title: A gardener's guide to 5 orchids that mimic animals, insects and even a naked man
full_text_raw:
Like most gardeners, I occasionally stumble upon fruits and flowers that resemble something else. But a naked man was not on my botanical bingo card.

Sure, tomatoes can be mischievous, taking on the shape of horned animals, Russian dolls, large-nosed characters and even unmentionables when exposed to extreme temperatures and vivid imaginations. But I thought orchids were more polite.

As it turns out, they aren't. You don't have to squint very hard to see the uncanny resemblance that some of them bear to animals, insects and even people. These are the five that impress and amuse me the most.

Let's get back to that naked man orchid

Meet Orchis italica, aka the naked man orchid, who smiles broadly as he hangs off the plant with his legs splayed and arms extended as if requesting a hug. Let's just say his decision to forgo pants is obvious.

Sometimes called "Italian orchid," naked man hails from the sunny Mediterranean region, which also may explain his decision to wear what resembles a hat. He thrives in partial shade and infertile soil, where the plant grows up to 20 inches tall before flowers make their midspring appearance.

Other orchid varieties resemble babies, doves, bees and monkeys

Swaddled baby (Anguloa uniflora) is a 2-foot tulip orchid that grows only in the Andes region of South America, where high humidity is essential for its survival. The flower's pale-pink-to-white petal formation resembles a newborn baby lovingly wrapped in a blanket.

Dove orchid (Peristeria elata) looks remarkably like its namesake, with blossoms that resemble the bird's head, beak, body, tail and purple-speckled wings.

The national flower of Panama, where the plant is called flor del Espíritu Santo (flower of the Holy Spirit), it has upright stems that can grow up to 3 feet long, each bearing a succession of as many as 20 blooms that open from late summer through early fall.

The dove orchid thrives in warm conditions and requires ample air circulation and consistently moist roots.

Bumble bee orchid (Ophrys bombyliflora) is probably the most cunning on this list, as its scent and flower bear an uncanny resemblance to a female solitary bee. The Mediterranean beauty's mimicry tricks mate-seeking male bees into landing on it, only to have their hopes dashed. They may leave disappointed, but not before inadvertently pollinating the flower and other nearby orchids, contributing to the propagation of the species.

Monkey orchid (Dracula chimaera) is native to the high-altitude, humid forests of the Andes mountains. The plant likes it cool, moist and at least partially shady. Growing just 6 to 12 inches tall and wide, its 2-inch-wide flowers each bear a striking resemblance to an adorable monkey's face.

Unlike malformed tomatoes, these orchids' appearances are exactly what nature intended. Although you may be able to find them for sale at specialty nurseries or in plant catalogs, growing them at home would require replicating their respective native climates, such as in a greenhouse or by providing humidifiers or other accommodations.

If that's not possible, you can simply delight in them from where you're sitting, just as I do.

title: Man of his word: Pope Leo speeches declared human-authored by Australian AI detection tool
full_text_raw:
Maps of Hope has been certified by Proudly Human, a company led by former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel

A collection of speeches and writings by Pope Leo XIV has been certified as human-authored less than two months after Leo declared artificial intelligence the greatest threat to humanity.

Proudly Human, the Australian company spearheaded by Australia's former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel, undertook a review of a collection of writings and speeches by the Pope, in collaboration with the publisher, the Australian Catholic University and cardinals in the Vatican.

Maps of Hope was published in the same week in May that Leo's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, warned of the dangers of artificial intelligence and the risks of the power of the technology being concentrated in the hands of a few.

In the encyclical, Leo said AI should be prevented "from dominating humanity," adding that the technology should be "human-friendly", accessible to all and opened to discussion and debate.

Finkel told Guardian Australia he had a "great deal of confidence" going into the Maps of Hope process that Leo's speeches would be written by a human, and within a day, Proudly Human had certified the collection as human-created.

The process typically requires authors or their representatives to sign up to the site, go through an ID check, and sign a declaration that they are operating within minimum standards: AI can't be used to write the first draft, or write sentences and paragraphs.

From there, Proudly Human uses AI detection tools that Finkel said "focus on different nuances" in writing and grammar.

"We use a suite of four or five of them and our own averaging algorithm, and we test that suite every night to make sure that they're really continuously fit for purpose," he said. "In this case, the book came through, as you would expect, is basically purely human."

The terms and conditions for the service outline that certifications are made "on the basis of information" provided and the checks performed, and the certifications can be refused or revoked if found to misrepresent authorship or "fall outside our published standards".

Finkel's hope is that in lieu of government regulation forcing people to disclose when something is created by AI, people can have information available through the trust mark that what they're reading was written by a human.

"They deserve to know. I actually think it's a fundamental right [for] human beings have," he said - particularly when it came to religious figures.

"If you're sitting in a church and you're expecting that that is the genuine expertise, religious wisdom, of the priest who's delivering the sermon," he said.

"The heart of what it is to be human is to engage with other people and to exchange ideas and exchange creative ideas."

The president and vice-chancellor of the Australian Catholic University, Prof Zlato Skrbis, said in a statement that given there was so much being generated so quickly, it was valuable to "say with confidence that a work is a product of human reflection and judgment".

title: Google wants to release 32 million sterile mosquitoes. Our Australian tests offer a valuable lesson | Nigel Beebe for the Conversation
full_text_raw:
Google's 'Debug' project in California and Florida aims to reduce mosquito numbers by releasing millions of sterilised males

In the United States, Google's (now Alphabet) Debug initiative has asked the federal government for permission to release up to 32 million sterilised male mosquitoes in California and Florida.

Male mosquitoes don't bite or carry disease. The hope is these millions of male mosquitoes will mate with disease-carrying females, the eggs won't hatch and mosquito numbers will fall.

Unsurprisingly, the US public has questions about the plan, including whether the release is safe and will work at scale, and what happens afterwards. Google/Alphabet's plan is to release more than 16 million mozzies each year, for two years.

More than a decade ago, I led a project with Google's life sciences division, (now known as Verily), to test a novel mosquito-control strategy in far north Queensland.

The results showed releasing specially bred male mosquitoes can dramatically suppress populations of the exotic, invasive mosquito species Aedes aegypti. This species is responsible for spreading deadly diseases such as dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever. Given the US is seriously considering this approach, our Australian experience offers important lessons.

Using mosquitoes against themselves

This story begins in 2015, when we travelled to Silicon Valley to meet Verily scientists interested in developing a mosquito suppression technology. Their goals aligned closely with our own research, supported by an Australian National Health and Medical Research Council grant, to develop environmentally friendly tools for suppressing invasive mosquitoes.

The strategy focuses on male mosquitoes because they don't bite, and female Aedes aegypti, which generally only mate once during their lifetime. If that mating event was incompatible - meaning the embryos don't develop - it could not produce viable offspring. Our challenge was to make mating ineffective.

The approach we ultimately tested relied on wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacterium found in many insects. Some wolbachia strains create a form of reproductive incompatibility, as described above.

The theory is simple: release enough wolbachia-carrying males into a population and, over time, the population declines. The released males are also beautifully evolved to search and find the last females - their large bushy antennae are super-radars for this job.

North Queensland the perfect laboratory

The Cassowary Coast in north Queensland provided ideal conditions for a large-scale trial of this approach. The region contained towns with abundant Aedes aegypti populations, while surrounding agricultural areas limited movement between communities. Equally important was the support of residents, local government and First Nations leaders.

Aedes aegypti likely arrived in Queensland in the late 1800s. It is distinct from our native mosquitoes because it is highly domesticated and feeds mainly on humans.

Before a single mosquito was released, the project team spent two years conducting field surveys and engaging with communities. We met with households, community organisations, First Nations leaders and local councils to discuss the technology and answer questions. The project, known as "Debug Innisfail", ultimately received regulatory approval from multiple authorities.

Releasing three million male mosquitoes

Field surveys began in 2015, involving a collaborative team spanning Australian and US institutions. During a 20-week release period in 2018, around three million wolbachia-carrying male mosquitoes were released into three treatment towns. Meanwhile, control towns where no mosquitoes were released were monitored.

The release system itself reflected Verily's engineering strengths. The company developed bespoke technologies, including machine-learning-based systems capable of separating male and female mosquitoes, crucial to ensuring only males were released.

The results were striking: when compared with control towns, mosquito populations in towns where mosquitoes were released began declining within four weeks. The findings, published in 2021, demonstrated incompatible male mosquito releases could achieve strong suppression.

In two treatment towns, suppression effects persisted into the following year. In one town, monitoring detected only a handful of Aedes aegypti 12 months later, corresponding to roughly 95% suppression.

What this means for the US

The Australian trials provide evidence-based answers to many of the concerns now being raised in the US.

First, ecological impacts are likely to be very small. Aedes aegypti is an invasive species in Australia and many other countries. Because it exclusively lives around humans and bites them, removing it from urban environments has minimal ecological consequences.

Second, the approach can work at scale. Although adult mosquitoes survive for only a few days, continuous releases of highly competitive males can substantially reduce populations across entire towns.

Third, benefits may persist after releases finish. This is because the suppression outcome does not necessarily disappear straight away, and can carry over into subsequent seasons. But that doesn't mean mosquito biology can be ignored - success depends on factors such as local ecology, mosquito movement patterns and community participation. The technology alone is not enough.

A model for future mosquito control

Perhaps the most important lesson from the trials is the value of collaboration. This project brought together researchers from six universities and Verily. Combining scientific expertise with industrial-scale engineering accelerated the journey from laboratory concept to real-world field trial in an incredibly short time.

We are still working towards biological and mechanical approaches to efficiently separating male mosquitoes, which would have better utility in developing countries.

As Aedes aegypti expands its range and insecticides fail to suppress it, using the mosquito against itself as the biological control tool will become increasingly important.

The Queensland trials helped lay the groundwork for programs now under way in the US. And they are a reminder that when science, technology and communities work together, it is possible to solve problems that matter.

title: Milky Way flipped in collision with dwarf galaxy 10bn years ago, astronomers say
full_text_raw:
Durham University researchers find cataclysmic direct hit with Gaia Sausage sent Milky Way into its current position

Astronomers have found evidence that the Milky Way was flipped on its side following a direct hit from a wayward galaxy long before the solar system was born.

The cataclysmic collision took place about 10bn years ago when the Milky Way was struck head-on by an incoming dwarf galaxy known - for purely astronomical reasons - as the Gaia Sausage.

The Milky Way tore the interloper to shreds and absorbed its stars, but the chaos unleashed in the event probably flipped the entire disc of the Milky Way by more than 90 degrees into the position seen today, researchers said.

Astronomers at Durham University used supercomputer simulations to show that Milky Way-like galaxies involved in head-on collisions with the Gaia Sausage were likely to experience a "disc flip" that dramatically, if slowly, reoriented the galaxy. "It probably takes at least a few hundred million years," said Kirill Batrakov, the lead researcher on the project.

The researchers made the discovery while investigating the curiously slow rotation of stars in the Milky Way's halo. The halo is the sparse, roughly ball-shaped cloud of stars that surrounds the galaxy. Most of the halo's stars originally formed in smaller galaxies that strayed too close to the Milky Way and merged over time.

Previous observations from the European Space Agency's Gaia mission show that stars in the Milky Way's disc orbit the heart of the galaxy at about 220km (137 miles) a second. But a longstanding mystery has surrounded those in the stellar halo, which rotate far more slowly, circling the galactic centre at about 25km a second.

In search of an explanation for the disparity, the Durham team turned to computer simulations of evolving Milky Way-like galaxies. title: The Dink review - pickleball comedy serves up engagingly silly laughs
full_text_raw:
Jake Johnson is delusional ex-tennis player The Hammer, who has to switch to the sport he loathes after injury

There's some funny stuff here in this engagingly silly sports comedy from producer-star Jake Johnson about the world of pickleball, and how this (allegedly) facile pseudo-tennis game for children and old people threatens to infantilise and dumb down the world of tennis itself.

Dusty (Johnson) is a middle-aged loser, delusionally nicknamed The Hammer, who once showed early promise at tennis before getting crushed by a humiliating teen encounter with the young Andy Roddick (playing himself in cameo). These days Dusty coaches at the tennis club owned by his dad (Ed Harris), who is scowlingly contemptuous of everything Dusty says and does. Only one thing allows poor Dusty to reclaim his self-respect as a man and a tennis player: his utter loathing for pickleball, whose followers are grudgingly permitted one of their toytown mini-courts at the club - and he duly gets a meet-cute quarrel with pickleball enthusiast Candace (Mary Steenburgen).

But Dusty's doctor (Ben Stiller) recommends pickleball as the best way to recover from a wrist injury, itself the pretext for a mountain of "jerking off" gags, and he discovers that he kind of likes the noble art, with its slower, more thoughtful pace and its prominent role for the humble "dink" drop shot. And he more than likes Candace as well ... although the film flinches from the reality of an age-gap relationship.

Inevitably for any comedy about tennis, John McEnroe has a funny walk-on, playing himself and commentating with baffling intensity on the climactic on-court confrontation between Dusty and his nemesis Roddick. There is nice support from Australian comic Aaron Chen as Dusty's cringingly submissive beta-male wingman PJ, as well as from Patton Oswalt as the pickleball partisan Slip - although 30 Rock fans will consider the film has supplied a pretty meagre role for Chris Parnell, the great Dr Spaceman in Tina Fey's TV comedy classic.

title: Tick bites are on the rise in the US and UK. Here's how to protect yourself
full_text_raw:
Experts share tips to avoid the blood-sucking pests that can transmit Lyme disease and other illnesses on to humans

I won't go into gory detail about the tick I found latched behind my ear approximately 35 hours after a hike in early June. Suffice it to say, the parasite was well fed, and I was horrified.

I am far from alone in making such a disgusting discovery. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), emergency room visits for tick bites have been unusually high in the US this year. Thirty-one million Americans are bitten by ticks annually - and the number has been trending up for over a decade. In the UK, ticks appear to be rising in number and species variety.

"Tick populations are expanding geographically because we're changing the climate," explains Vett Lloyd, a professor of biology at Mount Allison University in New Brunswick who studies ticks and the pathogens they transmit.

Milder winters and warmer summers raise ticks' survival rates. Additionally, human expansion - especially "mowing down forests and living in suburbs on previously forested land" - has expanded tick habitat dramatically, explains Lloyd.

Experts say that suburbs mean more prime habitat for mice, who thrive eating our garbage and harbor dangerous pathogens in their blood, like Lyme disease. More mice support more ticks, who feast on rodents as well as booming deer populations, lizards, birds and other creatures. Ticks can transmit diseases they pick up to human hosts. US rates of Lyme disease were 69% higher in 2022 compared with the 2017-2019 annual average. In England, cases of Lyme rose over 20% between 2024 and 2025.

"The pathogens are expanding almost exclusively because of human changes in how we live in the environment," says Lloyd.

Here's what you need to know to protect yourself from ticks.

How do you check for ticks?

"Ticks have a relatively boring life," says Lloyd. They hang out in moist, dark and shaded areas like leaf litter. When hungry, they crawl up blades of grass, where they wait to brush on to anything tasty that walks past, she says.

If a tick reaches your body, it typically climbs upward, seeking a dark, damp area, like the backs of knees, navel, groin, armpits or behind the ears, says Lloyd. There, they bite, injecting an anesthetic that prevents you from feeling pain or itchiness as they dig in.

The best time to find a tick is before it bites. "It can't give you a disease if it hasn't started drinking your blood," says Lloyd. Showering immediately after spending time outdoors may wash a tick off before it has a chance to latch.

Perform a tick check after being outdoors. This can be done alone with a mirror, and by lightly running your hands all over your body. Unfed ticks will feel like bumps the size of a poppy seed or a sesame seed. A fed tick can swell to the size of a blueberry. If you're comfortable with it, another person can help with the search.

The longer a tick feeds, the more likely it is to spread disease. Removing a tick before it's been on you for 24 hours greatly reduces the risk of disease transmission, per the CDC.

What should you do if you've been bitten by a tick?

"You want to try to get the whole tick out," says Dr Charlotte Mao, a pediatric infectious disease physician who works with the Bay Area Lyme Foundation. Mao recommends using "fine tip tweezers with firm gentle pressure" to grasp the tick at its head and pull it up. "You want to try to not have the mouth parts break off and stay stuck in the skin."

Wash the bite site and your hands thoroughly with soap and water or rubbing alcohol, she says.

Trying to remove it is better than leaving it in, even if you don't get the tick out perfectly. "While the tick is on you, it can be transmitting pathogens," notes Lloyd. "The mouth parts are organic; they will eventually dissolve, and the part of the tick that contains the pathogens is all in [its] body," she says. If you accidentally "pop" the tick, wash your hands well and disinfect the bite site, as these fluids can spread disease.

Both Mao and Lloyd suggest saving the tick in a Ziploc bag in your freezer, noting the date and geographic location it was found, if possible.

"It's not your ideal souvenir," says Lloyd, but if you begin to exhibit flu-like symptoms, facial drooping, severe headaches or any other worrisome new health issues in the month after your bite, you can get it tested. The Bay Area Lyme Foundation's website offers a list of laboratories that perform tick testing, some by mail. In the UK, you can mail your tick to the government's Tick Surveillance Scheme to help researchers map tick habitat, or to international tick test labs.

Consult your primary care provider after a bite, Mao says. They may give you an antibiotic prophylaxis - typically a single dose of doxycycline - to protect against Lyme, as well as other diseases commonly caused by ticks, like anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever. However, there are some tick-borne illnesses that cannot be treated with antibiotics, says Lloyd. These include alpha-gal, an allergy to red meat and other animal products, and babesiosis, a parasitic infection that causes flu-like symptoms and jaundice. If you notice any strange symptoms in the weeks after your tick bite, talk to a doctor right away.

If you identify an expanding solid red or bullseye-shaped rash near the site of your bite, this may be a sign of early Lyme disease. Your doctor may give you a longer course of antibiotics: one to two weeks, depending on the advice of your regional health authority.

Is there any way to prevent getting bitten by a tick?

To reduce your risk of tick bites, the CDC recommends wearing Environmental Protection Agency-approved insect repellants such as Deet or picaridin, long-sleeved shirts, long pants and closed shoes, and tumble-drying clothing on high after returning home to kill any lingering ticks. Stick to the open middle of trails while hiking rather than getting too close to brush or leaf litter.

Ticks aren't only a threat to hikers and hunters; depending on where you live, you can be bitten by a tick in your own back yard, notes Erika Machtinger, a medical and veterinary entomologist.

Machtinger recommends a few strategies for making your outdoor space safer.

Cutting back vegetation to prevent big shady areas and mowing your lawn frequently to reduce grassy habitat are the simplest interventions, she says. Stone walls are attractive to rodents, and have been shown to harbor high concentrations of ticks, says Machtinger. Seal up any nooks or replace them altogether.

"The single best way to manage ticks is with an acaricide," a tick-killing pesticide, Machtinger says.

Some homeowners are wary of the effect of acaricide on pollinators and other beneficial insects. A gentler, more targeted option is tick tubes: cardboard rolls stuffed with permethrin-treated cotton that mice discover and transport back to pad their nests, which basically treats them against ticks, Machtinger says.

Pet owners are at higher risk for tick bites, Machtinger says, because "they spend a lot of time with their pets outdoors". Pets can also transport ticks on their bodies. While Machtinger says cats are pretty good at grooming ticks off their bodies, she recommends checking dogs for ticks and combing their fur out before they come indoors.

title: India's Cockroach movement protesters show no sign of backing down
full_text_raw:
Thousands of people again on the streets of Delhi calling for education reforms despite police violence on Monday

Taru had come to the protest prepared this time. In one hand was an anti-government poster and in the other was a bicycle helmet. "We need to have protection in case Delhi police beat us up again," said the 25-year-old, who stood among her friends. "We are not scared of them and we won't run away, no matter what they do. We'll stay here till they listen."

On Tuesday, central Delhi still thronged with thousands of protesters, as an unprecedented expression of dissent against the powerful ruling Narendra Modi government showed no sign of abating.

Just 24 hours earlier, more than 50,000 people took to the streets in protest, swathes of them in their late teens and early 20s, mobilised by a new youth-led political movement that calls itself the Cockroach Janata party (CJP). Their rallying call was the resignation of the education minister and for reform of a corrupt and broken education system.

But what began peacefully on Monday - people fanning each other in the gruelling humidity, sharing snacks and chanting slogans - turned into scenes of brutality by the afternoon. Delhi police denied the protesters the right to march on parliament and kettled the expanding crowd into a restricted area. The internet was shut down and barricades were erected across the capital. The came the police batons and the teargas.

Police said they were responding to agitation but organisers and witnesses claimed the police carried out unprovoked attacks, including against women and children in the crowd. About 60 suffered injuries and at least one protester is on a ventilator in hospital intensive care.

"The day was so wholesome to start with, there was so much love," said Taru. "But after 3pm the police started attacking us. They were bashing us like anything. I saw them come up and hit people on the head as they were sitting down on the pavement doing nothing. And then as we were running, they opened up teargas on us."

Taru described the response by Delhi police - which are under central government control - as a "big mistake. Now we are more agitated than ever."

On Tuesday, the heavy hand of the Delhi police did little to keep supporters away from the historical site of Jantar Mantar in Delhi, which has become the focal point of the CJP protests over the past month. The crowds were thick and lively as they shouted slogans against the Modi government with abandon, calling for both the education minister and the prime minister to resign.

Some had travelled hundreds of miles to be there and said they intended to camp out until the government responded to the demands of the country's millions of young people. "The government needs to understand: we are not going anywhere," said Ranjit Verma, 23.

India's main opposition Congress party had also seized upon the mood, calling for Modi to resign "for destroying the future of India's youth" as it held its own protest in Delhi on Tuesday.

While the CJP movement has primarily focused on accountability for devastating leaks of exam papers and calling for the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, the overriding feeling in the aftermath of Monday's protest was that this was now so much bigger than one issue. For some, this was the moment India's youth - totalling more than 600 million - had found its political voice.

"The solidarity on the streets yesterday filled my heart," said Kuhoo Kaushik, 26, a content creator from Delhi. "How the government responded was really sad, police beating up 14-year-olds is horrible. But personally, I feel like it's really awoken something in me.

"That's why I've come back today: we won't be moved until the government listens to us. It's become about so much more than education - but one step at a time"'

Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke vowed that the protests would continue, though did not state what the next steps for the movement would be to capitalise on their momentum.

Standing by the stage at the protest site, Ratna Singh, a CJP spokesperson, said the movement was very aware of ways in which the Modi government had successfully cracked down on previous movements and figures of dissent during its 12 years in power.

"Anyone who has tried to speak up against this government has faced terrorism charges or tax raids or jail and there is so much fear," she said. "But I am very proud at how many people have showed up and come out on the streets. The police showed us no mercy - but no matter what barbaric treatment they give us, we will not be silenced."

While a senior government minister met two CJP spokespeople on Monday to discuss their demands, Singh said the government had not responded to them on Tuesday and the "prime minister has remained silent about what happened".

It was not only young people who returned to the protest site on Tuesday. Shobha Varma, 80, was attending with her granddaughter. "Our education system has been failing young people for years," she said. "But when I look out at everyone here, I really feel hope."

Regrettably, some will hunt and catch prey.

The best cat toys help any cat - indoor or outdoor - live out these behaviours safely, humanely, and often with their owner's involvement. Having a few within paw's reach is valuable to a pet cat's fitness, mood and fundamental felinity.

In my view, the best cat toys are interactive ones that come to life in a human's hand. It could be a teaser toy, a ball or a bravely proffered scatter toy - what matters is that you and your cat are playing together and growing closer as a result.

Of course, few among us lead lives of constant play, so you may also choose to get some toys that your cat can play with independently through the day. Laser toys with timers, electronic moving prey toys, or puzzle toys with moving parts can all add stimulation to a pet cat's alone time. When budgeting for cat toys, bear in mind that they tend to be shorter-term or repeat purchases, especially as cats tend to get bored of or enjoy destroying their favourite toys.

At a glance

* Best cat toy overall: Nature's Goodies colourful long raffia tail teaser sticks

* Best budget cat toy: Pets at Home scrunchie ball

* Best scented cat toy: Zebedee's valerian mouse

* Best electronic cat toy: PetSafe Peek-A-Bird

* Best catnip cat toy: Honeysuckle Cat Toys honeysuckle and catnip pouch

Why you should trust me

As a lifelong cat lover, I've spent untold hours playing with cats. These include my childhood pet, Jack; my current feline family member, Martha; and more than a dozen rescue cats I've fostered for Cat Action Trust 1977: a volunteer-run charity that provides help to feral and stray cats. There's nothing quite like watching a sweet kitty claw, kick or bite a toy into oblivion.

I'm also a journalist, and one of my most enjoyable gigs is reviewing products for the Filter. I treated the task of testing cat toys just as seriously as I took reviewing electric heaters - which are also adored by heat-loving cats.

How I tested

Spurning the temptation to dress up as a cat and test the toys in solitude, I engaged a panel of feline testers to play with each one. Most of the cats have a connection to Cat Action Trust 1977: a large group of kittens who were in the care of hand-rearing expert Dianne, and an adult cat named Hovis, who lives under the loving long-term care of fosterer Vanda. I also tested some of the toys with my own cat, Martha, because I didn't want her to feel left out.

Where possible, I tested each type of toy with multiple cats to accommodate differences in taste. As well as observing how the cats played with the toys, I considered the human's experience - especially how the toys encouraged interaction between pet and owner. After testing, the toys were left at the mercy of their new owners.

All of the kittens and cats who lent a claw with this article are now homed, but Cat Action Trust 1977 often has large numbers of foster cats in need of adoption.

The best cat toys in 2026

The best of the rest

What you need to know

What to do if a cat gets bored with a toy

As many cat owners know, cats will tend to become uninterested in a toy over time - sometimes within minutes. A University of Southampton study led by John Bradshaw, the author of Cat Sense, found that this disenchantment is typically with specific toys, rather than types of toys or play itself. So, it's worth replacing your cat's discarded old favourites with slightly different toys of the same types.

Of course, replacing cat toys frequently can become costly. Another option is using suitable household objects as toys, or making your own. In my experience, cats can have hours of fun with things like a ball of scrunched-up paper, the turned corner of a rug, or fronds of certain ornamental grasses (check the species is cat-safe before playtime).

With strongly scented toys, my fellow contributor Alan Martin has had some luck with putting them back in their bag in between plays to maintain the aromatic potency. A particularly pungent ferret toy was of far more interest to his cats after a spell back in its plastic pouch than when left out and about.

Why do cats play?

Felines have an instinct to play - or really, to hunt. If you have an indoor cat, playing with toys is their best opportunity to scratch, pummel, claw and kick that primal itch. Outdoor cats can also benefit from the variety and stimulation afforded by tantalising toys, and there's opportunity for all pet cats to grow closer to their human devotees through play.

Many of the best cat toys look, feel or move like mice, birds or other critters that scamper around on lower links of the food chain. Another interesting finding from John Bradshaw et al is that cats seem to retain interest in a toy for longer if it starts to fall apart during play - they value proof that the hunter is winning the fight with their prey.

All cats are individuals. Closely observing their behaviour may give you clues as to which play activities they'd enjoy - and therefore which toys you should buy. For instance, cats who bite loose threads or plant stems might appreciate a teaser with long strands for them to chase. Watch and play with your cat, and you'll get to know them.

title: A gardener's guide to 5 orchids that mimic animals, insects and even a naked man
full_text_raw:
Like most gardeners, I occasionally stumble upon fruits and flowers that resemble something else. But a naked man was not on my botanical bingo card.

Sure, tomatoes can be mischievous, taking on the shape of horned animals, Russian dolls, large-nosed characters and even unmentionables when exposed to extreme temperatures and vivid imaginations. But I thought orchids were more polite.

As it turns out, they aren't. You don't have to squint very hard to see the uncanny resemblance that some of them bear to animals, insects and even people. These are the five that impress and amuse me the most.

Let's get back to that naked man orchid

Meet Orchis italica, aka the naked man orchid, who smiles broadly as he hangs off the plant with his legs splayed and arms extended as if requesting a hug. Let's just say his decision to forgo pants is obvious.

Sometimes called "Italian orchid," naked man hails from the sunny Mediterranean region, which also may explain his decision to wear what resembles a hat. He thrives in partial shade and infertile soil, where the plant grows up to 20 inches tall before flowers make their midspring appearance.

Other orchid varieties resemble babies, doves, bees and monkeys

Swaddled baby (Anguloa uniflora) is a 2-foot tulip orchid that grows only in the Andes region of South America, where high humidity is essential for its survival. The flower's pale-pink-to-white petal formation resembles a newborn baby lovingly wrapped in a blanket.

Dove orchid (Peristeria elata) looks remarkably like its namesake, with blossoms that resemble the bird's head, beak, body, tail and purple-speckled wings.

The national flower of Panama, where the plant is called flor del Espíritu Santo (flower of the Holy Spirit), it has upright stems that can grow up to 3 feet long, each bearing a succession of as many as 20 blooms that open from late summer through early fall.

The dove orchid thrives in warm conditions and requires ample air circulation and consistently moist roots.

Bumble bee orchid (Ophrys bombyliflora) is probably the most cunning on this list, as its scent and flower bear an uncanny resemblance to a female solitary bee. The Mediterranean beauty's mimicry tricks mate-seeking male bees into landing on it, only to have their hopes dashed. They may leave disappointed, but not before inadvertently pollinating the flower and other nearby orchids, contributing to the propagation of the species.

Monkey orchid (Dracula chimaera) is native to the high-altitude, humid forests of the Andes mountains. The plant likes it cool, moist and at least partially shady. Growing just 6 to 12 inches tall and wide, its 2-inch-wide flowers each bear a striking resemblance to an adorable monkey's face.

Unlike malformed tomatoes, these orchids' appearances are exactly what nature intended. Although you may be able to find them for sale at specialty nurseries or in plant catalogs, growing them at home would require replicating their respective native climates, such as in a greenhouse or by providing humidifiers or other accommodations.

If that's not possible, you can simply delight in them from where you're sitting, just as I do.

title: Man of his word: Pope Leo speeches declared human-authored by Australian AI detection tool
full_text_raw:
Maps of Hope has been certified by Proudly Human, a company led by former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel

A collection of speeches and writings by Pope Leo XIV has been certified as human-authored less than two months after Leo declared artificial intelligence the greatest threat to humanity.

Proudly Human, the Australian company spearheaded by Australia's former chief scientist, Dr Alan Finkel, undertook a review of a collection of writings and speeches by the Pope, in collaboration with the publisher, the Australian Catholic University and cardinals in the Vatican.

Maps of Hope was published in the same week in May that Leo's first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, warned of the dangers of artificial intelligence and the risks of the power of the technology being concentrated in the hands of a few.

In the encyclical, Leo said AI should be prevented "from dominating humanity," adding that the technology should be "human-friendly", accessible to all and opened to discussion and debate.

Finkel told Guardian Australia he had a "great deal of confidence" going into the Maps of Hope process that Leo's speeches would be written by a human, and within a day, Proudly Human had certified the collection as human-created.

The process typically requires authors or their representatives to sign up to the site, go through an ID check, and sign a declaration that they are operating within minimum standards: AI can't be used to write the first draft, or write sentences and paragraphs.

From there, Proudly Human uses AI detection tools that Finkel said "focus on different nuances" in writing and grammar.

"We use a suite of four or five of them and our own averaging algorithm, and we test that suite every night to make sure that they're really continuously fit for purpose," he said. "In this case, the book came through, as you would expect, is basically purely human."

The terms and conditions for the service outline that certifications are made "on the basis of information" provided and the checks performed, and the certifications can be refused or revoked if found to misrepresent authorship or "fall outside our published standards".

Finkel's hope is that in lieu of government regulation forcing people to disclose when something is created by AI, people can have information available through the trust mark that what they're reading was written by a human.

"They deserve to know. I actually think it's a fundamental right [for] human beings have," he said - particularly when it came to religious figures.

"If you're sitting in a church and you're expecting that that is the genuine expertise, religious wisdom, of the priest who's delivering the sermon," he said.

"The heart of what it is to be human is to engage with other people and to exchange ideas and exchange creative ideas."

The president and vice-chancellor of the Australian Catholic University, Prof Zlato Skrbis, said in a statement that given there was so much being generated so quickly, it was valuable to "say with confidence that a work is a product of human reflection and judgment".

title: Google wants to release 32 million sterile mosquitoes. Our Australian tests offer a valuable lesson | Nigel Beebe for the Conversation
full_text_raw:
Google's 'Debug' project in California and Florida aims to reduce mosquito numbers by releasing millions of sterilised males

In the United States, Google's (now Alphabet) Debug initiative has asked the federal government for permission to release up to 32 million sterilised male mosquitoes in California and Florida.

Male mosquitoes don't bite or carry disease. The hope is these millions of male mosquitoes will mate with disease-carrying females, the eggs won't hatch and mosquito numbers will fall.

Unsurprisingly, the US public has questions about the plan, including whether the release is safe and will work at scale, and what happens afterwards. Google/Alphabet's plan is to release more than 16 million mozzies each year, for two years.

More than a decade ago, I led a project with Google's life sciences division, (now known as Verily), to test a novel mosquito-control strategy in far north Queensland.

The results showed releasing specially bred male mosquitoes can dramatically suppress populations of the exotic, invasive mosquito species Aedes aegypti. This species is responsible for spreading deadly diseases such as dengue, Zika, chikungunya and yellow fever. Given the US is seriously considering this approach, our Australian experience offers important lessons.

Using mosquitoes against themselves

This story begins in 2015, when we travelled to Silicon Valley to meet Verily scientists interested in developing a mosquito suppression technology. Their goals aligned closely with our own research, supported by an Australian National Health and Medical Research Council grant, to develop environmentally friendly tools for suppressing invasive mosquitoes.

The strategy focuses on male mosquitoes because they don't bite, and female Aedes aegypti, which generally only mate once during their lifetime. If that mating event was incompatible - meaning the embryos don't develop - it could not produce viable offspring. Our challenge was to make mating ineffective.

The approach we ultimately tested relied on wolbachia, a naturally occurring bacterium found in many insects. Some wolbachia strains create a form of reproductive incompatibility, as described above.

The theory is simple: release enough wolbachia-carrying males into a population and, over time, the population declines. The released males are also beautifully evolved to search and find the last females - their large bushy antennae are super-radars for this job.

North Queensland the perfect laboratory

The Cassowary Coast in north Queensland provided ideal conditions for a large-scale trial of this approach. The region contained towns with abundant Aedes aegypti populations, while surrounding agricultural areas limited movement between communities. Equally important was the support of residents, local government and First Nations leaders.

Aedes aegypti likely arrived in Queensland in the late 1800s. It is distinct from our native mosquitoes because it is highly domesticated and feeds mainly on humans.

Before a single mosquito was released, the project team spent two years conducting field surveys and engaging with communities. We met with households, community organisations, First Nations leaders and local councils to discuss the technology and answer questions. The project, known as "Debug Innisfail", ultimately received regulatory approval from multiple authorities.

Releasing three million male mosquitoes

Field surveys began in 2015, involving a collaborative team spanning Australian and US institutions. During a 20-week release period in 2018, around three million wolbachia-carrying male mosquitoes were released into three treatment towns. Meanwhile, control towns where no mosquitoes were released were monitored.

The release system itself reflected Verily's engineering strengths. The company developed bespoke technologies, including machine-learning-based systems capable of separating male and female mosquitoes, crucial to ensuring only males were released.

The results were striking: when compared with control towns, mosquito populations in towns where mosquitoes were released began declining within four weeks. The findings, published in 2021, demonstrated incompatible male mosquito releases could achieve strong suppression.

In two treatment towns, suppression effects persisted into the following year. In one town, monitoring detected only a handful of Aedes aegypti 12 months later, corresponding to roughly 95% suppression.

What this means for the US

The Australian trials provide evidence-based answers to many of the concerns now being raised in the US.

First, ecological impacts are likely to be very small. Aedes aegypti is an invasive species in Australia and many other countries. Because it exclusively lives around humans and bites them, removing it from urban environments has minimal ecological consequences.

Second, the approach can work at scale. Although adult mosquitoes survive for only a few days, continuous releases of highly competitive males can substantially reduce populations across entire towns.

Third, benefits may persist after releases finish. This is because the suppression outcome does not necessarily disappear straight away, and can carry over into subsequent seasons. But that doesn't mean mosquito biology can be ignored - success depends on factors such as local ecology, mosquito movement patterns and community participation. The technology alone is not enough.

A model for future mosquito control

Perhaps the most important lesson from the trials is the value of collaboration. This project brought together researchers from six universities and Verily. Combining scientific expertise with industrial-scale engineering accelerated the journey from laboratory concept to real-world field trial in an incredibly short time.

We are still working towards biological and mechanical approaches to efficiently separating male mosquitoes, which would have better utility in developing countries.

As Aedes aegypti expands its range and insecticides fail to suppress it, using the mosquito against itself as the biological control tool will become increasingly important.

The Queensland trials helped lay the groundwork for programs now under way in the US. And they are a reminder that when science, technology and communities work together, it is possible to solve problems that matter.
