title: This optical illusion is rarer than a rainbow and tricky to see in Australia. So what actually is a fogbow?
full_text_raw:
Visible when the sun is behind you and the fog is ahead, conditions have to be 'right in the Goldilocks spot' to see a fogbow

When Marie Johnson woke up one foggy morning, she just had a feeling it would be eye-catching.

"It was first thing in the morning, when I was heading into town to work. I just thought I'll quickly call in, get a photo of the fog with the old house," says Johnson, who lives on a historic farm in Cobar, in outback New South Wales.

But then she turned around and saw the ethereal archway. "Oh my God, look at that. What is this? It's like a rainbow, but it's white," she says.

The optical illusion, known as a fogbow, is rarer than a rainbow.

Ilana Cherny, a senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, says the conditions have to be just right to see one. "It really depends on you and the sun and the fog all being lined up in exactly the right way."

title: The children who loved a killer
full_text_raw:
The Carr family took in Steven Judy, hoping to 'save' a troubled teen. They didn't know he would become one of the most hated men in America

Childhood returns to Traci Carr in fragments.

Night-time. She is five. She wakes to shadows on the wall, her room strange in the dark. Her footie pyjamas slip against the wood as she pads downstairs and climbs into bed next to her foster brother, Steven Judy.

He scoots over, and the monsters recede. She burrows under the covers, feeling safe.

Morning. Traci and Steve share Froot Loops, their favorite cereal, the milk turning pink. He teases her, tells funny stories, acts extra goofy to make her laugh.

Later, they play hide and seek. He's all theater, snapping a belt in the air as he searches for Traci and her three older siblings. They collapse in giggles when he finds them.

Then one day, Steve disappears.

No one explains where he went. Her parents are away for long stretches, too. When they are home, conversations drop into whispers. Doors click shut. The television is switched off when she enters the room.

The year Traci turns seven, her parents take her on a car ride. At Conkle funeral home just outside Indianapolis, the room smells of carnations and furniture polish.

She is led to the coffin at the end of the room. She peers over the edge.

It's Steve.

His eyes are closed, his face composed. His hair isn't right - a wig, she'll learn later. But otherwise, he looks like himself.

Her mother, Mary, leans close. Touch him, she urges.

I don't want to.

Her mother insists. Don't be afraid. Just touch him. Traci extends a single finger. It leaves a dent in his cold skin.

Three days earlier, on 9 March 1981, the state of Indiana had executed Steven Judy. Traci would not fully grasp this for years.

Decades on, she still carries the confusion of that day. It flickers across her face as we sit in her kitchen, a plastic storage bin between us filled with his belts, his wallet, his watch, letters, photographs: the small, stubborn evidence of a brother they once loved. A brother whose grave drew hate-filled handwritten notes decades after his death.

For decades, Judy's crimes have been revisited in books, documentaries and true-crime retellings. His atrocities have been replayed, his psychology dissected. But Traci and her siblings are missing from those narratives. The families of condemned people are among the least visible casualties of capital punishment, even as the death penalty is on the rise again.

The Carr children loved and lost a foster brother the rest of the world called a monster. No one asked what it was like to be them. For decades, they were not ready to say.

I was there the day Judy died.

I was a young Associated Press journalist assigned to cover the family's side of the story and had arrived in Michigan City on Sunday, the day before the execution.

As reporters and photographers gathered outside the prison, I sat in a hotel room with the family. Over months of reporting, I had quietly slipped into their orbit. I wasn't a friend, exactly, but I had become a witness to their unraveling at a moment when most people looked away.

Eleven years earlier, a young man murdered my eighth-grade friend Cindy Winter in the Sonoran desert about a quarter of a mile from her home. We children had no language for this; neither did the grownups around us. After the first days of sorrow, we stopped speaking of Cindy altogether. Assigned to the Judy case, I did not yet understand that I was trying to report my way back into a story I already belonged to: violent death, bewildered survivors, and grief with nowhere to go.

That day, Traci had stayed home with a babysitter. In the afternoon, I went swimming with the other Carr children. We had lunch, and then dinner, though no one ate much.

Around 11pm, Judy's foster father, Bob Carr, left for the prison. He had reluctantly agreed to Judy's request that he witness the execution, which was scheduled shortly after midnight. By then, the kids were asleep, or appeared to be.

Mary thumbed through Polaroids of Judy that she had brought with her, sometimes glancing at the clock beside the bed. She smoked the way some people pray, steadily, wordlessly, through the waiting.

Shortly before 1am, Carr returned to our hotel with attorney Steve Harris. For Mary's benefit, he described Judy's final 71 minutes.

A shaved head. A cigarette. A phone call to a girlfriend who had sent him a last-minute telegram - Judy joked that if she proposed marriage, he might ask for a stay. A final Polaroid taken for the Carrs, never made public until now. A Valium to calm Judy's nerves before the end. Some tears, some jokes.

At 12.04am, the guards blindfolded Judy and led him a few paces to the chair in the next room. Harris and Carr moved to the witness room.

"I don't hold no grudges. This was my doing. I'm sorry it happened," Judy said from the chair before the switch was thrown.

Mary soaked in every detail, hanging on every word, sometimes asking Harris to repeat himself. The ashtray beside her filled with cigarette stubs.

Within the month, she admitted herself to a psychiatric hospital for a brief period, shattered by what had happened. I visited her there. Wearing a hospital gown, she seemed emptied of the force that had animated her for months - defending Judy, raging at the state, willing him somehow to survive. The fight had fled her body.

I spent months with the Carrs, but I shed no tears for Judy. I did not mistake him for an innocent man. Still, I could not believe justice had been served by strapping him into a chair and killing him. The state had not restored his victims to life; it had only widened the circle of suffering. Our world, as I saw it, had room for outrage, punishment and fascination, but little space for certain kinds of grief.

I did not yet know that this story would stay with me for the next 45 years.

The facts of the case are these: on the morning of 28 April 1979, around 6.30am, Judy, 22, raped and murdered Terry Lee Chasteen, 21, along the banks of White Lick Creek outside Indianapolis.

When her three children - ages two, four and five - cried, he threw them into the creek to drown.

It wasn't his first violent crime, but it was the one for which he would be executed.

The four bodies were discovered later that morning by mushroom hunters. Residents called it the worst crime Morgan county had ever seen.

A distinctive red and silver truck seen near the site of the killings was traced back to Bob Carr. He told police his foster son had borrowed it the night before. Judy was arrested the next day.

Public outrage hardened quickly. Even before all the evidence was presented, a grassroots group called Protect the Innocent demanded the death penalty.

At first, Judy said he couldn't remember what happened. Later, he confessed. Harris, the attorney, initially pursued an insanity defense, but two court-appointed psychiatrists concluded Judy was legally sane.

After the guilty verdict, Judy made his preference clear: death over life in prison. Determined to eliminate any possibility of leniency, he proposed leaping across the table to attack the prosecutor before sentencing.

"You can't do that," Harris told him. "There are 50 officers in that courtroom."

Instead, Judy asked to address the jury. He told them he knew their names, where they lived, where they worked, and would kill anyone who failed to vote for the electric chair. Then he turned toward the bench. "That goes for you too, bud," he said to the judge.

The jury deliberated 20 minutes before recommending the death penalty.

Forty-five years later, one of the people I most wanted to find was Harris. He had witnessed the crime's aftermath and Judy's final hours. I wondered what remained with him after all this time.

Before Judy, Harris had handled three other murder cases. After the execution, he vowed never to take another death penalty case. "It was time-consuming and emotional," he recalls now. "I just made the decision I would never do one again." He represented only one other murder defendant, then gradually left criminal law altogether.

He drove me to the bridge overlooking the stretch of White Lick Creek where the killings took place, about a mile and a half from his office. State Road 67 hums nearby now, busy and indifferent. Round the bend, the creek remains as secluded as it was then; teenagers still go there to hang out beyond the sight of their parents.

A rope swing dangles beneath a railroad bridge where someone has painted: "THE DEVIL WAS HERE." The water moves on.

Steve saved Randy Carr's life when Randy was two years old.

Randy was playing in a mud puddle in the alley behind their house when a family friend known as Stinky climbed into Bob Carr's truck and began backing it up, running over Randy's legs. Steve saw the scene unfold and began yelling and waving his arms.

"He stopped him," Randy says. "Another minute and Stinky would have run over my head."

After that, Steve became Randy's person. "The only one who paid me any attention," Randy recalls. Saturdays were their day. Together, they cleaned the basement, mowed the grass. When the chores were done, Steve took him for ice-cream. "Never failed," Randy remembers.

Steve entered the Carr family through a friendship with Randy's Uncle Tony. On the day of the Chasteen murders, Randy, who was nine, and his brother Bobby, who was 11, helped Steve clean out the garage. They drove trash to the dump. They swept out their father's pickup truck, the one Steve had been driving earlier that morning.

Then they went for ice-cream.

The next day, the police came. Steve was out with a friend, but they questioned the boys. They drove them back to the dump and asked where the trash had been thrown.

"I wasn't going to tell them," Randy says. "I pointed everywhere except where we dumped."

Back at home, Randy went to the window with a pair of binoculars and watched as officers dusted the truck for fingerprints. He watched them wait for Steve to come back. "I didn't grasp what was happening," he says. "Dad never told us anything."

After Steve's arrest, children at school avoided Randy. He began fighting. "I would get mad if anybody told me Steve was guilty of this. I couldn't see it in my mind. Steve couldn't do this."

Eventually, Steve told Randy himself.

"You've gotta let it go," Steve said. "I'm guilty of this. It's something I can't control."

He joked about the electric chair. "Man, I'm gonna ride that lightning."

Randy thought he meant an amusement park ride. "I still didn't understand," he says.

Years later, Randy came to believe Steve deserved to die. He says that plainly now. But then he adds, quietly, tearing up: "To this day, I hate that he did that. Because he was everything I had in life."

In the months before the execution, Randy started spiraling. He skipped school for the first time. He stole diet pills to get high. "I just felt like I needed to do something." When his mother told Steve during a prison visit that Randy was acting out, Steve wrote Randy a seven-page letter about his own childhood, about how he had started screwing up.

In a letter to Mary, Steve mentioned that he had written to Randy, and offered her some parenting advice: "Listen, Mary, I just wrote Randy that letter we talked about. It was hard, too. I don't know if it was exactly what you wanted but I think it will help if he listens. But you have to understand if you keep telling someone not to do this or that, it sometimes pushes them to do it anyway for spite."

Randy read the letter "a thousand times" when he was a kid. He never skipped school again. "I loved Steve to death. I defended him for a long time. I broke a lot of jaws of people who didn't really deserve it."

Randy begged Steve to appeal against the death penalty. "I cried with him for a long time. Finally Steve said: 'Look at me. Don't bring this up again. It's over with. Don't be sad, because this is what I need.'"

Randy visited Steve the afternoon before his execution. "I was so upset. But Steve was laughing and carrying on like nothing was happening. It just blows my mind how he knows he's going to his death, and he was just worried about how I was."

A few months after the funeral, Traci noticed the spine of a book jutting from a stack of papers on the kitchen countertop.

Burn Judy Burn.

Published between Judy's conviction and his execution, the book was written by Bette Nunn, managing editor of the Reporter-Times in Martinsville, Indiana.

Traci pulled it free and turned immediately to the photographs. One showed a small body just beneath the water's surface. Another showed a little boy lying on a metal table, his shirt half pulled up from his torso.

They were children, very small. She could tell they were close to her age.

"I was starting to piece it together," she told me. "I think I knew Steve had killed somebody. But I still didn't understand what had happened to him."

So she asked Randy. What happened to Steve? He told her what he could, as much as he understood.

She couldn't reconcile the brother she knew with the killer described in the book. Yet she kept returning to the photographs. "I had a morbid interest," she says. The more she grasped, the more terrified she became. The house itself seemed altered. When she returned from school and found no one there, she wouldn't go inside, pacing the sidewalk instead.

She didn't ask her parents any questions. She had already noticed the way her mother seemed always on the verge of tears, the way her parents argued in low, urgent voices. The whole house seemed stretched tight with things no one knew how to say aloud.

My editor at the Associated Press asked me to begin reporting on the case in early March 1980, 10 months after the murders of Terry Chasteen and her three children. Judy would become the first person executed in Indiana since 1961 and among the first handful nationally after the supreme court reinstated the death penalty in 1976.

I saw two possible ways into the story. I could try to reach Judy through his attorney, or I could try to understand the family waiting outside the prison walls.

I called Mary Carr. She invited me over immediately.

Mary worked as a drill operator at a manufacturing plant; Bob laid brick and stone for a living. Their house sat in a working-class neighborhood outside Indianapolis, small and crowded, every surface carrying its own accumulation of papers, toys, ashtrays, cups. Four children moved constantly through the rooms. Mary was not yet 31.

Bob was warm but reserved. Mary directed the energy of the house. Within minutes, she had seated me in a padded brown chair and placed a photo album in my lap. She pointed to photographs of Steven Judy.

"Look at him," she said. "He's handsome, isn't he? He's not cold and detached the way they say."

I felt myself recoil. I understood that I could never look at Judy the way Mary Carr did.

When I was in eighth grade, my friend Cindy Winter was murdered in Tucson while riding her bicycle to a close friend's house on a Sunday afternoon. Her body was found under a mesquite tree at the edge of a dry wash. The man who killed her was 24. He was arrested after he raped and killed another woman, leaving her two children alive beside the road.

The similarities between his case and Judy's were striking. Before Cindy's murder, we thought the desert between houses belonged to us. Afterward, the fear never fully left.

Meeting the Carrs conjured that dread back to life. After that first visit, I wrote in my journal: "Walking from my sturdy Scout to my apartment after midnight, the bushes seem to reach out as menacing men, and in the moonlight, I can see my fear."

I could never understand the killer. But I wanted to understand the family living in the aftermath of what he had done.

I began to spend time at the Carrs' kitchen table. I ate pizza with them, went swimming with the kids, phoned Mary to check in. Her warmth as a mother, I learned, was instinctive rather than structured. She wasn't the kind of parent who tracked homework or studied report cards. What she offered instead was openness, noise, food, a place to belong. She believed that when her family took Steve in, they were finally giving him something no one else had: a loving family, a permanent place at the table.

"She thought she could save him," Traci says. And that was exactly who Mary Carr was, a woman who believed in second chances, in the redemptive power of love and a full table. She had been raised by a mother who withdrew support, but Mary had chosen a different path: she made room. She fed people. She believed damage could be repaired if you loved hard enough and long enough.

This impulse would define the next eight years of her life, but Judy had arrived carrying damage the Carrs could not fully see.

In court records and later interviews, Judy described his childhood as violent and unstable. Both parents drank heavily. His father beat his mother and once, in a fit of fury, butchered a pet dog, leaving pieces scattered on the porch for the children to see. His mother brought men home; sometimes the children witnessed them having sex. She occasionally summoned Judy to kiss her while she was bathing or undressing, placing him on her lap and running her fingers through his hair. Pornographic magazines, he said, were kept openly in the house.

By age 10, he was pushing high school girls to the ground and molesting them. At 11, he began shoplifting; by 12, he was drinking. On 17 April 1970, at 13, he raped a 22-year-old woman and attacked her with a knife and a hatchet so severely that she required brain, abdominal and open-heart surgery to survive.

He was detained and transferred to the juvenile section of Indiana's Central State hospital. Opened in 1848 as the Indiana hospital for the "insane", central state closed in 1994 amid scandals over patient treatment and funding shortfalls. The old pathology building, where autopsies were once performed in search of the physical causes of madness, now houses the Indiana Medical History Museum. Brains sit in glass jars, labeled with names, dates, symptoms.

At Central State, Judy was diagnosed as a sexual psychopath. He became friends with Bob Carr's younger brother, Tony, who also was a resident after getting in trouble at school and home. Through him, he met the rest of the family.

When Judy was released at age 15, Mary and Bob agreed to take him in. As a juvenile, he needed to be released to adults; this must have felt like astonishing good fortune to him.

He lived with the Carrs, ate at their table, and worked construction for Bob. But the violence continued: more assaults, more jail time, a robbery.

The Carrs even paid his bond weeks before the Chasteen murders.

Throughout, "Mom always loved Steve," Traci recalls. "She never said anything bad about him, no matter what."

Prison life became a world of letters. Steve wrote and received hundreds of them.

Mary kept many of them in a bedroom drawer: letters from strangers who prayed for him, or from women who had never met him but said they loved him.

For Mary and Bob, he described his life in prison with flashes of humor and longing. Without his television set, he would "go bonkers", Steve wrote. "So far I've earned $15,000 on the Joker's Wild, gotten three dates on the Dating Game, and outdrawn Marshall Dillon twice."

"Tell the kids I said hi and I love them," he wrote time and again. Sometimes he mentioned them by name: "You tell Traci I said hi and that I love her too and that I've got a get-rich-quick scheme for us. I'm going to write the cereal company and tell them me and her are going to quit eating cereal and put them out of business unless they pay us a million dollars (50 cents anyway, ha ha)."

During prison visits, Steve offered Mary tips on staying safe and told her to pass them on to his foster sisters. Lock the car doors. Watch the blind spot. Don't pull over if a man waves you down.

After he was sentenced to death, Harris filed a routine appeal. But in October 1980, Judy told the court he did not want to pursue it, clearing the way for his execution six months later.

Steve wrote to his foster parents soon after. "I know you can't accept what I'm doing but I hope you don't hate me for it either," he told them. Mary had cried during a prison visit, and he had avoided telling her in front of the boys.

"I'm sorry you had to find it out like you did," he wrote. "I'm not going to get into my reasons and feelings on why I wanted it like this because I think it would be better to tell you here where we can look at each other's faces."

Steve was determined to carry through with the death penalty, but there were moments of fear. Right after he was transferred to death row in Michigan City, he wrote: "Mary, don't ever let anyone tell you this isn't bad, because it is, and I'm scared to death."

Later he wrote: "I'm worried about how the kids are taking it all. There's just so much on my mind that can't ever be put into words."

On 5 Febuary 1981, 32 days before the execution, he apologized for not writing. "I just let myself get so far down in the dumps that it was hard to do anything." He warned Mary that people might try to persuade her to intervene. "I know a few of them might try and get you to interfere but I hope you don't," he wrote. "About the only thing you could possibly do is cause a short delay and that would only hurt me." Then, as he often did, he turned back to the children: "Tell me, how are the kids doing? I really hope they're taking all this okay. Tell them I said hello and I send my love."

Steve considered Bob's mother, Rosita Mary Colvin, his foster grandmother. He affectionately called her "the old lady" and asked about her in letters. She wrote him shortly before his execution: "I have loved you from the first time I saw you at Central, your blond hair flying around, you and Tony playing basketball. You was a beautiful child. If you had been my own son, I could not have loved you more. I'm so sorry, Steve. I don't know what went wrong. I just want you to know you are loved by all of us and our lives will never be the same."

His last letter was written to his attorney. Judy told Harris that he had committed about 50 robberies and burglaries and 15 rapes. He confessed directly to one additional murder, indicated there was a second, and said he'd left women tied up so there might be others. He promised to list all his crimes in a letter to be opened after his death.

That last day, he gave Harris a thick sealed envelope.

Police knew this list of confessions was coming and they were waiting. Immediately after the execution, Harris opened the envelope.

In front of him was one page of writing followed by seven blank sheets.

When I visited Harris this year, he spread the letter on his desk so I could read it: "I'm sorry Steve [Harris] but I've decided to handle it this way because I care too much for my foster mom and family. I hope you can understand. Thank you for all you've done for me. Steve."

In his final photo, Judy stands next to Harris in the holding cell, minutes before the execution. His head is shaved. A cigarette rests between the fingers of his right hand. "I'm gonna give these things up," he quipped to Harris.

"It was kind of scary that he could be so dangerous and actually a likable person," Harris recalled. "He had a sense of humor."

Steve asked that he not be interred behind Indiana state prison, where prisoners whose families don't claim them are buried. The Carrs bought him a plot and headstone in Floral Park cemetery, less than a mile away from Central State hospital, where they first met him.

In the cemetery office, I asked for a map to help me locate the gravesite.

"Steven Judy," the clerk said slowly. Hate letters were regularly left on Steve's grave until about five years ago, he said. "Our groundskeepers removed them every morning. It became routine."

The story of death penalty cases is usually told through a narrow cast of characters: the victims, the condemned, sometimes the families of those murdered or the legal teams. Almost no one asks what happens to the families who loved the condemned, especially when they are children.

Scholars who study capital punishment have identified those families as a distinct and largely invisible group. Sociologist Susan Sharp began studying them in 1996. In her book Hidden Victims, she describes them as living in a kind of moral exile.

"They are tainted by association," Sharp told me. "We assume they must have done something wrong."

Sharp estimates that roughly 30% of death row prisoners have no family contact, either because of long estrangement or because relatives cut ties after the crime. For the other 70%, she said, the family's punishment can continue long after the condemned person is executed.

To outsiders, it can seem inexplicable that a family member can feel both horror for the victims and heartache for someone who has done monstrous harm. "We treat those family members as if they don't have a right to grieve. We take away their right to be human," Sharp says. "We fail to realize everyone is multifaceted. None of us is equal to the worst thing we've ever done."

Families who provide primary support to prisoners on death row, as the Carrs did, are likely to suffer from depression, anxiety and PTSD that often go untreated or unrecognized, according to a report by the Texas After Violence Project, a non-profit oral history organization.

Sociologist and death penalty scholar Michael L Radelet is deeply familiar with the Steven Judy case; it partly inspired his first book, Facing the Death Penalty. "The family members of the executed are among the most powerless in our communities," he told me. "The death penalty just doubles the number of innocent families who are mourning the loss of a loved one."

With no institutional support and little public sympathy, many families carry loss, shame and sorrow for decades. "They are victims of the system," Sharp said. "We need to find ways to intervene and help them make sense of it."

After the execution, threatening and abusive calls flooded the Carr home. They took the phone off the hook for days, but the noise did not stop.

Inside the house, Mary and Bob fought constantly, often about Steve, and Bob moved out. Traci found her mom's house chaotic and undisciplined so she went with her father; Randy and his brother stayed with Mary, who seemed unreachable, crying often, sunk in a sorrow with no clear edges.

Isolation hardened around them. Parents forbade their children from playing with the Carr kids. On the playground, though, the question surfaced anyway: Hey, what was he like, your brother? Traci refused to answer. "I wouldn't talk about it. I just wouldn't," she recalls. "I thought we did something wrong. I was really ashamed of it."

Randy kept getting into fights. Strong, athletic and ready to use his fists, he swung at anyone who tried to force him to accept what Steve had done.

The stain of being Steven Judy's foster siblings followed Traci and Randy through high school and beyond. It entered rooms before they did.

When Traci moved into her first apartment, eager for the ordinary independence of adulthood, she slept with the lights on. "The dark terrified me," she said.

Later, motherhood gave the fear somewhere new to live. She found herself watching her children obsessively, imagining dangers before they arrived. "The worst thoughts still pop in my head," she says. "I have to mentally block them out."

For a long time, Traci carried anger toward her parents for bringing Steve into their home, for not knowing more, for not protecting them better.

She has forgiven them now, at least mostly. "They grew later in life," she said. They were young. They didn't know the full extent of Steve's crimes. "Mom had the best intentions. She was always trying to rescue people. Steve was charming so she really thought she could turn it around for him and make something good out of something terrible. She was trusting to the end of her life. And it's a good quality."

Mary died in 2023, and her husband, Bob, died two years later. The bin containing Steve's belongings went to Traci. After we spent a day going through the bin together, Traci carried Steve's belongings back to a corner of her garage. She doesn't love having his stuff. "Was he wearing that belt when he did that? And that watch. Was he wearing that?" she asked. "I know Mom loved him, but I would never have kept this if it were up to me." But even now, the final act of throwing it away still feels impossible.

Asked what she would say to Steve today, knowing all she knows now, Traci hesitated.

"I'm sorry for what he had to go through as a child. It makes me sick to think about the things he had to witness." She paused. "Some people can pull through," she said, "and other people can't."

Mary's attachment to Steve did not end with his execution.

For 20 years, on the anniversary of his death, Mary would check into a hotel room alone and try to connect. She said she could feel him. She said he came to her. The kids sometimes teased her about this, but she just laughed good-naturedly. She was not religious, but recalled her grandmother communicating with spirits. She believed she came from a psychic family.

Though she kept a connection with Steve, Mary cut herself off from her parents for a time after the execution. "If anyone ever needed support and love from their family, I needed it this month," she wrote to her mother. "We buried Steve yesterday and not one member of my family was there. I think I know how Steve must have hurt when his family turned their back on him. My family did the same to me. And all I did was give a very lost kid some love."

Traci says when she discovered that letter, "it broke my heart. She never told me about any of that." It took Traci years to understand that her mother's grief carried its own kind of exile.

For Randy, the spiral that began after Judy's arrest never fully stopped. A star high school athlete, he later went to prison on drug-related charges. "Everybody always told me I was going to turn out like Steve, and I'm thinking I didn't mind that because I loved Steve to death," he said. "But I felt like everybody expected me to screw up, so it wasn't no big deal to meet their expectations."

Traci is married to a police officer. She works as a patient advocate at a hospital now. She sits with families in crisis, helping them navigate what they don't understand. In the evenings, she knits thick blankets, the yarn moving through her hands row by row.

Her mother has begun appearing again in her sleep: Mary holding her, comforting. Almost as if speaking aloud what had been buried for decades had called her mother back.

"Everyone hated Steve, and we were told we should too," Traci says. "For a long time, I thought we did something wrong, and I was ashamed. People treated us like we had raised a murderer. It's still how people remember us. I don't think Mom ever got to grieve properly. I don't think any of us did."

This year, somewhere in the United States, another family will be sitting in a hotel room like the one Mary sat in, waiting for a phone call.

Forty-seven executions took place in 2025, the most in any year since 2009. Fifteen more by early June of this year, with the federal government moving to add firing squads, electrocution and gas asphyxiation to how a life can be taken.

The methods have changed, but for families, what is on the other side of the execution has not.

Recently, I took a road trip with three friends I've known since elementary school. For the first time in decades, we spoke together about my childhood friend Cindy Winter, whose murder forced its way into our childhood before any of us really understood death, shattering trust and turning our Sonoran desert into a place of danger.

When Terry and her children were killed, Traci and Randy were younger than I had been when Cindy was murdered. What struck me in both cases was the force of the damage: how completely one person's violence could unmake life for children who had nothing to do with it.

But the Carrs carried something I never had to carry. Cindy's killer was a figure of fear to me. To them, Judy was the brother who was "everything I had", the protector who made room beneath the covers, the boy Mary could not stop trying to reach.

They had to go on knowing the worst thing about him, without being able to unknow the rest.

title: NYT Crossword Answers for July 22, 2026
full_text_raw:
WEDNESDAY PUZZLE -- It's hard to describe Wednesday crosswords. I think of them as the "You had to be there" puzzles of the solving week. They sometimes defy puzzle logic or pull off a whip-smart visual trick. Others contain rebus elements, and some are just plain witty.

I'd describe Rebecca Goldstein as something of a Wednesday whisperer, as crosswords go. It's not that she constructs Wednesday puzzles exclusively -- she has just four under her belt, in fact -- but that she knows how to keep us guessing, be it with clever sleights of word or visual magic. Today's crossword theme was another delight to uncover. There's a rebus square, a visual joke and a truly elegant design choice. Considering the puzzle's subject, that all seems more than, ahem, fair.

Today's Theme

Circled squares indicate themed fill, so that's probably where we'll find 38D's [Carnival game depicted in this puzzle]. Most of these circles contain standard letters: [Many a tech alum: Abbr.] at 49A is an ENGR -- a baffling shortening of "engineer," incidentally -- which gives us a circled R. The [Toxin in castor beans] at 40A is RICIN, which yields an I. Moving on from left to right, we've got an N from TALON (34A), a G from SINGH (41A) and ... something that doesn't quite fit at 52A and 23D.

The answer to [Risqué game that teenagers might give a whirl?] should be SPIN THE BOTTLE, but BOTTLE is too long a word for the entry spaces. 52A's [Pop top?] should be BOTTLE CAP, but we end up with the same issue. The logical conclusion: We're looking at a rebus square.

For the purposes of the Times Crossword we define rebuses simply as "crossword elements where solvers are asked to write multiple letters in the same square." In this case, those letters form the word BOTTLE. If we treat the square as the object itself, then the letters R, I, N and G arcing toward it amount to a RING TOSS (38D)!

Would it be a carnival game without a high-up [Prize dangling from a 38-Down booth] to be won? The biggest PLUSH TOY at 11A can be yours if you land the toss.

And while the connection probably wasn't intentional, I can't resist pointing out that the phrases at 17A and 60A, STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK, could serve as answers to the clue [Hawk's hook] -- as in, phrases used by carnival barkers hawking their games to hook players in. Eh?

Tricky Clues

14A. Blame the Canadian in me for defaulting to "Sorry!" as the [Cry after an accident] instead of OOPSY.

19A. The question mark at the end of [Seller's bottom lines, for short?] indicates a witty twist, likely in the literal interpretation of a figure of speech. "Bottom lines" refers to a product's bar code, also known as U.P.C.

43A. A question mark may also be a reminder to read the clue twice. It's [Get in bad with?], not "get in bed with." The answer is ABET.

1D. You don't need to get your hands grimy to [Spread dirt] in this sense, i.e., to GOSSIP.

40D. Tense is one of the "must match" elements of crossword clues, but it's easy to get tripped up by "-ed" endings, because past-tense verbs can end in other ways. The answer to [Trampled], for example, is RAN OVER.

51D. PIU is not a sound made at 59-Across, but an Italian-derived notation for [More, musically].

Constructor Notes

One of my favorite genres of crossword theme is the representation of an object or game. Lately I've been thinking about puzzles that depict movement, and looking at the timeline of this puzzle, that may have started earlier than I realized. My first stab at this theme was in late 2023. I had the circled elements in place, but the longer theme entries weren't quite coming together. Coming back to it in spring of 2025, the grid fell into place when I realized that STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK were the same length. I especially love the dangling vertical PLUSH TOY at the top of the grid. Hope this one doesn't throw you for a loop!

title: Monkeys Understand Shapes in Almost the Same Way as Humans
full_text_raw:
Our geometric intuition, long considered something that sets us apart, seems to be shared with other primates.

You (probably) won't find a monkey in a geometry class, but it looks like our fellow primates can swing the basics.

Just like people, monkeys seem to grasp the abstract qualities of geometric shapes, such as whether they are symmetrical, have parallel sides or contain right angles, according to a new study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. This ability allows the monkeys -- and us -- to understand when two shapes are the same, even when they've been rotated or resized.

This finding challenges a long-held notion that humans' geometric abilities are part of what makes our brains one of a kind. "Our hypothesis was that humans are not that unique," in possessing this mathematical understanding, said Jialin Li, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University and the lead author of the study.

In their experiment, Ms. Li and her colleagues decided to give monkeys (a total of eight rhesus macaques and olive baboons), preschoolers and adult humans with different education levels the same geometric task. That way, if humans truly had an innate advantage, it would show up when comparing the young children and the monkeys. And if the advantage was learned, it might show up when comparing the humans who had different levels of schooling.

It was a challenge to find a task simple enough that even preschool-aged children and monkeys could reasonably complete it, but the team eventually decided to have all the study participants do a matching task. All were shown a shape with a specific size and geometric form on a screen. Then they were asked to pick that same shape out of a group of others.

"By manipulating the similarity of the shapes, we were able to look at what kinds of rules they're using," said Jessica Cantlon, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University whose lab conducted the study.

title: Susumu Tonegawa Dies at 86; Nobel Laureate Showed How Antibodies Fight Infection
full_text_raw:
The first Japanese scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, he went on to discover how memories are stored, advancing understanding of how the brain works.

Susumu Tonegawa, a Japanese molecular biologist who won the Nobel Prize in 1987 for figuring out how the body can produce sufficient antibodies to combat a multitude of infections, and who later advanced the understanding of how the brain works by discovering how memories are stored, died on July 11 at his home in San Mateo, Calif. He was 86.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Dr. Tonegawa was a professor, announced his death.

"Few scientists have reshaped our understanding of biology as profoundly," Myriam Heiman, the director of M.I.T.'s Picower Institute for Learning and Memory, which Dr. Tonegawa founded in 1994, said in a statement. "His intellectual fearlessness, extraordinary creativity and relentless pursuit of fundamental questions opened entirely new frontiers in both immunology and neuroscience."

For decades, scientists were confounded by the antibodies created in the white blood cells known as B lymphocytes.

Those antibodies, which fight disease, are shaped like Y's, with two long and two short symmetrical chains of proteins built from amino acids, all bound together by bridges of sulfur atoms. Most of the long proteins and some of the short ones are considered constants because they are the same in all antibodies.

At the end of each strand are variable amino acids that allow the antibodies to bind to antigens on an array of infections, disabling them. A common analogy is that the constant amino acids are like the shaft of a key, and the variable ones are the notches that turn the lock. As with a key, each combination of notches is unique.

Even so, scientists were puzzled by how the antibodies could create enough combinations to fight millions of infections.

One suggestion was that it was an evolutionary adaptation, passed down from generation to generation in the genes, or what is known as the germ line. But the human body has only about 20,000 genes, so it seemed unlikely that there would be enough to create all the permutations required to fight so many diseases.

Another theory was that the body developed its defenses in somatic cells -- in other words, that there were a limited number of antibody genes at birth, but the body was capable of diversifying and building up its defenses over time by modifying those genes.

For a long time, scientists lacked the technology to do the kind of experiments that might have helped them solve the puzzle.

In 1974, while Dr. Tonegawa was working at the Basel Institute for Immunology in Switzerland, he decided to tackle the problem.

In a labor-intensive process that took months, he and an assistant made hybrid probes of messenger RNA -- the single-stranded molecule that conveys the genetic information of DNA to other genes -- to examine both the DNA of the cancer known as myeloma and that of the embryo tissue of mice. The probes bonded with complementary pieces of DNA, allowing the scientists to identify specific DNA sequences in the tissues they were analyzing. With that information, they were able to graph and compare the patterns in the myeloma and embryo tissues.

The results, which were entirely different, allowed them to see that antibodies were made by combining some of the variable amino acids, often in conjunction with constant amino acids, to create new amino acids. In creating some of the new amino acids, parts of the coding in the DNA strands had been altered; in some cases, the coding had been removed altogether.

Antibodies, they finally understood, could be created in a variety of ways, which is vital given the number of foreign antigens the body must confront.

The debate was over: The somaticeans, as Dr. Tonegawa called them, had won.

In 1976, he published the first in a series of influential papers on his findings. He continued to advance his research, working with others at the Basel lab, and in 1987 became the first Japanese scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, "for his discovery of the genetic principle for generation of antibody diversity."

The applications of Dr. Tonegawa's discovery, the Nobel committee noted, could include making vaccines more effective, developing immunological therapies and figuring out how to combat autoimmune diseases that occur when antibodies begin attacking healthy cells.

In 1994, as a professor at M.I.T., Dr. Tonegawa turned his attention to a new subject: neuroscience. After founding the M.I.T. Center for Learning and Memory (now the Picower Institute), he focused on understanding how memories are stored in the brain.

Using state-of-the-art technology, he looked at a group of cells known as engrams, in the hippocampus -- the part of the brain responsible for integrating new information into memory -- and elsewhere. Dr. Tonegawa discovered that memories are created in the engram cells from a variety of elements, including experiences and perceptions of space, time and the physical characteristics of objects.

In an interview, Li-Huei Tsai, a neuroscientist who succeeded Dr. Tonegawa as the director of the Center for Learning and Memory, equated the process to the way an orchestra combines multiple instruments to produce a piece of music.

In testing on mice, Dr. Tonegawa supplied engram cells with novel information, creating create new and distinct memories.

Those experiments with altering memory, Dr. Heiman said, may eventually be useful in treating PTSD and degenerative brain diseases like Alzheimer's by modifying or even suppressing negative memories.

Susumu Tonegawa was born on Sept. 5, 1939, in Nagoya, Japan, the second son of Tsutomu and Miyoko Tonegawa. His father was an engineer for a textiles company, and the family moved frequently for his job.

At Kyoto University, Susumu became fascinated with molecular biology. After graduating in 1963, he spent a couple of months working in the laboratory of Itaru Watanabe, at the university's Institute for Virus Research.

At Dr. Watanabe's suggestion, he left to study at the University of California San Diego, which had a new doctoral program in molecular biology. He earned his Ph.D. in 1968 and then did postdoctoral work at the nearby Salk Institute for Biological Studies, in the laboratory of Renato Dulbecco, a future Nobel laureate in medicine.

In 1971, Dr. Tonegawa went to work at the Basel Institute for Immunology. He was recruited to M.I.T. in 1981 by Salvador E. Luria, who had shared the Nobel in 1969 for his work on viruses.

Dr. Tonegawa's first marriage, to Kyoko Sakita, ended in divorce. He married Mayumi Yoshinari in 1985. She survives him, along with two children, Hidde and Hanna. A third child, Satto, died in 2011.

At a conference of Nobel winners in Tokyo in 2017, Dr. Tonegawa was asked to define creativity. "I don't feel I am a very creative scientist. I wish I could be more creative," he replied, to laughter.

"But if you force me to think about it," he added, "I can come up with three simple concepts. One is you have to be very curious about something. No. 2, you have to have an unfailing urge to address the question you have. No. 3, I think it helps to try to combine knowledge in at least two different fields where people don't necessarily interact."

title: Female Afghan Christian convert flees Taliban, only to risk deportation in Qatar
full_text_raw:
Taliban personnel detain a woman in Herat, Afghanistan, for allegedly violating the dress code.

Afghan Christian convert and former government official Ziba Mastoor says she fled to Qatar earlier this month after Taliban intelligence operatives pursued her from Afghanistan into Pakistan, leaving her dependent on a temporary visa and fearful that deportation could place her life in danger.

For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org

Her case reflects the risks confronting Afghan women and members of religious minorities who fled to neighboring countries after the Taliban seized power in August 2021. Pakistan and Iran have accelerated the expulsion of Afghans over the past year, raising concerns that vulnerable refugees and asylum seekers could be returned to Afghanistan to face further persecution.

Since retaking power, the Taliban has largely excluded women from public life. Girls are barred from secondary schools and universities, while women have faced sweeping restrictions on employment, travel and access to public spaces. Women who protest have reported arbitrary arrest and imprisonment.

The Organization of Islamic Cooperation and prominent Islamic scholars have rejected the Taliban's restrictions on women as lacking a basis in Islamic law. Rights advocates accuse the Taliban of using a rigid interpretation of Islam to enforce its rule while persecuting religious minorities.

Reports of intimidation, arbitrary detention, violence and discrimination have prompted members of minority communities to flee or conceal their identities.

Mastoor says she held a senior government position during the administration of former President Ashraf Ghani. She told The Media Line that Taliban intelligence operatives targeted her because of her faith and attempted to arrest her during a nighttime raid on her home, but she escaped.

Mastoor alleged that Taliban authorities later issued what she described as a sentence of "stoning to death" because she had converted to Christianity. She said officials also harassed and intimidated her parents while searching for her. The Media Line could not independently verify the existence of such a sentence.

Responding to a question from The Media Line, Mastoor said, "I converted to Christianity in 2019. My faith guided me to make this genuine and personal choice."

Her parents, who are ethnic Tajik Muslims, opposed her decision, she said.

Persistent harassment by Taliban intelligence operatives eventually forced Mastoor to flee Afghanistan for Pakistan, according to her account. Yet she said she found no lasting safety there and lived alone under the constant threat of forced return.

A trusted contact in Kabul later warned her that Taliban operatives were attempting to locate her in Pakistan, Mastoor said, prompting her to flee again.

She arrived in Qatar on a temporary visitor visa only days ago. Mastoor fears that she could be deported to Afghanistan when the visa expires, which she said would place her life at grave risk.

Afghanistan's Christian population is believed to be extremely small, and it is difficult to document because believers generally practice in secret. Mastoor estimated that only a few hundred Christians remain in the country.

She has appealed to Christian organizations worldwide for help in preventing her return to Afghanistan.

Fazal Ur Rehman Zadran, a Kabul-based political analyst, told The Media Line that determining the size of Afghanistan's Christian population was difficult because openly practicing or promoting Christianity is prohibited.

Zadran said that dozens of families from the Hazara Shiite community had converted to Christianity in previous years. Hazaras have long faced persecution, including attacks by the Islamic State group, and he suggested that such experiences may have contributed to some conversions.

After the Taliban returned to power, many Christian families were forced to conceal their religious identities, Zadran said. According to the information available to him, some fled to Pakistan and Iran in disguise.

Stricter deportation policies in both countries have left those families living in hardship and uncertainty, fearful that they could be returned to Afghanistan at any time, he explained.

Qaiser Khan Afridi, a spokesperson for the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) in Pakistan, expressed concern about Pakistan's policy of deporting Afghan refugees and asylum seekers.

He told The Media Line that while the UNHCR appreciates the people and government of Pakistan for "hosting millions of Afghan refugees with generosity for more than 45 years, despite facing their own economic and social challenges," refugees should not be compelled to return to a country where their lives or freedom could be endangered.

The UNHCR is particularly concerned about the risks facing women, girls and other vulnerable groups if they are sent back to Afghanistan, he said, and urged Pakistani authorities to ensure that any repatriation is voluntary, safe and dignified.

The Media Line also spoke with Zabihullah Mujahid, the Taliban's chief spokesperson, who categorically denied that a Christian community exists in Afghanistan.

Because there is no Christian community, Mujahid said, Christians have no official status in the country, and no churches are available for worship. He did not address Mastoor's allegations concerning her attempted arrest or reported sentence.

'The international response to Afghanistan's crisis has been marked by half-measures'

Rebecca Trotter, a St. Paul, Minnesota-based human rights activist, is the co-founder and co-director of Food for Thought Afghanistan, a US and Switzerland-based nongovernmental organization supporting Afghan civil society.

She told The Media Line that "the international response to Afghanistan's crisis has been marked by half-measures, symbolic gestures, and rhetorical condemnations rather than meaningful action."

She said that even measures imposed during the Taliban's first rule have largely not been reinstated, arguing that "the global community's commitment to defending fundamental human rights stands in stark contrast to the Taliban's determination to enforce its own agenda."

Trotter added that she believes the international community would have already openly normalized relations with Afghanistan's de facto authorities "had it not been for the relentless efforts of Afghan civil society, both inside the country and abroad, to resist such a course." Genuine international support for those efforts could fundamentally alter Afghanistan's future, she argued.

According to Trotter, "Food for Thought Afghanistan is working to relocate 60 at-risk Afghan women's rights activists from Pakistan to safe third countries." The organization successfully resettled 31 families last year, she said, while the remaining families continue to live in safe houses it established.

She said the organization had also pressed Pakistan to recognize the women's protection claims under international, Pakistani and Islamic law.

Hadia Sahibzada, the Tehran-based founder of the Afghanistan Women's Voice Movement and an advocate for Afghan refugees in Iran, told The Media Line that "women's rights in Afghanistan have become one of the world's gravest human rights crises."

Gender apartheid and a blatant violation of fundamental human rights

She described the Taliban's policies as gender apartheid and a blatant violation of fundamental human rights. Forced deportation places Afghan women at immediate risk of persecution, arbitrary detention, retaliation and severe punishment after their return, she said.

Repeated condemnations by the United Nations and foreign governments have failed to curb the Taliban's abuses, Sahibzada argued, while the absence of accountability has allowed violations to continue. She called for those responsible to be prosecuted under international law.

Sahibzada also urged governments not to normalize relations with the Taliban. Instead, she called for stronger diplomatic pressure, accountability measures, protection for Afghan women and the immediate reopening of schools and universities to girls.

For Mastoor, those debates are no longer abstract. Her immediate future depends on whether she can secure protection in Qatar or another country before her temporary visa expires. Without a safe destination, she fears that the long journey from Afghanistan through Pakistan may end where it began -- under the authority of the Taliban.

title: Here's how Andy Burnham really could end homelessness | Daniel Lavelle
full_text_raw:
Utilising empty homes, capping rents and fixing the benefits system would all help, but they'd require a serious fight

In January 2017, the then mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham, promised to end rough sleeping in the region by 2020 - a bold, frankly absurd promise that inevitably didn't materialise. Nearly a decade later, shortly after becoming prime minister, Burnham promised to end rough sleeping again, only this time for the whole of England. So why should we believe him this time around?

I have interviewed Burnham several times over the past decade. At the end of 2019, when it was clear he had not lived up to his promise, I asked him if he regretted making it in the first place. "I wasn't making what you would call a traditional target," the mayor said. "I issued my commitment to make it more of a wake-up call to the system. And I think it has had that effect." Burnham's advisers had told him to tone down the pledge, but he resisted. "The team here said I should have said: 'End the need for rough sleeping,' because you can't force people into a shelter ... In retrospect, if I had said 'end the need for', that probably would have been a wiser thing to have done. But I wasn't in the space of wanting to play semantics with it."

Official figures showed rough sleeping decreased by two-thirds in Manchester during his first five years as mayor. There are reasons I can quibble with this claim. First of all, it doesn't pass the eye test. Just walk through the city centre in the early hours, and you'll find people still bedding down in their dozens. Second, the statistics on rough sleeping are based on single-night snapshots, which involve council representatives walking around counting the people they find rough sleeping. The problem with this is obvious. Third, even those stats, as unreliable as they are, now show that rough sleeping in Manchester is three-quarters of what it was in 2017.

But let's forget all that, and give the prime minister the benefit of the doubt. Maybe his "promise" was merely a "wake-up call". He was a metro mayor after all, and for most of his time in office, he depended on the generosity of a Conservative government. He simply didn't have the resources to end rough sleeping. Let's also assume that Burnham means what he says. He didn't have to make his pledge back in 2017, and he certainly didn't have to make it on the steps of Downing Street on Monday.

The difference is that now he has control of the purse strings, so how does Burnham intend to honour his promise this time around? Initial signs are not encouraging. After Burnham finished his speech, his new government pledged an extra £340m, equivalent to £68m a year over five years, on top of the £3.5bn already allocated, to tackle homelessness. The UK can't quite agree on how many rough sleepers there are, but I think a sensible estimate is anywhere between 15,000-18,000 unique people over a 12-month period. So, £68m divided among 18,000 people amounts to £3,777 per head. That's about four months of rent if you're lucky. It's less a panacea, more like defending yourself from a tidal wave with a cocktail umbrella.

The government will say it is only targeting 3,000 of the most vulnerable rough sleepers with this cash, and they will receive closer to £22,000 per head. I don't know how one would qualify for the most-vulnerable list. Just how hopeless do you need to be in the new Burnham era?

If Burnham really wants to live up to his promise, he'll need to do a lot better than this. He should be aware from the start that rough sleeping represents the very tip of an enormous iceberg, and solving homelessness in this country will demand something close to a revolution. According to Shelter, there are 380,000 homeless people in England, and even that demoralising figure is almost certainly an underestimate. To permanently house those people would require an unprecedented social housebuilding programme that would make the postwar rebuild look like a casual game of Minecraft.

Burnham's government would also need to reverse 16 years of austerity. This is all quite spendy, and to fund it would require higher taxes, more borrowing and aggressive nationalisation of natural monopolies. An upheaval of the economy of such magnitude is unlikely to happen when so many Labour MPs have their fingernails firmly embedded in the market. If there's even a suggestion that Burnham intends to depart from turbo capitalism, then he will be out of SW1 faster than you can say Liz Truss.

So, what can Burnham realistically do about homelessness? There are several levers available to him to ease people's suffering in the short term, and they cost next to nothing in political or real capital.

His priority should be triggering a nationwide Housing First programme. Housing First, a policy pioneered in Finland that effectively eliminated rough sleeping, gives people a home with no preconditions, then tailors support to their individual needs. We know this works because we did it ourselves, only with a different name. The Everyone In campaign, established during the Covid-19 pandemic, virtually ended rough sleeping overnight by emergency block-booking hotels. Surely we can do the same thing again.

The next thing on the agenda should be removing the stick from the benefits system. Currently, the welfare state resembles a gameshow created by Kafka, where contestants have to complete a series of timed trials to win basic subsistence.

There are about 300,000 long-term empty homes in England. Housing people in some of these dwellings might be a good idea; capping rents at an affordable rate would be another, as would fast-tracking asylum applications and enabling asylum seekers to receive benefits and temporary work visas while their claims are processed.

I'm not confident that Burnham will do any of these things. Not because I think he doesn't care or lacks the political will, but because government apparatus is smothered in molasses, and most Labour politicians are Tories in all but name.

But let's see what Burnham does before writing him off as yet another neoliberal metronome with fine words and dry parsnips. Let's give the man his honeymoon period, but the "king of the north" should keep this in mind: winter is coming, and he must act quickly, not just for his premiership, but for the poor souls he has promised to get off the streets.
