title: The children who loved a killer
full_text_raw:
The Carr family took in Steven Judy, hoping to 'save' a troubled teen. They didn't know he would become one of the most hated men in America

Childhood returns to Traci Carr in fragments.

Night-time. She is five. She wakes to shadows on the wall, her room strange in the dark. Her footie pyjamas slip against the wood as she pads downstairs and climbs into bed next to her foster brother, Steven Judy.

He scoots over, and the monsters recede. She burrows under the covers, feeling safe.

Morning. Traci and Steve share Froot Loops, their favorite cereal, the milk turning pink. He teases her, tells funny stories, acts extra goofy to make her laugh.

Later, they play hide and seek. He's all theater, snapping a belt in the air as he searches for Traci and her three older siblings. They collapse in giggles when he finds them.

Then one day, Steve disappears.

No one explains where he went. Her parents are away for long stretches, too. When they are home, conversations drop into whispers. Doors click shut. The television is switched off when she enters the room.

The year Traci turns seven, her parents take her on a car ride. At Conkle funeral home just outside Indianapolis, the room smells of carnations and furniture polish.

She is led to the coffin at the end of the room. She peers over the edge.

It's Steve.

His eyes are closed, his face composed. His hair isn't right - a wig, she'll learn later. But otherwise, he looks like himself.

Her mother, Mary, leans close. Touch him, she urges.

I don't want to.

Her mother insists. Don't be afraid. Just touch him. Traci extends a single finger. It leaves a dent in his cold skin.

Three days earlier, on 9 March 1981, the state of Indiana had executed Steven Judy. Traci would not fully grasp this for years.

Decades on, she still carries the confusion of that day. It flickers across her face as we sit in her kitchen, a plastic storage bin between us filled with his belts, his wallet, his watch, letters, photographs: the small, stubborn evidence of a brother they once loved. A brother whose grave drew hate-filled handwritten notes decades after his death.

For decades, Judy's crimes have been revisited in books, documentaries and true-crime retellings. His atrocities have been replayed, his psychology dissected. But Traci and her siblings are missing from those narratives. The families of condemned people are among the least visible casualties of capital punishment, even as the death penalty is on the rise again.

The Carr children loved and lost a foster brother the rest of the world called a monster. No one asked what it was like to be them. For decades, they were not ready to say.

I was there the day Judy died.

I was a young Associated Press journalist assigned to cover the family's side of the story and had arrived in Michigan City on Sunday, the day before the execution.

As reporters and photographers gathered outside the prison, I sat in a hotel room with the family. Over months of reporting, I had quietly slipped into their orbit. I wasn't a friend, exactly, but I had become a witness to their unraveling at a moment when most people looked away.

Eleven years earlier, a young man murdered my eighth-grade friend Cindy Winter in the Sonoran desert about a quarter of a mile from her home. We children had no language for this; neither did the grownups around us. After the first days of sorrow, we stopped speaking of Cindy altogether. Assigned to the Judy case, I did not yet understand that I was trying to report my way back into a story I already belonged to: violent death, bewildered survivors, and grief with nowhere to go.

That day, Traci had stayed home with a babysitter. In the afternoon, I went swimming with the other Carr children. We had lunch, and then dinner, though no one ate much.

Around 11pm, Judy's foster father, Bob Carr, left for the prison. He had reluctantly agreed to Judy's request that he witness the execution, which was scheduled shortly after midnight. By then, the kids were asleep, or appeared to be.

Mary thumbed through Polaroids of Judy that she had brought with her, sometimes glancing at the clock beside the bed. She smoked the way some people pray, steadily, wordlessly, through the waiting.

Shortly before 1am, Carr returned to our hotel with attorney Steve Harris. For Mary's benefit, he described Judy's final 71 minutes.

A shaved head. A cigarette. A phone call to a girlfriend who had sent him a last-minute telegram - Judy joked that if she proposed marriage, he might ask for a stay. A final Polaroid taken for the Carrs, never made public until now. A Valium to calm Judy's nerves before the end. Some tears, some jokes.

At 12.04am, the guards blindfolded Judy and led him a few paces to the chair in the next room. Harris and Carr moved to the witness room.

"I don't hold no grudges. This was my doing. I'm sorry it happened," Judy said from the chair before the switch was thrown.

Mary soaked in every detail, hanging on every word, sometimes asking Harris to repeat himself. The ashtray beside her filled with cigarette stubs.

Within the month, she admitted herself to a psychiatric hospital for a brief period, shattered by what had happened. I visited her there. Wearing a hospital gown, she seemed emptied of the force that had animated her for months - defending Judy, raging at the state, willing him somehow to survive. The fight had fled her body.

I spent months with the Carrs, but I shed no tears for Judy. I did not mistake him for an innocent man. Still, I could not believe justice had been served by strapping him into a chair and killing him. The state had not restored his victims to life; it had only widened the circle of suffering. Our world, as I saw it, had room for outrage, punishment and fascination, but little space for certain kinds of grief.

I did not yet know that this story would stay with me for the next 45 years.

The facts of the case are these: on the morning of 28 April 1979, around 6.30am, Judy, 22, raped and murdered Terry Lee Chasteen, 21, along the banks of White Lick Creek outside Indianapolis.

When her three children - ages two, four and five - cried, he threw them into the creek to drown.

It wasn't his first violent crime, but it was the one for which he would be executed.

The four bodies were discovered later that morning by mushroom hunters. Residents called it the worst crime Morgan county had ever seen.

A distinctive red and silver truck seen near the site of the killings was traced back to Bob Carr. He told police his foster son had borrowed it the night before. Judy was arrested the next day.

Public outrage hardened quickly. Even before all the evidence was presented, a grassroots group called Protect the Innocent demanded the death penalty.

At first, Judy said he couldn't remember what happened. Later, he confessed. Harris, the attorney, initially pursued an insanity defense, but two court-appointed psychiatrists concluded Judy was legally sane.

After the guilty verdict, Judy made his preference clear: death over life in prison. Determined to eliminate any possibility of leniency, he proposed leaping across the table to attack the prosecutor before sentencing.

"You can't do that," Harris told him. "There are 50 officers in that courtroom."

Instead, Judy asked to address the jury. He told them he knew their names, where they lived, where they worked, and would kill anyone who failed to vote for the electric chair. Then he turned toward the bench. "That goes for you too, bud," he said to the judge.

The jury deliberated 20 minutes before recommending the death penalty.

Forty-five years later, one of the people I most wanted to find was Harris. He had witnessed the crime's aftermath and Judy's final hours. I wondered what remained with him after all this time.

Before Judy, Harris had handled three other murder cases. After the execution, he vowed never to take another death penalty case. "It was time-consuming and emotional," he recalls now. "I just made the decision I would never do one again." He represented only one other murder defendant, then gradually left criminal law altogether.

He drove me to the bridge overlooking the stretch of White Lick Creek where the killings took place, about a mile and a half from his office. State Road 67 hums nearby now, busy and indifferent. Round the bend, the creek remains as secluded as it was then; teenagers still go there to hang out beyond the sight of their parents.

A rope swing dangles beneath a railroad bridge where someone has painted: "THE DEVIL WAS HERE." The water moves on.

Steve saved Randy Carr's life when Randy was two years old.

Randy was playing in a mud puddle in the alley behind their house when a family friend known as Stinky climbed into Bob Carr's truck and began backing it up, running over Randy's legs. Steve saw the scene unfold and began yelling and waving his arms.

"He stopped him," Randy says. "Another minute and Stinky would have run over my head."

After that, Steve became Randy's person. "The only one who paid me any attention," Randy recalls. Saturdays were their day. Together, they cleaned the basement, mowed the grass. When the chores were done, Steve took him for ice-cream. "Never failed," Randy remembers.

Steve entered the Carr family through a friendship with Randy's Uncle Tony. On the day of the Chasteen murders, Randy, who was nine, and his brother Bobby, who was 11, helped Steve clean out the garage. They drove trash to the dump. They swept out their father's pickup truck, the one Steve had been driving earlier that morning.

Then they went for ice-cream.

The next day, the police came. Steve was out with a friend, but they questioned the boys. They drove them back to the dump and asked where the trash had been thrown.

"I wasn't going to tell them," Randy says. "I pointed everywhere except where we dumped."

Back at home, Randy went to the window with a pair of binoculars and watched as officers dusted the truck for fingerprints. He watched them wait for Steve to come back. "I didn't grasp what was happening," he says. "Dad never told us anything."

After Steve's arrest, children at school avoided Randy. He began fighting. "I would get mad if anybody told me Steve was guilty of this. I couldn't see it in my mind. Steve couldn't do this."

Eventually, Steve told Randy himself.

"You've gotta let it go," Steve said. "I'm guilty of this. It's something I can't control."

He joked about the electric chair. "Man, I'm gonna ride that lightning."

Randy thought he meant an amusement park ride. "I still didn't understand," he says.

Years later, Randy came to believe Steve deserved to die. He says that plainly now. But then he adds, quietly, tearing up: "To this day, I hate that he did that. Because he was everything I had in life."

In the months before the execution, Randy started spiraling. He skipped school for the first time. He stole diet pills to get high. "I just felt like I needed to do something." When his mother told Steve during a prison visit that Randy was acting out, Steve wrote Randy a seven-page letter about his own childhood, about how he had started screwing up.

In a letter to Mary, Steve mentioned that he had written to Randy, and offered her some parenting advice: "Listen, Mary, I just wrote Randy that letter we talked about. It was hard, too. I don't know if it was exactly what you wanted but I think it will help if he listens. But you have to understand if you keep telling someone not to do this or that, it sometimes pushes them to do it anyway for spite."

Randy read the letter "a thousand times" when he was a kid. He never skipped school again. "I loved Steve to death. I defended him for a long time. I broke a lot of jaws of people who didn't really deserve it."

Randy begged Steve to appeal against the death penalty. "I cried with him for a long time. Finally Steve said: 'Look at me. Don't bring this up again. It's over with. Don't be sad, because this is what I need.'"

Randy visited Steve the afternoon before his execution. "I was so upset. But Steve was laughing and carrying on like nothing was happening. It just blows my mind how he knows he's going to his death, and he was just worried about how I was."

A few months after the funeral, Traci noticed the spine of a book jutting from a stack of papers on the kitchen countertop.

Burn Judy Burn.

Published between Judy's conviction and his execution, the book was written by Bette Nunn, managing editor of the Reporter-Times in Martinsville, Indiana.

Traci pulled it free and turned immediately to the photographs. One showed a small body just beneath the water's surface. Another showed a little boy lying on a metal table, his shirt half pulled up from his torso.

They were children, very small. She could tell they were close to her age.

"I was starting to piece it together," she told me. "I think I knew Steve had killed somebody. But I still didn't understand what had happened to him."

So she asked Randy. What happened to Steve? He told her what he could, as much as he understood.

She couldn't reconcile the brother she knew with the killer described in the book. Yet she kept returning to the photographs. "I had a morbid interest," she says. The more she grasped, the more terrified she became. The house itself seemed altered. When she returned from school and found no one there, she wouldn't go inside, pacing the sidewalk instead.

She didn't ask her parents any questions. She had already noticed the way her mother seemed always on the verge of tears, the way her parents argued in low, urgent voices. The whole house seemed stretched tight with things no one knew how to say aloud.

My editor at the Associated Press asked me to begin reporting on the case in early March 1980, 10 months after the murders of Terry Chasteen and her three children. Judy would become the first person executed in Indiana since 1961 and among the first handful nationally after the supreme court reinstated the death penalty in 1976.

I saw two possible ways into the story. I could try to reach Judy through his attorney, or I could try to understand the family waiting outside the prison walls.

I called Mary Carr. She invited me over immediately.

Mary worked as a drill operator at a manufacturing plant; Bob laid brick and stone for a living. Their house sat in a working-class neighborhood outside Indianapolis, small and crowded, every surface carrying its own accumulation of papers, toys, ashtrays, cups. Four children moved constantly through the rooms. Mary was not yet 31.

Bob was warm but reserved. Mary directed the energy of the house. Within minutes, she had seated me in a padded brown chair and placed a photo album in my lap. She pointed to photographs of Steven Judy.

"Look at him," she said. "He's handsome, isn't he? He's not cold and detached the way they say."

I felt myself recoil. I understood that I could never look at Judy the way Mary Carr did.

When I was in eighth grade, my friend Cindy Winter was murdered in Tucson while riding her bicycle to a close friend's house on a Sunday afternoon. Her body was found under a mesquite tree at the edge of a dry wash. The man who killed her was 24. He was arrested after he raped and killed another woman, leaving her two children alive beside the road.

The similarities between his case and Judy's were striking. Before Cindy's murder, we thought the desert between houses belonged to us. Afterward, the fear never fully left.

Meeting the Carrs conjured that dread back to life. After that first visit, I wrote in my journal: "Walking from my sturdy Scout to my apartment after midnight, the bushes seem to reach out as menacing men, and in the moonlight, I can see my fear."

I could never understand the killer. But I wanted to understand the family living in the aftermath of what he had done.

I began to spend time at the Carrs' kitchen table. I ate pizza with them, went swimming with the kids, phoned Mary to check in. Her warmth as a mother, I learned, was instinctive rather than structured. She wasn't the kind of parent who tracked homework or studied report cards. What she offered instead was openness, noise, food, a place to belong. She believed that when her family took Steve in, they were finally giving him something no one else had: a loving family, a permanent place at the table.

"She thought she could save him," Traci says. And that was exactly who Mary Carr was, a woman who believed in second chances, in the redemptive power of love and a full table. She had been raised by a mother who withdrew support, but Mary had chosen a different path: she made room. She fed people. She believed damage could be repaired if you loved hard enough and long enough.

This impulse would define the next eight years of her life, but Judy had arrived carrying damage the Carrs could not fully see.

In court records and later interviews, Judy described his childhood as violent and unstable. Both parents drank heavily. His father beat his mother and once, in a fit of fury, butchered a pet dog, leaving pieces scattered on the porch for the children to see. His mother brought men home; sometimes the children witnessed them having sex. She occasionally summoned Judy to kiss her while she was bathing or undressing, placing him on her lap and running her fingers through his hair. Pornographic magazines, he said, were kept openly in the house.

By age 10, he was pushing high school girls to the ground and molesting them. At 11, he began shoplifting; by 12, he was drinking. On 17 April 1970, at 13, he raped a 22-year-old woman and attacked her with a knife and a hatchet so severely that she required brain, abdominal and open-heart surgery to survive.

He was detained and transferred to the juvenile section of Indiana's Central State hospital. Opened in 1848 as the Indiana hospital for the "insane", central state closed in 1994 amid scandals over patient treatment and funding shortfalls. The old pathology building, where autopsies were once performed in search of the physical causes of madness, now houses the Indiana Medical History Museum. Brains sit in glass jars, labeled with names, dates, symptoms.

At Central State, Judy was diagnosed as a sexual psychopath. He became friends with Bob Carr's younger brother, Tony, who also was a resident after getting in trouble at school and home. Through him, he met the rest of the family.

When Judy was released at age 15, Mary and Bob agreed to take him in. As a juvenile, he needed to be released to adults; this must have felt like astonishing good fortune to him.

He lived with the Carrs, ate at their table, and worked construction for Bob. But the violence continued: more assaults, more jail time, a robbery.

The Carrs even paid his bond weeks before the Chasteen murders.

Throughout, "Mom always loved Steve," Traci recalls. "She never said anything bad about him, no matter what."

Prison life became a world of letters. Steve wrote and received hundreds of them.

Mary kept many of them in a bedroom drawer: letters from strangers who prayed for him, or from women who had never met him but said they loved him.

For Mary and Bob, he described his life in prison with flashes of humor and longing. Without his television set, he would "go bonkers", Steve wrote. "So far I've earned $15,000 on the Joker's Wild, gotten three dates on the Dating Game, and outdrawn Marshall Dillon twice."

"Tell the kids I said hi and I love them," he wrote time and again. Sometimes he mentioned them by name: "You tell Traci I said hi and that I love her too and that I've got a get-rich-quick scheme for us. I'm going to write the cereal company and tell them me and her are going to quit eating cereal and put them out of business unless they pay us a million dollars (50 cents anyway, ha ha)."

During prison visits, Steve offered Mary tips on staying safe and told her to pass them on to his foster sisters. Lock the car doors. Watch the blind spot. Don't pull over if a man waves you down.

After he was sentenced to death, Harris filed a routine appeal. But in October 1980, Judy told the court he did not want to pursue it, clearing the way for his execution six months later.

Steve wrote to his foster parents soon after. "I know you can't accept what I'm doing but I hope you don't hate me for it either," he told them. Mary had cried during a prison visit, and he had avoided telling her in front of the boys.

"I'm sorry you had to find it out like you did," he wrote. "I'm not going to get into my reasons and feelings on why I wanted it like this because I think it would be better to tell you here where we can look at each other's faces."

Steve was determined to carry through with the death penalty, but there were moments of fear. Right after he was transferred to death row in Michigan City, he wrote: "Mary, don't ever let anyone tell you this isn't bad, because it is, and I'm scared to death."

Later he wrote: "I'm worried about how the kids are taking it all. There's just so much on my mind that can't ever be put into words."

On 5 Febuary 1981, 32 days before the execution, he apologized for not writing. "I just let myself get so far down in the dumps that it was hard to do anything." He warned Mary that people might try to persuade her to intervene. "I know a few of them might try and get you to interfere but I hope you don't," he wrote. "About the only thing you could possibly do is cause a short delay and that would only hurt me." Then, as he often did, he turned back to the children: "Tell me, how are the kids doing? I really hope they're taking all this okay. Tell them I said hello and I send my love."

Steve considered Bob's mother, Rosita Mary Colvin, his foster grandmother. He affectionately called her "the old lady" and asked about her in letters. She wrote him shortly before his execution: "I have loved you from the first time I saw you at Central, your blond hair flying around, you and Tony playing basketball. You was a beautiful child. If you had been my own son, I could not have loved you more. I'm so sorry, Steve. I don't know what went wrong. I just want you to know you are loved by all of us and our lives will never be the same."

His last letter was written to his attorney. Judy told Harris that he had committed about 50 robberies and burglaries and 15 rapes. He confessed directly to one additional murder, indicated there was a second, and said he'd left women tied up so there might be others. He promised to list all his crimes in a letter to be opened after his death.

That last day, he gave Harris a thick sealed envelope.

Police knew this list of confessions was coming and they were waiting. Immediately after the execution, Harris opened the envelope.

In front of him was one page of writing followed by seven blank sheets.

When I visited Harris this year, he spread the letter on his desk so I could read it: "I'm sorry Steve [Harris] but I've decided to handle it this way because I care too much for my foster mom and family. I hope you can understand. Thank you for all you've done for me. Steve."

In his final photo, Judy stands next to Harris in the holding cell, minutes before the execution. His head is shaved. A cigarette rests between the fingers of his right hand. "I'm gonna give these things up," he quipped to Harris.

"It was kind of scary that he could be so dangerous and actually a likable person," Harris recalled. "He had a sense of humor."

Steve asked that he not be interred behind Indiana state prison, where prisoners whose families don't claim them are buried. The Carrs bought him a plot and headstone in Floral Park cemetery, less than a mile away from Central State hospital, where they first met him.

In the cemetery office, I asked for a map to help me locate the gravesite.

"Steven Judy," the clerk said slowly. Hate letters were regularly left on Steve's grave until about five years ago, he said. "Our groundskeepers removed them every morning. It became routine."

The story of death penalty cases is usually told through a narrow cast of characters: the victims, the condemned, sometimes the families of those murdered or the legal teams. Almost no one asks what happens to the families who loved the condemned, especially when they are children.

Scholars who study capital punishment have identified those families as a distinct and largely invisible group. Sociologist Susan Sharp began studying them in 1996. In her book Hidden Victims, she describes them as living in a kind of moral exile.

"They are tainted by association," Sharp told me. "We assume they must have done something wrong."

Sharp estimates that roughly 30% of death row prisoners have no family contact, either because of long estrangement or because relatives cut ties after the crime. For the other 70%, she said, the family's punishment can continue long after the condemned person is executed.

To outsiders, it can seem inexplicable that a family member can feel both horror for the victims and heartache for someone who has done monstrous harm. "We treat those family members as if they don't have a right to grieve. We take away their right to be human," Sharp says. "We fail to realize everyone is multifaceted. None of us is equal to the worst thing we've ever done."

Families who provide primary support to prisoners on death row, as the Carrs did, are likely to suffer from depression, anxiety and PTSD that often go untreated or unrecognized, according to a report by the Texas After Violence Project, a non-profit oral history organization.

Sociologist and death penalty scholar Michael L Radelet is deeply familiar with the Steven Judy case; it partly inspired his first book, Facing the Death Penalty. "The family members of the executed are among the most powerless in our communities," he told me. "The death penalty just doubles the number of innocent families who are mourning the loss of a loved one."

With no institutional support and little public sympathy, many families carry loss, shame and sorrow for decades. "They are victims of the system," Sharp said. "We need to find ways to intervene and help them make sense of it."

After the execution, threatening and abusive calls flooded the Carr home. They took the phone off the hook for days, but the noise did not stop.

Inside the house, Mary and Bob fought constantly, often about Steve, and Bob moved out. Traci found her mom's house chaotic and undisciplined so she went with her father; Randy and his brother stayed with Mary, who seemed unreachable, crying often, sunk in a sorrow with no clear edges.

Isolation hardened around them. Parents forbade their children from playing with the Carr kids. On the playground, though, the question surfaced anyway: Hey, what was he like, your brother? Traci refused to answer. "I wouldn't talk about it. I just wouldn't," she recalls. "I thought we did something wrong. I was really ashamed of it."

Randy kept getting into fights. Strong, athletic and ready to use his fists, he swung at anyone who tried to force him to accept what Steve had done.

The stain of being Steven Judy's foster siblings followed Traci and Randy through high school and beyond. It entered rooms before they did.

When Traci moved into her first apartment, eager for the ordinary independence of adulthood, she slept with the lights on. "The dark terrified me," she said.

Later, motherhood gave the fear somewhere new to live. She found herself watching her children obsessively, imagining dangers before they arrived. "The worst thoughts still pop in my head," she says. "I have to mentally block them out."

For a long time, Traci carried anger toward her parents for bringing Steve into their home, for not knowing more, for not protecting them better.

She has forgiven them now, at least mostly. "They grew later in life," she said. They were young. They didn't know the full extent of Steve's crimes. "Mom had the best intentions. She was always trying to rescue people. Steve was charming so she really thought she could turn it around for him and make something good out of something terrible. She was trusting to the end of her life. And it's a good quality."

Mary died in 2023, and her husband, Bob, died two years later. The bin containing Steve's belongings went to Traci. After we spent a day going through the bin together, Traci carried Steve's belongings back to a corner of her garage. She doesn't love having his stuff. "Was he wearing that belt when he did that? And that watch. Was he wearing that?" she asked. "I know Mom loved him, but I would never have kept this if it were up to me." But even now, the final act of throwing it away still feels impossible.

Asked what she would say to Steve today, knowing all she knows now, Traci hesitated.

"I'm sorry for what he had to go through as a child. It makes me sick to think about the things he had to witness." She paused. "Some people can pull through," she said, "and other people can't."

Mary's attachment to Steve did not end with his execution.

For 20 years, on the anniversary of his death, Mary would check into a hotel room alone and try to connect. She said she could feel him. She said he came to her. The kids sometimes teased her about this, but she just laughed good-naturedly. She was not religious, but recalled her grandmother communicating with spirits. She believed she came from a psychic family.

Though she kept a connection with Steve, Mary cut herself off from her parents for a time after the execution. "If anyone ever needed support and love from their family, I needed it this month," she wrote to her mother. "We buried Steve yesterday and not one member of my family was there. I think I know how Steve must have hurt when his family turned their back on him. My family did the same to me. And all I did was give a very lost kid some love."

Traci says when she discovered that letter, "it broke my heart. She never told me about any of that." It took Traci years to understand that her mother's grief carried its own kind of exile.

For Randy, the spiral that began after Judy's arrest never fully stopped. A star high school athlete, he later went to prison on drug-related charges. "Everybody always told me I was going to turn out like Steve, and I'm thinking I didn't mind that because I loved Steve to death," he said. "But I felt like everybody expected me to screw up, so it wasn't no big deal to meet their expectations."

Traci is married to a police officer. She works as a patient advocate at a hospital now. She sits with families in crisis, helping them navigate what they don't understand. In the evenings, she knits thick blankets, the yarn moving through her hands row by row.

Her mother has begun appearing again in her sleep: Mary holding her, comforting. Almost as if speaking aloud what had been buried for decades had called her mother back.

"Everyone hated Steve, and we were told we should too," Traci says. "For a long time, I thought we did something wrong, and I was ashamed. People treated us like we had raised a murderer. It's still how people remember us. I don't think Mom ever got to grieve properly. I don't think any of us did."

This year, somewhere in the United States, another family will be sitting in a hotel room like the one Mary sat in, waiting for a phone call.

Forty-seven executions took place in 2025, the most in any year since 2009. Fifteen more by early June of this year, with the federal government moving to add firing squads, electrocution and gas asphyxiation to how a life can be taken.

The methods have changed, but for families, what is on the other side of the execution has not.

Recently, I took a road trip with three friends I've known since elementary school. For the first time in decades, we spoke together about my childhood friend Cindy Winter, whose murder forced its way into our childhood before any of us really understood death, shattering trust and turning our Sonoran desert into a place of danger.

When Terry and her children were killed, Traci and Randy were younger than I had been when Cindy was murdered. What struck me in both cases was the force of the damage: how completely one person's violence could unmake life for children who had nothing to do with it.

But the Carrs carried something I never had to carry. Cindy's killer was a figure of fear to me. To them, Judy was the brother who was "everything I had", the protector who made room beneath the covers, the boy Mary could not stop trying to reach.

They had to go on knowing the worst thing about him, without being able to unknow the rest.

title: Many US patients opt for obesity drug injections, defying some expectations
full_text_raw:
NEW YORK, July 22 (Reuters) - Many patients have opted for injectable forms of the wildly popular GLP-1 obesity medications through a pilot program of the U.S. government's Medicare health insurance program for Americans aged 65 and older, according to early indications from doctors and analysts.

The U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services this month launched an 18-month trial program that for the first time opens access to Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO), opens new tab Wegovy and Eli Lilly's (LLY.N), opens new tab Foundayo and Zepbound as weight-loss treatment alone for a monthly cost of $50.

Millions of people are expected to qualify, and doctors are already being flooded with interest from patients aged 65 and older. For the most part, they say the process is going well -- with some hiccups.

Many pharmaceutical industry experts had expected that patients would prefer pills over injections, for convenience. Novo's U.S. chief Jamey Millar in June said the firm's research indicated that Medicare beneficiaries prefer the oral pill to the injectable on a two-to-one basis.

Yet eight of 10 doctors interviewed by Reuters and three pharma sector analysts said many are opting ⁠for the injectables.

"Hands down -- these patients are asking for injections as they know they work and it has been so costly in the past," said Dr. Sarah Ro, director of University of North Carolina Health's weight-management program.

Ro said patients who meet the criteria have been generally receiving approvals quickly once the clinicians became familiar with the process.

COMPARING WEIGHT-LOSS DATA

U.S. approvals for injectable Zepbound and Wegovy were based on separate trials in which the Lilly drug helped patients lose more than 22% of their weight after 72 weeks, while Wegovy led to 15% weight loss after 68 weeks.

Oral Wegovy led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, and Foundayo about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, in separate studies.

"Prescribing patterns have evolved over time as new options have become available, but the majority of patients are still prescribed injectable therapies," said analysts with investment bank William Blair in a July 13 note, citing a call with an obesity medicine specialist.

To be sure, demand for the Wegovy pill has been strong, and analysts said the most recent publicly available data from data firm IQVIA show that prescriptions for ⁠Lilly's pill Foundayo jumped in the week to July 10. IQVIA did not confirm the data.

But patients generally seem to be opting for the injectables once they learn about the efficacy.

"A year ago if you'd asked me, I would have thought people would be jumping at the pill," said RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh. "But it turns out that for most people, it's all about efficacy."

Spokespeople for Lilly and Novo said they were pleased with the new Medicare program. The Lilly spokesperson said the program is "working very well" and the firm is encouraged by the strong interest. Neither drugmaker provided any details about specific ⁠volumes.

FRUSTRATIONS OVER MIXED ACCESS

A CMS spokesperson said the Medicare program's first weeks have been "positive" with most authorizations completed in under 12 hours.

But patients' ability to get coverage under the demo has been mixed, according to both doctors and patients.

Katie Smith, who asked her doctor to send in the prescription on July 1, said she is still waiting for word if she'll be covered. The Virginia retiree said she is ⁠frustrated after years of being unable to access these medications due to cost. The companies' direct-to-consumer prices range from $149 to $449 per month.

"I'm not really sure what's happening," she said.

The process has also been "cumbersome" for doctors, said Dr. Amanda Velazquez, director of obesity medicine at Cedars-Sinai's Center for Weight Management and Metabolic Health in Los Angeles.

"This has required numerous hours and numerous clinical staff ⁠and clinicians to come together to make standardized protocols, order sets, and troubleshoot to try to get through the red tape to get access to GLP1RAs for our patients," she said.

Still, many are seeing success. Dr. Christina Nguyen of weight-loss clinic Knownwell in Atlanta said nationwide it had received approvals for about 200 patients in the first week.

"We're getting several approvals every day, if the patient meets the criteria," she said.

title: US food illnesses climb as authorities struggle to identify source
full_text_raw:
A US outbreak of a serious gastrointestinal illness caused by a food-borne parasite has continued to grow by hundreds of cases per day as authorities struggle to identify the source.

Michigan, the centre of the outbreak, reported over 400 new cases of cyclosporiasis on Tuesday for a total of 6,571 since June 21, skyrocketing above the state average of 50 cases per year. Other states in the Midwest and Northeast have also reported hundreds of cases apiece.

Michigan's state health department first publicly identified an uptick in cyclosporiasis on July 1. As cases mounted, initial investigative efforts pointed to lettuce provided by grower Taylor Farms to Taco Bell restaurants.

The Mexican-themed fast-food chain voluntarily pulled Taylor Farms lettuce from its menus nationwide on Friday. Foot traffic at Taco Bell dropped nearly 19 per cent on Friday compared to the day-of-the-week average this year, according to market researcher Placer.ai.

However, the Food and Drug Administration on Sunday walked back test results identifying the cyclospora parasite on lettuce from Taylor Farms, saying the result was a "false positive".

Epidemiological efforts to trace the pathogen still show a "strong signal" towards lettuce or salad greens as a source of the outbreak, according to the Michigan state health department.

The state has also seen cases where patients "report neither consuming lettuce nor eating at any particular fast-food chain", said Natasha Bagdasarian, chief medical executive for the state of Michigan. "It is possible, with the types of numbers that we are seeing, that there are two separate things happening," she said.

Taylor Farms is continuing with its recall of iceberg lettuce despite the FDA test retraction. The brand recalled lettuce grown in central Mexico and will not source from the region for the rest of the growing season, it said in a statement.

Neither Taylor Farms nor Taco Bell responded to a request for comment.

Cyclospora is very difficult to identify in lab tests, said Karen Levy, a professor researching foodborne illnesses at the University of Washington. "There's a lot of potential for false positives," she said.

In general, it is "not unusual" for an outbreak investigation to identify a contamination source entirely by interviewing patients, without ever obtaining a definitive test result, said Jodie Guest, senior vice-chair of epidemiology at Emory University.

Michigan and other states are tracing the outbreak via interviews with patients, which take about 45 minutes each and require patients to recall to health officials everything they've eaten in a two-week period.

Bagdasarian said the Trump administration's 2025 funding cuts to the Centers for Disease Control reduced Michigan's public health staff by over 100 workers and have "absolutely" slowed the current investigation.

The cyclosporiasis outbreak is a "canary in the coal mine" for a public health system "stretched to the breaking point" by funding cuts and staff shortages, said Levy, the University of Washington researcher.

The CDC did not respond to a request for comment. The FDA said in a statement to the FT that it is "currently investigating Cyclospora outbreaks using established epidemiological, laboratory and traceback tools in close co-ordination with the CDC and state and local partners".

No deaths are associated with the cyclosporiasis outbreak, but hundreds have been hospitalised for cases of gastrointestinal distress including explosive diarrhoea, which can last up to a month without treatment.

title: Government Overhauls Teen Pregnancy Program to Focus on Marriage and Starting Families
full_text_raw:
The administration canceled federal grants to organizations across the country, accusing them of encouraging premarital sex. New criteria say programs should stress abstinence.

A few weeks ago, Rena Dixon, the head of Fact Forward, a South Carolina nonprofit that offers adolescent health and sex education classes, got a letter from the Trump administration with crushing news. The government was terminating the organization's $1.6 million grant from a federal program to reduce teen pregnancies, effective immediately.

The administration's priorities, it said, do not align with "content that encourages, normalizes or promotes sexual activity for minors."

The move is the latest in a campaign that began in the first Trump administration to defund or overhaul the 16-year-old, $100 million initiative. Courts blocked the effort in 2018, but this time the administration, which abruptly canceled 53 of the program's 67 grants last month, has been taking steps to be on firmer legal ground.

The letter from the assistant secretary for health accused Fact Forward of including lessons with "advice on making condom use more pleasurable" and discussions that normalize "use of pornography." A video, it said, contained a "scenario of adolescents engaging in sexual activity."

"That information was just not true," said Dr. Dixon. The organization had never used the lessons specified, she said. The video "is about one teen telling another that she had had sex, and her friend responding, 'That's a big no-no!'"

In interviews, other directors also said that the government had distorted their content. They pointed out that the grant had required them to use courses from a federally approved list shown by research to be age-appropriate and effective.

Healthy Futures of Texas, a nonprofit that serves teenagers in Dallas, San Antonio and the Rio Grande Valley, won renewal of its grant less than a year ago, following a rigorous federal review of its material.

"Today those same materials are being cited as the reason for termination, with no opportunity to address those concerns," said Ginger Mullaney, the organization's chief executive. "So we're all struggling a little bit to understand."

Now dozens of grant holders face an existential dilemma, as they wrestle with whether to submit applications due this week for the next round of grants, under the administration's new rules.

The new criteria say that grant recipients must teach abstinence as the only means to prevent teen pregnancy. Courses must stress the importance of marriage and procreation and instruct young people how to safeguard their fertility. They make scant reference to preventing sexually transmitted infections and virtually none to lesbian, gay and transgender sexuality.

The Department of Health and Human Services declined to comment on the new requirements or the litigation. But these conditions mirror blueprints laid out in Project 2025 as well as in other position papers by the Heritage Foundation, which argue that teen pregnancy prevention programs falsely presume that adolescent sex is inevitable and also undermine parental authority.

Last week, three programs that lost funding and a nonprofit that works with them filed a lawsuit in federal court against the Department of Health and Human Services and its secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The programs seek to block the terminations and the new requirements that, they say, create an ideologically based framework that violates the intent of the federally mandated one.

"Congress plainly did not intend H.H.S. to focus on teaching young women strategies to become pregnant in a pregnancy prevention program," wrote Democracy Forward, a national legal advocacy nonprofit, in the lawsuit.

The five-year projects funded by the Teen Pregnancy Prevention grants had supported topics in sex education, including consent, decision-making and healthy relationships, adjusted for age as well as a local community's values and culture. Locations ranged from schools to juvenile detention centers to foster care settings. The programs also hold communication workshops with teens and trusted adults.

The teenage birthrate has been plummeting steadily for over two decades. Researchers say explanations are varied, but include increased teen access to forms of long-acting birth control, abortion pills and even smartphones.

Public health scholars and bipartisan congressional committees have also attested to the influence of the federal prevention programs on teen behavior, including delayed sexual initiation.

The birthrate among girls 15 to 19 has dropped by more than 65 percent during the time the program has been in effect, to 11.7 births per 1,000 in 2025 from 34.3 births per 1,000 in 2010, according to the latest provisional data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Yet at a time when the overall American birthrate is declining, a trend decried by many conservatives and others, the new, 89-page grant application requires programs to draw from a curriculum known as "sexual risk avoidance," which connects abstinence during the teenage years to maturity and readiness for marriage and parenthood.

It often lifts language almost wholesale from The Body Literacy Project, a curriculum praised by some conservative thinkers and religious leaders as an alternative to public school sex education. The project's website says its courses were developed to align closely with the administration's priorities for the teen pregnancy prevention program.

Applicants must provide separate modules on male and female reproductive health. Young women should recognize "ovulation as the central event and primary indicator of hormonal health and fertility." Although gynecologists often prescribe birth control pills to treat irregular cycles and extreme menstrual pain, courses must include "an overview of approaches to managing menstrual health concerns, including the advantages and disadvantages of ovarian suppression."

Body literacy courses for boys should include strategies for managing "spontaneous arousal in ways that support self-regulation, health and future fertility." And they should address "how repeated or artificially stimulated arousal may affect neural development and behavior over time."

Layoffs and cancellations

Fact Forward's federal grant covered 80 percent of its pregnancy prevention project. Since receiving the termination letter, Dr. Dixon had to lay off half her staff and cancel training for local educators and programming for teen summer activities. The organization reaches some 6,000 young people ages 13 to 21.

"When people hear teen pregnancy prevention program, they think it's all about raining condoms from the sky," said Dr. Dixon, who has a doctorate in public health. But in conservative states like South Carolina, where state law requires public school health classes to emphasize abstinence, Fact Forward operates within tight boundaries and has a faith advisory board.

It runs workshops in church basements, teen clubs, public libraries, health care centers and college campuses. Recently, it sponsored "Game Changers," a daylong summit for 300 middle schoolers with sessions on reproductive health, consent and healthy relationships, with a break room set up like an arcade.

In Bozeman, Mont., Bridgercare, a center that provides adolescent reproductive health care and education, just lost its $1 million federal pregnancy prevention grant. In summertime, it trained school nurses and health teachers from across the state, and established a corps of teen educators.

Em Williamson, 18, was among a group of teens who led discussions about puberty with sixth graders, about consent with eighth graders and about safe sex and birth control with high school students. In private schools and sororities, she explained how to use condoms correctly.

After her own middle school health teacher erroneously warned about contracting a sexually transmitted infection from a toilet seat, Ms. Williamson said she became determined to arm students with the knowledge and skills to make their own decisions about sex, urging them to communicate with supportive adults.

"I also say that abstinence is the only 100 percent way to prevent pregnancy and the contraction of S.T.I.s," Ms. Williamson said. "Except that we don't expect that everyone will be choosing abstinence."

In compliance with Montana's strict parental opt-out laws, Bridgercare educators provided materials to parents in advance of sessions. Students who showed up in class were those whose parents did not object.

Stephanie McDowell, Bridgercare's executive director, has two teenagers. "I want my kids to get good sex ed in school, where they're all getting accurate information together. Then they can talk about values with each other and the adults they trust. But the removal of this funding makes the decision for me as a parent about what education will now be available."

The grant cancellations and new application criteria reflect a tactical shift from July 2017, when the first Trump administration, without explanation, alerted all 81 grantees in the program that their federal funding would end in a year. In 2018, federal courts ordered the funding to be restored, saying the terminations were at odds with the health department's own regulations.

This time, the administration is trying to lay a foundation to argue that the newly terminated programs run afoul of the government's priorities. Last year it issued executive orders and a statement of priorities, barring pregnancy prevention programs from promoting material that "depicts, describes, exposes or presents obscene, indecent or sexually explicit content, including content that encourages, normalizes or promotes sexual activity for minors."

Since the federal grants began in 2010, teen birthrates in South Carolina have dropped 59 percent. Yet as of 2024, when the latest federal data was completed, the state still ranked at No. 11 nationwide in teen births. Dr. Dixon, like some other program directors, has decided to adjust to the new criteria; the funding is too crucial. Fact Forward will turn in its application this week.

"It's a real disservice to what we know works best in our state," Dr. Dixon said. "But if I can keep some of our programs from closing so that young people are still hearing about healthy relationships, something is better than nothing. I don't know if we'll be successful, but at least I'm going to try."

title: 8 Books to Help You Navigate Divorce
full_text_raw:
Whether you're contemplating a split, or in the process of one, these books can help.

There is no single way or universal timeline to go through a divorce. Some people spend years deciding, while others are thrust into it. But no matter the specifics, the process can bring up common challenges: grief, uncertainty, logistical stress and questions about what comes next.

"You'll need practical and therapeutic help," said Kathryn Smerling, a psychotherapist in New York City. "Books can be a good source of both."

While books aren't a replacement for a good lawyer, financial adviser, therapist or support system, Dr. Smerling added, they can fill in gaps and empower you throughout the process.

So we asked psychologists, therapists and other relationship experts to share the books they suggest to their clients, whether they're considering divorce, in the thick of the process or navigating the aftermath.

If you're contemplating the subject

Loving Bravely

by Alexandra H. Solomon

In this 2017 book, Dr. Solomon, a clinical psychologist and adjunct professor at Northwestern University, unpacks relational self-awareness, or the ability to understand one's own patterns, expectations and emotional responses within relationships. This, she argues, is foundational to better connection with others.

Using guided reflections that help readers explore their beliefs and habits, Dr. Solomon encourages people to take responsibility for what they bring to their relationships.

"It's written for people at the beginning of love, but I reach for it most often with people who are somewhere in the middle of losing it," said Moe Ari Brown, a relationship therapist in Maryland who has seen divorce discussions change course with the help of this book.

If you're unsure what to do

The D Word

by Kate Anthony

This candid, decision-focused guide, published in 2023, helps readers work through the often murky question of whether to stay or leave a marriage, Dr. Solomon explained in an interview. Ms. Anthony, a high-conflict divorce coach and host of "The Divorce Survival Guide Podcast," tackles common sources of uncertainty, like whether to make the marriage work for the kids and whether a relationship dynamic is abusive.

Dr. Solomon praised the book for its comprehensive approach, addressing the emotional, logistical, legal and financial aspects of the process. Ms. Anthony "has worked intensively with women through every stage of the divorce process from contemplation to completion," Dr. Solomon said. "She's so good at helping people address the uncomfortable but necessary realities of divorce."

If you want to end things 'well'

Conscious Uncoupling

by Katherine Woodward Thomas

Katherine Woodward Thomas, a marriage and family therapist, lays out a five-step framework for ending a relationship with mutual respect instead of resentment. The method begins with working through the difficult emotions of separation and ends with looking ahead to life after the relationship. Reframing this transition as an opportunity for growth instead of failure, Ms. Thomas breaks down common misconceptions around what it means to break up and guides readers forward in a more intentional, self-aware way.

Divorce is often shaped by an "inherently adversarial" legal system, and this 2015 book can help couples stay grounded in their values throughout the process, Dr. Solomon said. "While there is no such thing as an 'easy divorce,' the tools that Thomas teaches point readers toward a path that allows for endings to be done with care and integrity," she said.

If you have children

'The Parent's Guide to Divorce'

by Erica Komisar

Drawing on decades of clinical experience and research, Ms. Komisar, a psychoanalyst who specializes in parenting, offers a comprehensive map for navigating parenting issues like talking to your children about what's happening and maintaining routines. According to Dr. Solomon, the "practical and thoughtful" guide, published in March, is full of specific tools and scripts that parents can use to support their children through divorce.

The book also helps parents maintain a stable environment, as family dynamics change. Ms. Komisar "gives very good, very simple advice on how to get along with your ex-partner as a business relationship -- the business being your children," said Dr. Smerling, who also recommended the book.

If you need financial guidance

Divorce & Money

by Lina Guillen

Originally published in 1992, and now in its 14th edition, this book lays out the financial side of divorce in clear, practical terms. On top of covering topics like determining the value of assets and understanding support payments, this practical guide comes with worksheets, checklists and other resources to keep handy throughout the divorce process.

While the book doesn't touch on many of the emotional pains of divorce, Dr. Smerling emphasizes that sometimes "you need to get practical first, so that you can get on with your life and work on letting go."

If you Have a lot of feelings to process

Broken Open

by Elizabeth Lesser

Ms. Lesser, co-founder of the Omega Institute retreat center, blends memoir and practical guidance to explore how people weather major life disruptions, including divorce. Julie Newman, a couples counselor in New York, likes how Ms. Lesser "gently reframes pain not as something to rush through or fix, but as something that can lead to meaningful internal transformation."

Ms. Newman often recommends the book to clients in need of a compassionate, empowering example in the early stages of divorce. "Her writing is warm, hopeful and grounding, showing the reader exactly how much control they have," she said.

If it's happening later in life

Divorce After 50

by Janice Green

"Gray divorces," breakups among people 50 and older, are on the rise -- and they often come with unique challenges, Dr. Smerling explained. In addition to the emotional fallout of ending a long-term partnership, people splitting up in their 50s and beyond may also be navigating retirement planning and health care concerns with the complicated family dynamics.

"Divorce After 50," now in its sixth edition, covers this all and more, Dr. Smerling said, the reason she often recommends the book to her older clients. Plus, it includes "survival stories" to help readers see what this transition can look like realistically, she added.

If you're ready to move On

Breakup Bootcamp

by Amy Chan

Amy Chan, a relationship columnist and the creator of the Renew Breakup Bootcamp , filled this 2020 book with exercises, prompts and somatic practices for anyone feeling heartbroken and stuck after the end of a relationship. Mixing research, expert interviews and anecdotes, Ms. Chan outlines how heartbreak can be a catalyst for change, and she walks readers through how to identify and break destructive relationship habits.

While it's not specific to divorce, Ms. Newman recommended "Breakup Bootcamp" for anyone who's ready to reflect on patterns and to actively work toward healthier relationships. "Much of healing comes from turning insight into meaningful action, and this book does exactly that," Ms. Newman said.

title: The Use of Computational Thinking Skills, Difficulties, and Strategies of Introductory Programming Students Solving Bebras Tasks
inverted_pyramid_lead: Computational thinking (CT) is regarded as a fundamental skill set everyone should learn. Identifying when and how CT skills are used is challenging but important to inform interventions supporting their development. Previous research has examined how students and experts apply CT skills when solving introductory computational problems. However, the extent to which higher education students in introductory programming courses do so in depth is underexplored. We address this gap by examining how those students apply CT skills when solving computational problems, the difficulties they encounter, and the strategies they employ. We collected plans and solutions to Bebras tasks (short problems introducing CS concepts and considered effective for eliciting CT skills) in an introductory programming course for non-CS majors. We gathered 241 submissions from 58 students across five tasks, along with post-task comments and reflections on strategies. We analyzed the data using descriptive statistics, applied an existing coding scheme to identify CT skills, and conducted thematic analysis to identify difficulties and strategies. Submissions varied in structure and level of detail. The most prevalent CT skills were algorithmic thinking, abstraction, and decomposition, while evaluation and generalization appeared much less frequently. CT skill presence was positively associated with correct answers. Students faced challenges in four areas, including understanding the tasks and making a plan, and reported various problem-solving strategies. Consolidating and extending prior research on CT skills and problem solving, our findings show that students in introductory programming apply CT skills but can struggle to solve problems systematically and explain their reasoning. Furthermore, Bebras tasks create opportunities for this population to engage CT skills and could be used in future research.

title: Time-dependent structural equation modeling of fans' football fever using activity tracking data during the 2025 DFB Cup final
inverted_pyramid_lead: Football fans frequently exhibit pronounced emotional and physiological reactions during high-stakes matches. However, the temporal dynamics of this football fever are rarely modeled as a latent process. Using intensive longitudinal data from Arminia Bielefeld supporters who wore smartwatches during the 2025 German Football Association (DFB) Cup final, we investigate how football fever unfolds. The devices recorded heart rate, stress level, and related indicators in short intervals, allowing us to construct a latent variable for football fever and model its dynamics. We specify a time-dependent structural equation model with latent growth components and autoregressive effects to capture both overall trends and short-term carry-over effects in fans' physiological responses. Results are aggregated across multiple imputations of missing measurements. Model fit is evaluated using adjustments for the high data dimensionality. The results show that football fever follows a V-shaped trajectory: high at kick-off, followed by a steady decline until the renewed arousal in the second half, with substantial between-fan heterogeneity in both baseline level and temporal dynamics. Our findings demonstrate that football fever can be adequately represented as a latent variable using structural equation modeling and reflected by wearable technology data. This highlights the importance of accounting for temporal dependence when studying dynamic emotional phenomena, e. g., in sports spectatorship.

title: Early Prediction of Student Performance Using Bayesian Updating with Informative Priors Across Cohorts
inverted_pyramid_lead: Early identification of at risk students in higher education depends on predictive models that maintain accuracy across successive cohorts -- a requirement that single-cohort modeling approaches fail to meet. This study evaluates Bayesian updating with informative priors from a previous cohort to improve cross-cohort prediction robustness using digital trace data. We fit weekly Bayesian linear, logistic, and ordinal regression models with either uninformative default priors or informative priors derived from posterior distributions of a preceding cohort. Models were applied to six weekly self-regulated learning (SRL)-aligned engagement indicators from two consecutive cohorts of students in a blended first-year mathematics course (N1 = 307; N2 = 323). Outcomes were exam points, final grades, and a binary at risk indicator. The models were evaluated weekly based on accuracy, sensitivity, and RMSE. In the source cohort, performance was already substantial by week 6. In the target cohort, informative priors improved early classification: Logistic models with priors reduced misclassification by 22% and false negatives by 38% in week 3 relative to the uninformative default. Ordinal models with priors similarly showed the strongest improvements in early weeks, reducing misclassification by 42% in week 2 and reaching an accuracy of .77 by week 4. Linear models showed little benefit from prior information. These findings demonstrate that Bayesian updating is a viable method for improving early classification performance across cohorts, with gains concentrated in the early weeks of the semester when current-cohort data are scarce.

title: Concave Statistical Utility Maximization Bandits via Influence-Function Gradients
inverted_pyramid_lead: We study stochastic multi-armed bandits in which the objective is a statistical functional of the long-run reward distribution, rather than expected reward alone. Under mild continuity assumptions, we show that the infinite-horizon problem reduces to optimizing over stationary mixed policies: each weight vector \(w\) on the simplex induces a mixture law \(P^w\), and performance is measured by the concave utility \(U(w)=\mathfrak U(P^w)\). For differentiable statistical utilities, we use influence-function calculus to derive stochastic gradient estimators from bandit feedback. This leads to an entropic mirror-ascent algorithm on a truncated simplex, implemented through multiplicative-weights updates and plug-in estimates of the influence function. We establish regret bounds that separate the mirror-ascent optimization error from the bias caused by estimating the influence function. The framework is developed for general concave distributional utilities and illustrated through variance and Wasserstein objectives, with numerical experiments comparing exact and plug-in influence-function implementations.

title: Informed Asymmetric Dirichlet Priors for Multivariate Bernoulli Mixture Models
inverted_pyramid_lead: Clustering multivariate binary data is of interest in many scientific fields, including ecology, biomedicine, and social policy. Beyond heuristic clustering algorithms, such data can be modelled using multivariate Bernoulli mixture models. Many Bayesian implementations of these models involve a trade-off between computational efficiency and full posterior inference. We propose instead a Bayesian approach able to provide both aspects. The method fixes the total number of components to a large value and employs an asymmetric Dirichlet prior on the mixture weights. The asymmetric Dirichlet hyperparameters are elicited using the popular Penalized Complexity prior framework, which provides an intuitive way for users to inform the induced distribution of the number of clusters. An efficient MCMC algorithm is then developed to fit the model. Simulations and real-world applications demonstrate that the method is competitive with existing alternatives and can outperform them in certain settings. The proposal is illustrated using an ecological dataset about presence-absence of species across multiple sites, where cluster-specific parameters are modelled on the basis of environmental conditions. Overall, the proposed method provides a computationally efficient, fully Bayesian, and interpretable framework for clustering multivariate binary data, with potential applications across diverse scientific domains.

title: A Non-stationary, Amortized, Transfer Learning Approach for Modeling Italian Air Quality
inverted_pyramid_lead: Air quality monitoring in Italy relies on sparse, irregular, ground-based stations that provide high-quality but incomplete measurements of pollution. Chemical transport models (CTMs) offer full spatial and temporal coverage but smooth over local variability. We develop a spatial transfer-learning framework that integrates these two data sources to produce daily, fine-grid predictions of nitrogen dioxide (NO$_2$) concentrations across Italy for 2023, with uncertainty quantification. The resulting maps provide a resource for decision making in downstream applications such as epidemiology and environmental policy. Our approach builds on the geostatistical LatticeKrig framework, which uses compactly supported basis functions and coefficients governed by a sparse precision matrix. We learn a nonstationary, anisotropic correlation structure from the gridded CTM outputs using an image-to-image neural architecture that estimates millions of spatially varying parameters in a matter of seconds. The basis-function representation enables this covariance structure to be transferred to the point-level station data and projected onto a finer prediction grid, a key extension for handling the change of support between data sources. A likelihood-based refinement step then adjusts the correlation range to recover fine-scale variability smoothed out by the gridded data. The proposed methodology results in a flexible, non-stationary, and anisotropic representation of the spatial process, better accommodating the complex geography of Italy. Performance is assessed through experiments on both gridded CTM outputs and point-level station measurements, demonstrating improvements over the stationary formulation.

title: A Quasi-Regression Method for the Mediation Analysis of Zero-Inflated Single-Cell Data
inverted_pyramid_lead: Recent advances in single-cell technologies have advanced our understanding of gene regulation and cellular heterogeneity at single-cell resolution. Single-cell data contain both gene expression levels and the proportion of expressing cells, which makes them structurally different from bulk data. Currently, methodological work on causal mediation analysis for single-cell data remains limited and often requires specific distributional assumptions. To address this challenge, we present QuasiMed, a mediation framework specialized for single-cell data. Our proposed method comprises three steps, including (i) screening mediator candidates through penalized regression and marginal models (similar to sure independence screening), (ii) estimation of indirect effects through the average expression and the proportion of expressing cells, (iii) and hypothesis testing with multiplicity control. The key benefit of QuasiMed is that it specifies only the mean functions of the mediation models through a quasi-regression framework, thereby relaxing strict distributional assumptions. The method performance was evaluated through the real-data-inspired simulations, and demonstrated high power, false discovery rate control, and computational efficiency. Lastly, we applied QuasiMed to ROSMAP single-cell data to illustrate its potential to identify mediating causal pathways. R package is freely available on GitHub repository at https://github.com/sjahnn/QuasiMed.

title: On Data Thinning for Model Validation in Small Area Estimation
inverted_pyramid_lead: Small area estimation produces estimates of population parameters for geographic and demographic subgroups with limited sample sizes. Such estimates are critical for policy decisions, yet principled validation of these models remains a challenge. Unlike conventional predictive settings, validation data are rarely available. Data thinning splits a single observation into independent training and test components. It enables out-of-sample validation using only the area-level summary statistics routinely available, requiring only their Gaussianity and known sampling variances. However, the properties of thinning-based model comparison have not been formally studied. In this paper, we develop these properties. We construct an unbiased estimator of thinned-data mean squared error and show that it differs systematically from its full-data counterpart; for the standard Fay-Herriot model, the gap admits a closed-form expression that depends on the candidate model's shrinkage behavior. We further show that the estimator variance increases sharply as the training fraction approaches one, producing a bias-variance tradeoff with no universally optimal thinning parameter. Practical recommendations balancing these forces are informed by theory and verified empirically. Design-based simulations using American Community Survey microdata show that the recommended data thinning approach is competitive with information-criterion and simulation-based methods, and substantially more stable across heterogeneous sampling designs.

inverted_pyramid_lead: Spousal bereavement severely deteriorates mental health. While palliative care benefits dying patients, its "stress-buffering" effect on survivors' depression remains empirically elusive due to acute small-$N$ constraints in longitudinal dyadic data. This study evaluates the causal impact of palliative care on bereaved spouses while introducing Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) to resolve sample attrition in quasi-experimental designs. Using SHARE panel data, we augment the sparse treated cohort via a Conditional Tabular GAN, anchoring synthetic trajectories to empirical baseline constraints to preserve causal pathways. A Matched Difference-in-Differences estimator applied to the high-fidelity augmented dataset evaluates the treatment effect. Results reveal a non-linear psychological response. Palliative care initially exacerbates acute depressive symptoms at the time of loss ($β_0 = 0.218,\ p < 0.05$), reflecting the intense emotional confrontation of the intervention. However, a sustained stress-buffering effect emerges in subsequent periods ($β_2 = -0.763,\ p < 0.01$), indicating an accelerated long-term recovery compared to standard care. Estimates are highly robust to unobserved confounding (Oster's $δ> 1$). Substantively, we advocate for reconceptualizing end-of-life care as a dyadic public health intervention. Methodologically, we establish SDG as a robust analytical tool capable of powering fragile quasi-experiments in longitudinal social surveys.

title: How Proxy Race Distorts Regression-Based Fairness Audits
inverted_pyramid_lead: Proxy-based race inference is increasingly used to conduct fairness assessments when protected-class data are unavailable or legally restricted -- most prominently in U.S. fair-lending enforcement, and now explicitly contemplated in emerging insurance regulation, including Colorado's draft SB21-169 testing framework and New York's Insurance Circular Letter No. 7. Despite this growing regulatory relevance, little is known about how standard regression-based discrimination analyses behave when race is measured with error through proxies such as Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) or Bayesian Improved First Name and Surname Geocoding (BIFSG). This paper studies the consequences of using proxy-imputed race as a categorical regressor in regression-based fairness assessments. Treating proxy race as a categorical covariate subject to misclassification, we show that proxy-based coefficients become weighted mixtures of true group effects, systematically shrinking estimated disparities toward the majority group -- even when overall classification accuracy is high. Empirically, using a linked North Carolina voter-insurance dataset with self-reported race and ZIP-level auto insurance premiums, we demonstrate two mechanisms through which it distorts inference: (i) the intrinsic mixing of group effects implied by misclassification, and (ii) structured errors that vary with ZIP-level racial composition and socioeconomic conditions and remain correlated with pricing residuals after controls. As a result, regression-based disparity estimates can be attenuated or amplified relative to analogous analyses based on self-reported race. Our findings caution against treating proxy race as a plug-in substitute in regulatory testing and highlight design implications for proxy-based audit frameworks in insurance and other high-stakes domains.

title: Republican blocks bill to halt retrofit of Qatari-gifted Air Force One
full_text_raw:
President Donald Trump exits the new Air Force One, a plane gifted by Qatar, in Belle Fourche-Cheyenne Valleys, South Dakota, on July 3. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

A Republican senator blocked a Democratic bill Wednesday that would bar the Defense Department from spending more money to retrofit a luxury jet given to the United States by the government of Qatar.

President Donald Trump ordered the plane -- a Boeing 747-800 worth about $400 million -- and had it modified to serve as the new Air Force One despite ethical and national security concerns. He started flying on it this month, using it to travel to the NATO summit in Turkey, but he left Ankara on an older jet.

title: A Statistically Reliable Optimization Framework for Bandit Experiments in Scientific Discovery
inverted_pyramid_lead: Scientific experimentation is largely driven by statistical hypothesis testing to determine significant differences in interventions. Traditionally, experimenters allocate samples uniformly between each intervention. However, such an approach may lead to suboptimal outcomes - multi-armed bandits (MABs) addresses this problem by allocating samples adaptively to maximize outcomes. Yet, two challenges have hindered the use of MABs in scientific domains. First, common hypothesis tests (e.g., $t$-tests) become invalid under adaptive sampling without correction, leading to inflated type~I and type~II errors. This is an understudied problem, and prior solutions suffer from issues such as low statistical power which prevent adoption in many practical settings. Second, practitioners must explicitly balance cumulative reward with statistical efficiency, yet no general methodology exists to quantify this trade-off across algorithms. In this paper, we study assumption modification and critical region correction approaches for hypothesis testing that enable common tests to be applied to adaptively collected data. We provide heuristic justification for its power efficiency and show in simulation that it achieves higher power than existing approaches. Further, we derive a theoretically and practically motivated objective function for adaptive experiment evaluation, which we integrate into a unified experimental framework. Our framework asks experimenters to specify an experiment extension cost for their problem, and based on that enables our proposed optimization procedure to select the bandit algorithm that best balances reward and power in their setting. We show that our approach enables practitioners to improve outcomes with only slightly more steps than uniform randomization, while retaining statistical validity.

title: The Uncertain Policy Price of Scaling Direct Air Capture
inverted_pyramid_lead: Direct air carbon capture and storage (DACCS) is a promising CO2 removal technology, but its deployment at scale remains speculative. Yet, its technological, economic, and policy-related uncertainties have often been overlooked in mitigation pathways. This paper conducts the first uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis of DACCS on technological, market, financial and public support drivers, using a detailed-process Integrated Assessment Model and newly developed sensitivity algorithms. We find that DACCS deployment exhibits a fat-tailed distribution: most scenarios show modest technology uptake, but there is a small but non-zero probability (4-6%) of achieving gigaton-scale removals by mid-century. Scaling DACCS to gigaton levels requires subsidies that always exceed 200-330 USD/tCO2 and are sustained for decades, resulting in a public support programme of 900-3000 USD Billions. Such an effort pays back by mid-century, but only if accompanied by strong emission reduction policies. These findings highlight the critical role of climate policies in enabling a robust and economically sustainable CO2 removal strategy.
