WEDNESDAY PUZZLE -- It's hard to describe Wednesday crosswords. I think of them as the "You had to be there" puzzles of the solving week. They sometimes defy puzzle logic or pull off a whip-smart visual trick. Others contain rebus elements, and some are just plain witty.

I'd describe Rebecca Goldstein as something of a Wednesday whisperer, as crosswords go. It's not that she constructs Wednesday puzzles exclusively -- she has just four under her belt, in fact -- but that she knows how to keep us guessing, be it with clever sleights of word or visual magic. Today's crossword theme was another delight to uncover. There's a rebus square, a visual joke and a truly elegant design choice. Considering the puzzle's subject, that all seems more than, ahem, fair.

Today's Theme

Circled squares indicate themed fill, so that's probably where we'll find 38D's [Carnival game depicted in this puzzle]. Most of these circles contain standard letters: [Many a tech alum: Abbr.] at 49A is an ENGR -- a baffling shortening of "engineer," incidentally -- which gives us a circled R. The [Toxin in castor beans] at 40A is RICIN, which yields an I. Moving on from left to right, we've got an N from TALON (34A), a G from SINGH (41A) and ... something that doesn't quite fit at 52A and 23D.

The answer to [Risqué game that teenagers might give a whirl?] should be SPIN THE BOTTLE, but BOTTLE is too long a word for the entry spaces. 52A's [Pop top?] should be BOTTLE CAP, but we end up with the same issue. The logical conclusion: We're looking at a rebus square.

For the purposes of the Times Crossword we define rebuses simply as "crossword elements where solvers are asked to write multiple letters in the same square." In this case, those letters form the word BOTTLE. If we treat the square as the object itself, then the letters R, I, N and G arcing toward it amount to a RING TOSS (38D)!

Would it be a carnival game without a high-up [Prize dangling from a 38-Down booth] to be won? The biggest PLUSH TOY at 11A can be yours if you land the toss.

And while the connection probably wasn't intentional, I can't resist pointing out that the phrases at 17A and 60A, STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK, could serve as answers to the clue [Hawk's hook] -- as in, phrases used by carnival barkers hawking their games to hook players in. Eh?

Tricky Clues

19A. The question mark at the end of [Seller's bottom lines, for short?] indicates a witty twist, likely in the literal interpretation of a figure of speech. "Bottom lines" refers to a product's bar code, also known as U.P.C.

One of my favorite genres of crossword theme is the representation of an object or game. title: Tiny Love Stories: 'A Full, Hiccuping Meltdown Over Nothing'
full_text_raw:
Modern Love in miniature, featuring reader-submitted stories of no more than 100 words.

My daughter's birthday falls three days after my late brother's. Every July, while I hang lanterns and fill gift bags, grief flashes through me. My daughter is 6 and doesn't know she should have an Uncle Jay. He was nine years my junior, a boy I mothered, adored and eventually couldn't save from untreated schizophrenia and suicide. I thought telling her about him would only pass down pain. But grief is not the whole story of his life, or our bond. Soon, I will tell my daughter about my brother, confident that I'll also be able to pass down love. -- Ashley Womble

'Steady as the Sun'

I called my high school friends Anvi and Ashwini in a full, hiccuping meltdown over nothing, a PMS spiral that felt stupidly enormous. Now roommates, both happened to be working from home. Twenty minutes later, they were at my door. No questions, just action: They pulled me out of bed, put shoes on my feet and drove me to get ice cream. We relaxed in the grass in Dolores Park, sharing two pints, watching San Francisco buzz around us. They sat beside me, steady as the sun above, reminding me, without saying a word, that I was never alone. -- Kaanthi Pandhigunta

He Saw Me Before I Could

Fifth grade, hazel eyes, curly hair, honey-toned skin. I was infatuated with him, already tailoring plans for us to fall in love. I confessed my feelings. He gently replied, "Tiff, you're like my boy; you don't really see me that way, do you?" Years passed, his question lingering in my mind. Then one day, walking along the boardwalk, hand in hand with my girlfriend, I saw him again. I smiled, introducing them. His hazel eyes brightened with happiness when he saw that I had found myself and my sexual identity, something he seemed to understand long before I ever could. -- Tiffany Pippins

Never Too Old to Be Mothered

I thought I wanted to be alone with my husband after my son was born, but then my mother brought me breakfast in bed -- banana pancakes, right off the stove, with warmed syrup on the side. She cut them into pieces so I could eat with one hand while holding the baby. They tasted so good that I cried. Today we were with my son at the park. As I chased him with his hat, my mother asked, "Did you get sunscreen on?" "Yes, just need to get his legs," I said. "Not him," she replied, smiling. "You!" -- Virginia Craig

title: Monkeys Understand Shapes in Almost the Same Way as Humans
full_text_raw:
Our geometric intuition, long considered something that sets us apart, seems to be shared with other primates.

You (probably) won't find a monkey in a geometry class, but it looks like our fellow primates can swing the basics.

Just like people, monkeys seem to grasp the abstract qualities of geometric shapes, such as whether they are symmetrical, have parallel sides or contain right angles, according to a new study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. This ability allows the monkeys -- and us -- to understand when two shapes are the same, even when they've been rotated or resized.

This finding challenges a long-held notion that humans' geometric abilities are part of what makes our brains one of a kind. "Our hypothesis was that humans are not that unique," in possessing this mathematical understanding, said Jialin Li, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University and the lead author of the study.

In their experiment, Ms. Li and her colleagues decided to give monkeys (a total of eight rhesus macaques and olive baboons), preschoolers and adult humans with different education levels the same geometric task. That way, if humans truly had an innate advantage, it would show up when comparing the young children and the monkeys. And if the advantage was learned, it might show up when comparing the humans who had different levels of schooling.

It was a challenge to find a task simple enough that even preschool-aged children and monkeys could reasonably complete it, but the team eventually decided to have all the study participants do a matching task. All were shown a shape with a specific size and geometric form on a screen. Then they were asked to pick that same shape out of a group of others.

"By manipulating the similarity of the shapes, we were able to look at what kinds of rules they're using," said Jessica Cantlon, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University whose lab conducted the study.

title: German conservatives to appoint Merz confidant to lead faction after surrogacy row
full_text_raw:
BERLIN, July 22 (Reuters) - Germany's ruling conservatives will appoint a close ally of Chancellor Friedrich Merz as their new parliamentary faction chief, officials said on Wednesday, after the abrupt exit of party heavyweight Jens Spahn in a row over a surrogacy baby.

Thorsten Frei, the head of Merz's chancellery, will replace Spahn, two conservative party sources and a member of the Social Democrats both told Reuters, confirming an earlier media report by the Bild newspaper.

A government spokesperson declined to comment on Frei's appointment.

Spahn resigned on Saturday after having a baby born to a ⁠surrogate mother in the United States, a move at odds with his own party's opposition to surrogacy. Spahn had at one time been seen as a potential challenger to Merz.

Frei, a longtime Merz confidant, has been responsible for coordinating government business from the chancellery, a role that has drawn scrutiny during the coalition's rocky first year.

German media have reported criticism within the ruling parties -- at a time of low public approval for Merz and his government -- that coordination between the ⁠chancellery, ministries, parliamentary groups and coalition partners has often been poor.

Frei's supporters see him as better suited to the parliamentary post, saying he has strong backing in the faction and is well connected there. Discussions regarding who will succeed Frei as head of the chancellery ⁠are continuing, officials said.

Spahn, 46, the parliamentary leader of Merz's Christian Democratic Union and its sister Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), drew heavy criticism after news emerged that he had become a ⁠parent with his husband through the surrogate mother.

Surrogacy is prohibited in Germany, although it is not illegal to bring up a child born of a surrogate mother ⁠outside Germany. The CDU voted to uphold the ban on surrogacy inside Germany at its party conference in February.

title: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests
full_text_raw:
Finding widens selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable

Mars once had rivers of magma bubbling beneath its crust, new research suggests. The surprise find makes it more probable that Mars could have supported life and widens the selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable.

Researchers at the University of Oxford studied data gathered by Nasa's Insight Lander, which recorded seismic waves caused by meteorite impacts and Martian quakes. They used the seismic data to analyse a mysterious boundary 15 miles (24km) below the surface of Mars. Their findings, published in Nature Astronomy, showed that the most likely cause for this boundary was molten rock pooling deep underground and stretching sideways for hundreds or even thousands of miles.

Scientists had previously assumed that the volcanoes on Mars were underlain by simple isolated magma chambers, but the new finding suggests a more complex interconnected plumbing system. Such a system would have the potential to make a chemically complex crust, capable of recycling elements and supporting the kind of processes needed to generate an atmosphere and ocean on the surface.

This would also help to regulate the climate - previously thought only to be possible on planets with plate tectonics. And that means rocky planets previously dismissed as uninhabitable because of their lack of plate tectonics now deserve a second look.

title: Should Queer Parents Have Zingers Ready for Boneheaded Questions?
full_text_raw:
Two moms who are tired of intrusive comments about sperm donation and "mom names" want quippy comebacks they can roll out as needed. Is there a better way?

My wife and I are the queer mothers of a baby. We would like some zingers to use for the surprising number of people who say stupid things to us -- for instance, "What are your mom names?" (We're both Mom, duh!) We are friends with our sperm donor, and sometimes people refer to him as our baby's "dad," which is also annoying. And many women feel the need to tell us that they would never allow their boyfriends to donate sperm. (Got it! We won't ask for any.) I wish that these things didn't annoy us, but they do. And we'd like to experiment with comebacks. What have you got?

MOM

Congratulations on the baby! Over my long gay life, I have known dozens of gay and lesbian parents, and in every case, their children used different names for each parent to distinguish between them: Mom and Mama, Daddy and Pop, and my favorite, Mommy and Pom-Pom. Your baby may not be talking yet, but when that day comes, I doubt your child will use the same name for the two most important people in his or her life. Besides, it's such an innocuous question: Why clap back?

Don't misunderstand me: You have no responsibility to educate other people about the mechanics of your family life. And I understand that muddled vocabularies ("dad" versus "donor") and unsolicited feedback about family planning might get annoying. But these people wouldn't know anything about your sperm donor if you hadn't told them.

My feeling is that zingers are not the solution here. (I used to think they were!) But it so often feels as if there are only two camps these days: steadfast allies and sworn enemies. Slapping down nice people for clueless errors may look like fun, but there is often a bitter aftertaste, in my experience. Better to help people who are trying to understand and ignore the rest. In the absence of ill will, just focus on your wonderful family.

Speechless at a Relative's Generosity

My husband and I are well off. We don't have children, and we like to use our money to improve the lives of others. We were close with my late cousin's son when he was a young child. He is now in his late 20s. When he graduated from college, we offered to help him pay off some of his substantial student loan debt. Initially, he refused, saying he didn't need any help. But when he and his wife decided to buy a home, he changed his mind. So, for three years, we have been paying off one of his loans directly. But he's never once thanked us! We think he must be ashamed of accepting our help. We would like to talk to him about this and offer to stop paying if that would make him feel better. We are not happy that our gift has never been acknowledged. Thoughts?

title: Laptopitis: the hidden health cost of working from home
full_text_raw:
Working from home is fueling back, neck and shoulder pain as poor laptop setups, couch-based work and too little movement take a cumulative toll; what can be done to prevent this from becoming chronic pain?

Working from home started as a dream: no traffic jams, no distracting hallway chatter, fresh coffee from your own kitchen and the ability to throw a load of laundry into the washing machine between Zoom meetings. However, after a few years of hybrid work, it turns out this routine is not doing the body any favors.

Laptopitis is the unofficial term gaining traction in the media to describe this phenomenon. It refers to the collective aches and injuries caused by prolonged laptop use: neck pain, lower back pain, shoulder tension, wrist strain and occasional headaches and muscle fatigue.

Medical professionals use formal terms such as Repetitive Strain Injuries (RSI) and Work-related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WMSDs). The truth is, dining tables, couches and laptops resting on laps were never engineered for working eight to ten hours straight in front of a screen.

Data gathered in recent years by international health organizations reveals the true scale of the issue: over 65% of remote employees report developing new musculoskeletal pain or experiencing worsening symptoms since transitioning to hybrid work. The lack of ergonomic workstations serves as a primary risk factor, significantly increasing physical strain.

To avoid letting temporary aches turn into permanent damage, here are the most common remote-work mistakes and straightforward ways to fix them:

Before you start working: Gentle mobility exercises that engage the joints and prevent stiffness are essential preparation for hours of little active movement. It is best to start with head and neck rolls. Tilt your head toward your shoulder for a gentle stretch, then move on to rolling your shoulders forward and backward, rounding your back and bringing your shoulder blades together.

Next, stand firmly next to a desk or kitchen counter, place your hands down for support and perform wide pelvic circles to loosen the lower back joints. This movement stimulates joint fluids, boosts circulation and perfectly prepares the musculoskeletal system for prolonged sitting.

The couch is not an office: Slouching on a soft surface without lower back support creates cumulative stress on the spine and neck muscles. When sitting correctly, the upper body's center of gravity rests directly over the pelvis and thighs, allowing a natural, straight alignment for the lower back, neck and head.

Conversely, sinking into an overly soft armchair causes the pelvis to tilt backward and round out. This compromised posture triggers a chain reaction: the upper back and neck bend forward, the head thrusts outward and the shoulders round, a combination that invites long-term musculoskeletal issues.

Therefore, if a dedicated home office is unavailable, working at a sturdy table with a standard dining chair is far better than spending hours with a laptop on your lap.

Smart computing practices: Placing a laptop directly on your lap is a surefire recipe for pain: the screen sits too low, forcing the neck to stay bent forward for hours. Meanwhile, hovering your mouse hand in the air without proper support overworks the wrist muscles. Simple solutions like a laptop stand, an external keyboard and a mouse will completely transform your posture and relieve immense pressure from your neck and shoulders.

Ergonomically adjusting the workspace, ensuring the right proportion between chair and desk height, keeps the head straight and eye level right at the top of the screen without forcing a neck tilt. Choose a chair that provides solid lower back support, make sure your feet rest flat on the floor or a footrest and keep your knees at or slightly below hip level. If the screen remains too low, use an adjustable monitor or prop it up. Incorporating a sit-stand desk allows for alternating positions throughout the day. It is also crucial to pause every 30 to 45 minutes to stand up, walk around and do light stretches to prevent the body from locking into a single position.

Remote work has eliminated the incidental movement built into office life: walking from the car, moving between offices or stepping out for lunch. When the distance between your bed, desk and refrigerator is just five steps, it helps to artificially create short walks throughout the day. Try a brief walk outside before starting the day or take phone calls while standing up. The goal is to build movement directly into the workday routine, rather than treating it as an afterthought when the pain has already started.

title: NHS trust investigated for corporate manslaughter after Nottingham attacks
full_text_raw:
Police open investigation into Nottinghamshire service that treated Valdo Calocane, who killed three people in 2023

The NHS trust which treated the triple killer Valdo Calocane in the years before the Nottingham attacks is being investigated by police for corporate manslaughter.

Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia, was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after he fatally stabbed the 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, and the 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, on 13 June 2023.

A public inquiryinto the events leading up to the 2023 attacks heard how the Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation trust had sectioned Calocane four times between 2020 and 2022.

Evidence given to the inquiry detailed a string of violent incidents that Calocane had committed in the years before the Nottingham attacks and his repeated refusal to take medication. During his second hospital admission, the inquiry heard how a doctor warned Calocane could "end up killing someone".

Despite this, Calocane was discharged from mental health services in September 2022 because he had failed to attend his appointments and healthcare workers "couldn't find him".

Northumbria police confirmed they were carrying out the criminal inquiry on behalf of the Nottinghamshire force. The NHS trust said it was cooperating with the investigation, which could result in substantial fines and changes to its leadership.

Charges of corporate manslaughter, a serious criminal offence, can only apply to certain organisations, including public bodies such as local authorities and NHS trusts, to ensure they can "be held properly accountable for very serious failings resulting in death", according the Crown Prosecution Service.

The public inquiry into the attacks, which is expected to publish its findings next year, heard that there had been a warrant out for Calocane's arrest at the time of the Nottingham attacks after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer.

Nottinghamshire and Leicestershire police forces apologised during the inquiry for failing to act on the warrant, which according to the Times is why the Northumbria force will carry out the investigation into the NHS trust.

The Nottingham trust has been under close scrutiny since the 2023 attacks. A 2026 report by the Care Quality Commission said it needed to make significant improvements.

A trust spokesperson said: "Northumbria police, acting on behalf of Nottinghamshire police, have begun an investigation into matters relating to the care and treatment of Valdo Calocane.

"We know how important the independent inquiry and police investigation are for the affected families, the survivors and our local communities.

"We will, of course, be cooperating fully with Northumbria police, as we have with the statutory inquiry."

A spokesperson for force said: "Our thoughts are very much with the victims, their families and all those impacted by the tragic events in Nottingham in June 2023.

"We are in contact with the victims' families and survivors and are committed to supporting them throughout this process."

title: Why hot weather and chocolate can go together

title: How to turn beetroot leaves into a classic south Indian vegetable dish - recipe | Waste not
full_text_raw:
Simple spices, fresh coconut and a handful of lentils or nuts is enough to transform leaves normally destined for the compost

Poriyal is south India's version of sauteed spiced vegetables, and it can be made with just about any vegetable, though green beans or a leafy green such as spinach, moringa or amaranth are most commonly used. The vegetables are fried with onions and spices, a spoon of urad dal is added for texture (if you don't have urad dal, a handful of cashews makes a delicious alternative), and it's finished with a grating of fresh coconut. This fragrant, spicy and flavoursome side dish also works brilliantly with the earthy flavour of beetroot leaves, and I like to serve it with boiled beetroot, yoghurt, chapatis or/and rice.

Beetroot leaf poriyal, or south Indian-style sauteed greens

I've adapted this recipe from the incredible Maunika Gowardhan, author of Curry, one of the New York Times best cookbooks of 2025. She writes: "The key to cooking spinach poriyal is to let the greens cook without any water. As they wilt and release their moisture, they begin to take on the flavour of the spices." Beetroot leaves, which feature in a lot of Indian recipes, cook just like spinach leaves, and I like to use the stalks, too, not least because they impart a lovely red colour to the dish. It's best to add them with the onions to make sure they cook through. I love the addition of freshly grated coconut at the end, and bought one especially; it is optional, however, and can be replaced with rehydrated desiccated coconut.

Serves 2-4 as a side dish

1 bunch beetroot leaves (roughly 160g), or another leafy green (spinach, kale, cabbage)

1½ tbsp neutral oil, or ghee

1 tsp black (or white/yellow) mustard seeds

1 dried red chilli (optional)

6-10 fresh curry leaves, or to taste

2 tsp urid dal, or 1 small handful crushed cashews

1 small onion, peeled and roughly chopped

¼-½ tsp chilli powder

35g freshly grated coconut, or 10g desiccated coconut, pre-soaked in a little warm water for 10 minutes

1 handful fresh coriander, chopped from stem to leaf

To serve (all optional)

Boiled beetroot, cut into wedges

Yoghurt

Chapatis or/and rice

Wash the bunch of beetroot leaves and strip the leaves off the stalks. Shred the leaves and cut the stalks into 1cm lengths.

Put a wok or frying pan on a medium heat, add the oil or ghee and, once it's hot, stir in the mustard seeds and optional dried chilli. When the seeds start to pop, add a few curry leaves and the urad dal or a handful of crushed cashews, then add the chopped onion, beetroot stems and chilli powder to taste. Saute, stirring, for five minutes, or until translucent, then add the leaves and saute until wilted. Season to taste, then stir in the freshly grated coconut with a few more curry leaves and a handful of chopped coriander, and serve.

title: NYT Crossword Answers for July 23, 2026
full_text_raw:
Damon Gulczynski puzzles over the mysteries of the universe.

THURSDAY PUZZLE -- A warm welcome back to Damon Gulczynski, who makes his 49th appearance in the New York Times Crossword today. While his puzzles have run on every day of the week, he's really in the pocket on the back half. Some of Mr. Gulczynski's wily Thursday themes have included phonetic mistranslations, in-grid punctuation and clues written with letter substitution, and he has uncorked another winner today. That's not meant to intimidate newer Thursday solvers; today's puzzle hides its trick cleverly, but fairly. And, as always, the Wordplay column and its friendly commentariat are here to help. Onward!

Today's Theme

You would be forgiven if you thought that today's puzzle was a rebus crossword, a grid with squares that contain multiple letters. After all, this puzzle has several answers that are evidently correct, but don't fit in the grid -- a telltale sign of a shove-'em-in rebus. Picking up on those signals is an excellent solving instinct, and one that will serve you well for sussing out the tricks of late-week puzzles. But when you anticipate a Thursday puzzle's zig, sometimes it zags. There are no squares that require multiple letters in today's puzzle. In fact, all of the letters are there -- some are just hidden.

At 1-Across, [More than just a disapproving look], describes a "death stare." But only DEATH STAR, the planet-destroying space station from "Star Wars," fits. If you investigate the crossing entry where the E should be, at 14-Down, you'll find that it also has the letter unaccounted for. [Champion, as a cause] should be "espouse," but only SPOUSE fits. The E isn't missing; it's represented by the black square at the intersection of DEATH STAR(E) and (E)SPOUSE.

The same trick appears right next door, at 10-Across. [Scruff of the neck] describes "nape," but only APE fits. The hidden letter is intersected by 15-Down, which is clued with [Budding] to mean "nascent," but only ASCENT works. This time, it's the letter N that's represented by the black square where (N)APE and (N)ASCENT meet.

Why hide these letters in black squares, and how many can you expect to find in the puzzle? The theme revealer's clue provides the key. At 62-Across, [Proposed cosmological phenomenon that could make up 70% of the universe -- and six squares in this puzzle's grid?] solves to DARK ENERGY. There are six dark squares in this puzzle that represent a letter. When read from top to bottom, those hidden letters spell "energy." Note that every entry with a hidden letter is an acceptable word whether the letter is included or not: "Nape" and APE are both valid entries, as are "nascent" and ASCENT. See if you can discover the remaining dark squares, or hit the links below to have the mysteries of the universe revealed.

Tricky Clues

16A. You didn't hear this from me, but ["The Devil's radio"] is another way to describe IDLE GOSSIP. George Harrison, no stranger to the rumor mill, released a song titled "Devil's Radio" in 1987. It was reportedly inspired by a church billboard he had seen that read, "Gossip: The Devil's Radio ... Don't Be a Broadcaster."

19A. [What a pointless game has?] plays with the multiple meanings of "pointless." It's not about a nonsensical game, but rather one with NO SCORE. Sports are a rich vein of coinages and turns of phrase that mean "zero." Other than "goose egg," soccer often also uses "nil" for zero, and shutouts are referred to as "clean sheets." In tennis, "love" means zero, and shutouts are called "bagels."

43A. The [Desert for which an African country is named] is the NAMIB Desert, which stretches along the continent's southwestern coast from Angola to South Africa, though a vast majority of it lies in Namibia, the country in question. The Namib is mostly uninhabited and has a fitting etymology: Its name comes from the Nama language and means "an area where there is nothing."

53A. There's a lot going on in the clue [Wholly, but not holey or holy, e.g.: Abbr.]. To make it more digestible, I set aside the "Abbr." and focus on the remainder. While they're all homophones, "holey" and "holy" are adjectives and only "wholly" is an adverb. The word "adverb" can be abbreviated as ADV.

2D. This one may trip up solvers unfamiliar with American football. The [Word after tight or defensive] is END; tight end and defensive end are both positions in the sport. The Cleveland Browns trading Myles Garrett, the best defensive end in the N.F.L., to the Los Angeles Rams was one of the biggest stories this off-season. Still, it didn't generate the headlines that the off-season activities of a certain tight end did.

WEDNESDAY PUZZLE -- It's hard to describe Wednesday crosswords. I think of them as the "You had to be there" puzzles of the solving week. They sometimes defy puzzle logic or pull off a whip-smart visual trick. Others contain rebus elements, and some are just plain witty.

I'd describe Rebecca Goldstein as something of a Wednesday whisperer, as crosswords go. It's not that she constructs Wednesday puzzles exclusively -- she has just four under her belt, in fact -- but that she knows how to keep us guessing, be it with clever sleights of word or visual magic. Today's crossword theme was another delight to uncover. There's a rebus square, a visual joke and a truly elegant design choice. Considering the puzzle's subject, that all seems more than, ahem, fair.

Today's Theme

Circled squares indicate themed fill, so that's probably where we'll find 38D's [Carnival game depicted in this puzzle]. Most of these circles contain standard letters: [Many a tech alum: Abbr.] at 49A is an ENGR -- a baffling shortening of "engineer," incidentally -- which gives us a circled R. The [Toxin in castor beans] at 40A is RICIN, which yields an I. Moving on from left to right, we've got an N from TALON (34A), a G from SINGH (41A) and ... something that doesn't quite fit at 52A and 23D.

The answer to [Risqué game that teenagers might give a whirl?] should be SPIN THE BOTTLE, but BOTTLE is too long a word for the entry spaces. 52A's [Pop top?] should be BOTTLE CAP, but we end up with the same issue. The logical conclusion: We're looking at a rebus square.

For the purposes of the Times Crossword we define rebuses simply as "crossword elements where solvers are asked to write multiple letters in the same square." In this case, those letters form the word BOTTLE. If we treat the square as the object itself, then the letters R, I, N and G arcing toward it amount to a RING TOSS (38D)!

Would it be a carnival game without a high-up [Prize dangling from a 38-Down booth] to be won? The biggest PLUSH TOY at 11A can be yours if you land the toss.

And while the connection probably wasn't intentional, I can't resist pointing out that the phrases at 17A and 60A, STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK, could serve as answers to the clue [Hawk's hook] -- as in, phrases used by carnival barkers hawking their games to hook players in. Eh?

Tricky Clues

14A. Blame the Canadian in me for defaulting to "Sorry!" as the [Cry after an accident] instead of OOPSY.

19A. The question mark at the end of [Seller's bottom lines, for short?] indicates a witty twist, likely in the literal interpretation of a figure of speech. "Bottom lines" refers to a product's bar code, also known as U.P.C.

43A. A question mark may also be a reminder to read the clue twice. It's [Get in bad with?], not "get in bed with." The answer is ABET.

1D. You don't need to get your hands grimy to [Spread dirt] in this sense, i.e., to GOSSIP.

40D. Tense is one of the "must match" elements of crossword clues, but it's easy to get tripped up by "-ed" endings, because past-tense verbs can end in other ways. The answer to [Trampled], for example, is RAN OVER.

51D. PIU is not a sound made at 59-Across, but an Italian-derived notation for [More, musically].

Constructor Notes

One of my favorite genres of crossword theme is the representation of an object or game. Lately I've been thinking about puzzles that depict movement, and looking at the timeline of this puzzle, that may have started earlier than I realized. My first stab at this theme was in late 2023. I had the circled elements in place, but the longer theme entries weren't quite coming together. Coming back to it in spring of 2025, the grid fell into place when I realized that STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK were the same length. I especially love the dangling vertical PLUSH TOY at the top of the grid. Hope this one doesn't throw you for a loop!

title: Monkeys Understand Shapes in Almost the Same Way as Humans
full_text_raw:
Our geometric intuition, long considered something that sets us apart, seems to be shared with other primates.

You (probably) won't find a monkey in a geometry class, but it looks like our fellow primates can swing the basics.

Just like people, monkeys seem to grasp the abstract qualities of geometric shapes, such as whether they are symmetrical, have parallel sides or contain right angles, according to a new study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. This ability allows the monkeys -- and us -- to understand when two shapes are the same, even when they've been rotated or resized.

This finding challenges a long-held notion that humans' geometric abilities are part of what makes our brains one of a kind. "Our hypothesis was that humans are not that unique," in possessing this mathematical understanding, said Jialin Li, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University and the lead author of the study.

In their experiment, Ms. Li and her colleagues decided to give monkeys (a total of eight rhesus macaques and olive baboons), preschoolers and adult humans with different education levels the same geometric task. That way, if humans truly had an innate advantage, it would show up when comparing the young children and the monkeys. And if the advantage was learned, it might show up when comparing the humans who had different levels of schooling.

It was a challenge to find a task simple enough that even preschool-aged children and monkeys could reasonably complete it, but the team eventually decided to have all the study participants do a matching task. All were shown a shape with a specific size and geometric form on a screen. Then they were asked to pick that same shape out of a group of others.

"By manipulating the similarity of the shapes, we were able to look at what kinds of rules they're using," said Jessica Cantlon, a cognitive neuroscientist at Carnegie Mellon University whose lab conducted the study.

title: European Parliament demands Pakistan free 13-year-old Christian girl in forced marriage, conversion
full_text_raw:
Maria Shahbaz, a 13-year-old Christian who was forced to convert to Islam after being abducted last year, must be provided with access to her family and psychological support, Members of the European Parliament demanded while passing a new resolution on the human rights situation in Pakistan earlier this month.

Shahbaz was married to her abductor in March, despite most provinces requiring a person to be at least 18 to marry.

She was abducted on July 26, 2025, by a 30-year-old man and immediately married to him after police in Lahore delayed filing the family's first information report (FIR) and influenced the judge to dismiss their abduction complaint, according to the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom.

Five days after her abduction, the Model Town court of Judicial Magistrate Hassan Sarfaraz Cheema awarded custody of Shahbaz to her captor after accepting falsified documents claiming she was 18 years old, while ignoring evidence provided by her family proving otherwise.

In March 2026, the Federal Constitutional Court upheld the decision, formalizing her marriage.

Forced conversions, marriages major issue amongst Christian Pakistanis

Forced conversion through marriage is a common issue faced by Christians in Pakistan, according to UN figures. Twenty-five percent of those forced to abandon their faith in this manner are Christian, while the majority are Hindu women and girls. According to International Christian Concern, as many as 1,000 Christian, Hindu and Sikh girls are abducted each year.

Only five years before Shahbaz's abduction, a 14-year-old Christian girl with the exact same name was abducted from Faisalabad. She was forcibly converted to Islam and married to her abductor, but was later able to escape, though courts had earlier ruled in her abductor's favor, overturning a protection order and returning her to his custody.

The European Parliament urged Pakistan's authorities to implement the national framework to end child marriage and create a national mechanism for handling complaints from families whose loved ones have been abducted and forced to convert.

Calling on Pakistan to do more to protect minorities, the MEPs demanded that perpetrators be prosecuted, the country's judicial framework be strengthened, and abducted girls be returned safely.

'Deeply entrenched, systemic pattern of human rights abuses'

Christian Solidarity Worldwide's Deputy Team Leader for South Asia, "Simon," told The Jerusalem Post, "This timely resolution by the European Parliament exposes a deeply entrenched, systemic pattern of human rights abuses where Pakistan's judicial system has failed to protect vulnerable girls belonging to religious minority communities.

CSW echoes the European Parliament's urgent demand that Pakistani authorities immediately secure Maria's safety, provide her with independent legal and psychological support, and transparently overhaul its legal and enforcement mechanisms to criminalize forced conversions once and for all.

"CSW also welcomes the passage of the Child Marriage Restraint Bill by the Punjab Assembly in April 2026 and urges lawmakers across the country, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, where the legal age for marriage is currently 16 for girls, to follow suit and amend all existing laws governing marriages of Muslims and religious minorities and to standardize the legal age of 18 years for marriage.

"We also urge the government to go further and enact legislation that explicitly criminalizes forced conversion, ensuring that perpetrators and those complicit in such acts are held to account, and introduce legal safeguards to prevent the misuse of religious conversion claims in cases involving minority girls."

title: Can 'Brand Burnham' survive the move to Number 10?
full_text_raw:
With a down-to-earth speaking style and a blokeish, quip-heavy persona on social media, new UK prime minister Andy Burnham appears determined to break the mould of a traditional leader.

This was on display on Monday when he addressed the nation outside Number 10 with no notes or lectern.

His favoured wardrobe of a T-shirt and zip-up jacket has been the first casualty of his arrival in office this week -- a suit and tie are now the order of the day.

The question is whether Burnham can balance his everyman brand with the demands of high office.

As mayor of Greater Manchester he was known for fostering an easy-going connection with the public, in contrast with the previous prime minister, Sir Keir Starmer.

One of his former colleagues suggested this direct appeal to voters was reflected in his speech on Monday.

"He was talking straight down the lens, talking to the public and saying 'the care of people is at the heart of my plan'," Tracy Brabin, West Yorkshire mayor, told Sky News.

Jo Tanner, political communications strategist and managing partner at Rud Pedersen UK, said it was an effective opening gambit. "He's definitely going to do it his way and I think that is right for him," she said.

Nevertheless, speaking without notes is "risky" as prime minister, said Tanner, "especially when nuance in language can be misinterpreted" by the markets or foreign leaders.

"It's going to be hard to continue to do when you have a PM's diary to cope with, where every five minutes is accounted for."

While he was mayor, Burnham held weekly radio phone-ins, monthly public Q&A sessions and regular press conferences at which journalists could ask him anything.

But since a press conference at the launch of his Makerfield by-election campaign in May, his communications have been more controlled.

That approach has continued since his return to Westminster. He has hired Sarah Brown, a respected and long-serving aide to London's mayor Sir Sadiq Khan, as his director of communications.

He took no questions at his first speech as an MP in Manchester last month, after inviting London-based journalists north to hear him. On Monday, the Westminster press pack complained that he took only three questions in a huddle immediately after his entrance to Number 10.

His team has been advised to prioritise regional and local journalists during his summer tour of the nation.

It is an approach that has not always worked for prime ministers -- Liz Truss was savaged during a round of local BBC radio interviews after 2022's disastrous "mini" Budget.

While taking a more controlled approach to the traditional media, Burnham has also upped his TikTok and Instagram output to project an informal yet carefully curated style. As mayor he ran his own X account, regularly responding to critics, but Makerfield marked a turning point in his online approach.

He has twice taken questions on Reddit in recent weeks, a process his team can closely control. Burnham has also shown a preference for podcasters, giving a big interview to Gary Lineker just before taking power.

Since becoming prime minister, his social media strategy has been led by Abby Tomlinson, known for her "Milifandom" campaign backing Ed Miliband more than a decade ago and, more recently, her work on Labour's social media content during the 2024 general election.

This week's output has included a series of TikTok and Instagram reels featuring Burnham, including a tie-up with Ukrainian influencer Max Klymenko talking about his first job as a football pools collector.

Burnham is still in the process of building his presence on those platforms, with 383,000 followers on Instagram versus Starmer's 862,000. Starmer joined in 2017, whereas Burnham's account was only set up in May.

James Lyons, former No 10 director of communications and a partner at Penta Group, said that while both prime ministers had used the same platforms, "the difference is, Andy's a lot more natural, comfortable and prepared to take a risk, as we saw with him fluttering his eyelashes [in a recent video]".

Social media gives Burnham "a brilliant opportunity to connect directly with voters where they are and where they consume information", he said, adding that so far he has come across as "fluent, confident and optimistic".

But Lyons adds: "You can't avoid the traditional media as well . . . for good or ill, print and broadcast media in this country still frame the debate." In fact, they often influence content on social media, he said.

"He comes across as very warm and empathetic," he said. "He needs to hold on to that authenticity."

title: Bus fare cap coming from aid budget will hit world's poorest, Burnham told
full_text_raw:
Funding proposal for cost of living policy 'throws global south countries under the bus', says ActionAid UK director

The world's most vulnerable people will be put at risk by Andy Burnham's decision to use the aid budget to pay for cheaper bus fares in England, charities have said.

The prime minister announced on Wednesday that he would reduce the fare cap from £3 per journey to £2 for next year, funded mainly by changing international climate donations into repayable loans.

The switch allows the government to borrow more against those loans without violating its borrowing rules. But experts say it will also leave people in the poorest parts of the world more vulnerable to the effects of the climate crisis.

It comes after the government indicated the new aid minister, Kirsty McNeill, would not attend cabinet as her immediate predecessors did, prompting concerns the government is downgrading its commitment to international development.

Joanne O'Neill, the co-director of advocacy at ActionAid UK, said: "The prime minister's fare cap scheme is a welcome initiative but his funding proposal throws global south countries under the bus, penalising those most impacted by a climate crisis they did not create."

She added: "Delivering international climate finance as loans instead of grants pushes countries deeper into debt and forces them to divert funding away from essential public services such as education, health and social protection - which disproportionately impacts women and girls."

Monica Harding, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for international development, said Burnham's decision would "further undermine the UK's standing as a reliable global partner". She said: "Swapping crucial climate grants for loans will ultimately fall on the backs of the world's poorest, racking developing nations with more destabilising debt. This will only harm Britain's security in the long run, fuelling more migration and instability abroad."

Romilly Greenhill, the chief executive of Bond, which represents aid organisations, said: "It is disappointing that the new prme minister is picking up where the previous one left off, by continuing to raid the diminished UK aid budget to prop up much-needed funding for the cost of living crisis here in the UK.

"The cost of living crisis in the UK needs to be urgently addressed, but robbing Peter to pay Paul is not the answer and pitches marginalised communities here in the UK against marginalised communities in lower-income and climate-vulnerable countries."

Danny Gross, a climate campaigner at Friends of the Earth, said: "With the UK already doing far below its fair share on international climate finance, funding [the fare cap] by replacing climate grants with loans is nothing short of a travesty."

Burnham made the bus fare cap his second major policy announcement in office, coming a day after he said he would cut VAT on electricity bills.

During a visit to Bath, the prime minister said the move would "really help people with the cost of living pressures they're facing". He added: "It's there for the whole of 2027, and I think it will put money in people's pockets."

Downing Street said on Wednesday the move would cost more than £500m next year, £400m of which will be funded by switching international climate investment to loans.

Officials said the switch would enable the money to go to international financing schemes such as the Tropical Forests Forever Facility, an anti-deforestation initiative set up last year by the Brazilian president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Changing donations to loans, however, means money is more likely to go to countries that can repay them, which are more likely to be middle-income countries such as India or Brazil than some of the world's poorest.

The switch could also reduce the amount of money the UK gives as international aid, which the previous government promised would stay at 0.3% of national income after cutting it in half to pay for more defence spending.

Though loans can count towards overseas development spending, that will depend on the terms on which they are given. Only loans given at a significant discount to market rates will count.

Experts say some of the money is likely to have been allocated already, leaving ministers potentially having to renege on agreed donations.

The government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Samsung details features of its smart glasses as it enters market dominated by Meta
full_text_raw:
Samsung on Wednesday detailed the features of its upcoming smart glasses, including gesture controls, as it looks to mount its first challenge to Meta in the device category.

The South Korean tech giant had previously unveiled the "intelligent eyewear" at Google I/O conference in May, showing off two products designed with its partners Gentle Monster and Warby Parker. At the time, Samsung gave very few details about the design and functionality.

At Samsung's Galaxy Unpacked event on Wednesday, the company said the glasses have a built-in camera, as CNBC first reported earlier this year. The camera can capture content that the user is seeing such as taking a video. It can also read content on a whiteboard or presentation and organize the key information into notes.

The device can summarize long messages that a person receives on their smartphone. This can be heard from the built-in speakers in the glasses.

title: Sperm whales change 'vowel' sounds when boats are nearby, scientists discover
full_text_raw:
Researchers listening off the Caribbean island of Dominica found variations in the mammals' audible clicks when marine traffic was close

Sperm whales produce a specific pattern of clicking noises when they hear the noise of boats, researchers have found. The pattern is so distinct that the scientists who identified it said they can now use it to predict when ships are nearby.

Researchers from Project Ceti (the Cetacean Translation Initiative), a non-profit research organisation working to decode sperm whale communication, spent four years tuning in on the calls of 15 sperm whales off the coast of Dominica.

They discovered specific differences in sperm whale "codas", the discrete and distinctive patterns of clicks that this species utters to communicate when those whales encountered shipping. Individual click sequences became shorter, and one type became more prominent than another. Their findings are published in the journal Ecological Informatics.

"This research begs the question: are whales talking about the ships, or is it an impact on their voices because the ships are around?," said David Gruber, the founder and chief executive of Project Ceti. "And then if we're able to discern what they're saying about the ships, how might that impact policy and laws?"

Under normal conditions, recordings from one of the whales, named "Atwood", picked up one type of coda comprising five clicks in a 1-1-3 pattern (two clicks preceding three quicker ones), which, Gruber explained, is unique to this specific clan of sperm whales off the Caribbean coast of Dominica. With the background hum of a ship, Atwood issued the same 1-1-3 click rhythm but noticeably faster, with the whale reducing the intervals between each click.

The association was so strong that "in general, from their vocalisations alone, we can predict whether ships are around," said Gašper Beguš, linguistics lead at Project Ceti.

For the study, Beguš and colleagues recorded more than 1,000 codas from the 15-strong sperm whale pod, using audio tags attached to whales by drones to be minimally invasive. Where background shipping noise was detected, it was verified using digital geolocation data to confirm that vessels were in the whale's vicinity when the recording was made.

Several studies have shown that marine animals increase the volume of their vocalisations when there is noise pollution, but the researchers were surprised not to see this trend in the sperm whales, finding that the creatures instead seemed to prioritise altering not just the speed but the types of codas they produced.

This related to previous studies where Project Ceti researchers described the "use of vowels" in sperm whales. Communication among sperm whales has long been viewed as a series of morse code-like clicks, but in that work the team found that if the gaps between individual clicks in a coda sequence were condensed to speed up the recording, they formed a continuous unit of sound that resembled two human vowels - the sounds "aaaa" and "iiii".

In the latest research, in addition to the changing coda tempo, the team identified differences in the prevalence of these two vowel-like sounds in noisy conditions, with sperm whales using the "aaaa" coda more frequently.

"The study is actually one of the first glimpses that the vowels that we discovered might actually carry meaningful information. Because in the presence of shipping noise, they change the way they use those vowels," Beguš said.

Some researchers have criticised Ceti's previous studies, finding fault with its methods and saying that describing whale communication using terms such as "vowels" and "language" stretches the associations between whale and human communication too far. Gruber says they try to address this concern by using terms such as "vowel-like" or "language-like".

Nathan Merchant, an underwater noise specialist at the UK government marine research agency Cefas, who was not involved in the research, said there could be other unknown factors driving the change in whale vocalisations aside from shipping noise. But he said his "hunch" was that the relationship was causal.

A large body of work now showed changes in behaviour and call volume when marine animals encountered shipping noise, Merchant noted. "Something that marks this study out is that it shows changes to the fine-scale content of those calls," he said. "It really adds another dimension of nuance to that story about how underwater noise can affect cetaceans."

He added that it would take more research to determine what these audible changes meant.

"Are they [the whales] just struggling to say the same thing, or are they saying something different in the presence of this noise?" he said. "It's a really intriguing question."

title: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests
full_text_raw:
Finding widens selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable

Mars once had rivers of magma bubbling beneath its crust, new research suggests. The surprise find makes it more probable that Mars could have supported life and widens the selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable.

Researchers at the University of Oxford studied data gathered by Nasa's Insight Lander, which recorded seismic waves caused by meteorite impacts and Martian quakes. They used the seismic data to analyse a mysterious boundary 15 miles (24km) below the surface of Mars. Their findings, published in Nature Astronomy, showed that the most likely cause for this boundary was molten rock pooling deep underground and stretching sideways for hundreds or even thousands of miles.

Scientists had previously assumed that the volcanoes on Mars were underlain by simple isolated magma chambers, but the new finding suggests a more complex interconnected plumbing system. Such a system would have the potential to make a chemically complex crust, capable of recycling elements and supporting the kind of processes needed to generate an atmosphere and ocean on the surface.

This would also help to regulate the climate - previously thought only to be possible on planets with plate tectonics. And that means rocky planets previously dismissed as uninhabitable because of their lack of plate tectonics now deserve a second look.

title: Laptopitis: the hidden health cost of working from home
full_text_raw:
Working from home is fueling back, neck and shoulder pain as poor laptop setups, couch-based work and too little movement take a cumulative toll; what can be done to prevent this from becoming chronic pain?

Working from home started as a dream: no traffic jams, no distracting hallway chatter, fresh coffee from your own kitchen and the ability to throw a load of laundry into the washing machine between Zoom meetings. However, after a few years of hybrid work, it turns out this routine is not doing the body any favors.

Laptopitis is the unofficial term gaining traction in the media to describe this phenomenon. It refers to the collective aches and injuries caused by prolonged laptop use: neck pain, lower back pain, shoulder tension, wrist strain and occasional headaches and muscle fatigue.

Medical professionals use formal terms such as Repetitive Strain Injuries (RSI) and Work-related Musculoskeletal Disorders (WMSDs). The truth is, dining tables, couches and laptops resting on laps were never engineered for working eight to ten hours straight in front of a screen.

Data gathered in recent years by international health organizations reveals the true scale of the issue: over 65% of remote employees report developing new musculoskeletal pain or experiencing worsening symptoms since transitioning to hybrid work. The lack of ergonomic workstations serves as a primary risk factor, significantly increasing physical strain.

To avoid letting temporary aches turn into permanent damage, here are the most common remote-work mistakes and straightforward ways to fix them:

Before you start working: Gentle mobility exercises that engage the joints and prevent stiffness are essential preparation for hours of little active movement. It is best to start with head and neck rolls. Tilt your head toward your shoulder for a gentle stretch, then move on to rolling your shoulders forward and backward, rounding your back and bringing your shoulder blades together.

Next, stand firmly next to a desk or kitchen counter, place your hands down for support and perform wide pelvic circles to loosen the lower back joints. This movement stimulates joint fluids, boosts circulation and perfectly prepares the musculoskeletal system for prolonged sitting.

The couch is not an office: Slouching on a soft surface without lower back support creates cumulative stress on the spine and neck muscles. When sitting correctly, the upper body's center of gravity rests directly over the pelvis and thighs, allowing a natural, straight alignment for the lower back, neck and head.

Conversely, sinking into an overly soft armchair causes the pelvis to tilt backward and round out. This compromised posture triggers a chain reaction: the upper back and neck bend forward, the head thrusts outward and the shoulders round, a combination that invites long-term musculoskeletal issues.

Therefore, if a dedicated home office is unavailable, working at a sturdy table with a standard dining chair is far better than spending hours with a laptop on your lap.

Smart computing practices: Placing a laptop directly on your lap is a surefire recipe for pain: the screen sits too low, forcing the neck to stay bent forward for hours. Meanwhile, hovering your mouse hand in the air without proper support overworks the wrist muscles. Simple solutions like a laptop stand, an external keyboard and a mouse will completely transform your posture and relieve immense pressure from your neck and shoulders.

Ergonomically adjusting the workspace, ensuring the right proportion between chair and desk height, keeps the head straight and eye level right at the top of the screen without forcing a neck tilt. Choose a chair that provides solid lower back support, make sure your feet rest flat on the floor or a footrest and keep your knees at or slightly below hip level. If the screen remains too low, use an adjustable monitor or prop it up. Incorporating a sit-stand desk allows for alternating positions throughout the day. It is also crucial to pause every 30 to 45 minutes to stand up, walk around and do light stretches to prevent the body from locking into a single position.

Remote work has eliminated the incidental movement built into office life: walking from the car, moving between offices or stepping out for lunch. When the distance between your bed, desk and refrigerator is just five steps, it helps to artificially create short walks throughout the day. Try a brief walk outside before starting the day or take phone calls while standing up. The goal is to build movement directly into the workday routine, rather than treating it as an afterthought when the pain has already started.

title: NHS trust investigated for corporate manslaughter after Nottingham attacks
full_text_raw:
Police open investigation into Nottinghamshire service that treated Valdo Calocane, who killed three people in 2023

The NHS trust which treated the triple killer Valdo Calocane in the years before the Nottingham attacks is being investigated by police for corporate manslaughter.

Calocane, who has paranoid schizophrenia, was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order after he fatally stabbed the 19-year-old students Barnaby Webber and Grace O'Malley Kumar, and the 65-year-old caretaker Ian Coates, on 13 June 2023.

A public inquiryinto the events leading up to the 2023 attacks heard how the Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation trust had sectioned Calocane four times between 2020 and 2022.

Evidence given to the inquiry detailed a string of violent incidents that Calocane had committed in the years before the Nottingham attacks and his repeated refusal to take medication. During his second hospital admission, the inquiry heard how a doctor warned Calocane could "end up killing someone".

Despite this, Calocane was discharged from mental health services in September 2022 because he had failed to attend his appointments and healthcare workers "couldn't find him".

Northumbria police confirmed they were carrying out the criminal inquiry on behalf of the Nottinghamshire force. The NHS trust said it was cooperating with the investigation, which could result in substantial fines and changes to its leadership.

Charges of corporate manslaughter, a serious criminal offence, can only apply to certain organisations, including public bodies such as local authorities and NHS trusts, to ensure they can "be held properly accountable for very serious failings resulting in death", according the Crown Prosecution Service.

The public inquiry into the attacks, which is expected to publish its findings next year, heard that there had been a warrant out for Calocane's arrest at the time of the Nottingham attacks after he failed to appear in court for the alleged assault of a police officer.

Nottinghamshire and Leicestershire police forces apologised during the inquiry for failing to act on the warrant, which according to the Times is why the Northumbria force will carry out the investigation into the NHS trust.

The Nottingham trust has been under close scrutiny since the 2023 attacks. A 2026 report by the Care Quality Commission said it needed to make significant improvements.

A trust spokesperson said: "Northumbria police, acting on behalf of Nottinghamshire police, have begun an investigation into matters relating to the care and treatment of Valdo Calocane.

"We know how important the independent inquiry and police investigation are for the affected families, the survivors and our local communities.

"We will, of course, be cooperating fully with Northumbria police, as we have with the statutory inquiry."

A spokesperson for force said: "Our thoughts are very much with the victims, their families and all those impacted by the tragic events in Nottingham in June 2023.

"We are in contact with the victims' families and survivors and are committed to supporting them throughout this process."

title: Why hot weather and chocolate can go together
full_text_raw:
Fridge-friendly nougat, malty ice-cream and a hybrid brownie-chocolate bar - your summer bites are sorted

The summer heat requires special treatment of chocolate. Few experts would agree with keeping it in the fridge, but sometimes you have to gently shh them and do what feels right. Heist's Milk and Honey Nougat is like a choc-covered torrone morbido: a big slab of milk chocolate covering honey-laced pistachio and almond nougat. It's a disaster in hot weather. But, kept in the fridge ... wow. The pre-marked pieces are so big and generous you can't disobey them, slice your knife into it and then eat the piece within, say, three minutes before the whole lot turns molten in your fingers.

Pump Street has just launched a Walnut Brownie 60% Dark Milk Bar with Haitian beans. It features brownie crumb with English Sharpham Park caramelised, hand-chopped walnuts. It's rich and deep in flavour.

My father used to have an ice-cream shop, and he made the best chocolate ice-cream (which I think is difficult to get right) because he'd mix the chocolate with chestnuts to give the gelato a wonderful mouthfeel. I keep meaning to try to emulate it. Not the same but a very worthy chocolate ice-cream, since it's the weather for it, is Ottolenghi's Salted Malted Chocolate ice-cream made with 73% cocoa Ecuadorian chocolate.

Soon I'll be writing about making your own chocolate treats, but I am in love with Dominique Ludwig's salted caramel bars, which feature an oat and almond base, nut butter and dates whizzed up into a dreamy caramel and drizzled with (for me, very high cocoa content) chocolate. I customise her recipe with more nut butter than she suggests and sprinkle a few roasted peanuts into the caramel innards to make a bastard child of a Twix and a Snickers. Shop-bought can go hang.

WEDNESDAY PUZZLE -- It's hard to describe Wednesday crosswords. I think of them as the "You had to be there" puzzles of the solving week. They sometimes defy puzzle logic or pull off a whip-smart visual trick. Others contain rebus elements, and some are just plain witty.

I'd describe Rebecca Goldstein as something of a Wednesday whisperer, as crosswords go. It's not that she constructs Wednesday puzzles exclusively -- she has just four under her belt, in fact -- but that she knows how to keep us guessing, be it with clever sleights of word or visual magic. Today's crossword theme was another delight to uncover. There's a rebus square, a visual joke and a truly elegant design choice. Considering the puzzle's subject, that all seems more than, ahem, fair.

Today's Theme

Circled squares indicate themed fill, so that's probably where we'll find 38D's [Carnival game depicted in this puzzle]. Most of these circles contain standard letters: [Many a tech alum: Abbr.] at 49A is an ENGR -- a baffling shortening of "engineer," incidentally -- which gives us a circled R. The [Toxin in castor beans] at 40A is RICIN, which yields an I. Moving on from left to right, we've got an N from TALON (34A), a G from SINGH (41A) and ... something that doesn't quite fit at 52A and 23D.

The answer to [Risqué game that teenagers might give a whirl?] should be SPIN THE BOTTLE, but BOTTLE is too long a word for the entry spaces. 52A's [Pop top?] should be BOTTLE CAP, but we end up with the same issue. The logical conclusion: We're looking at a rebus square.

For the purposes of the Times Crossword we define rebuses simply as "crossword elements where solvers are asked to write multiple letters in the same square." In this case, those letters form the word BOTTLE. If we treat the square as the object itself, then the letters R, I, N and G arcing toward it amount to a RING TOSS (38D)!

Would it be a carnival game without a high-up [Prize dangling from a 38-Down booth] to be won? The biggest PLUSH TOY at 11A can be yours if you land the toss.

And while the connection probably wasn't intentional, I can't resist pointing out that the phrases at 17A and 60A, STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK, could serve as answers to the clue [Hawk's hook] -- as in, phrases used by carnival barkers hawking their games to hook players in. Eh?

Tricky Clues

14A. Blame the Canadian in me for defaulting to "Sorry!" as the [Cry after an accident] instead of OOPSY.

19A. The question mark at the end of [Seller's bottom lines, for short?] indicates a witty twist, likely in the literal interpretation of a figure of speech. "Bottom lines" refers to a product's bar code, also known as U.P.C.

43A. A question mark may also be a reminder to read the clue twice. It's [Get in bad with?], not "get in bed with." The answer is ABET.

1D. You don't need to get your hands grimy to [Spread dirt] in this sense, i.e., to GOSSIP.

40D. Tense is one of the "must match" elements of crossword clues, but it's easy to get tripped up by "-ed" endings, because past-tense verbs can end in other ways. The answer to [Trampled], for example, is RAN OVER.

51D. PIU is not a sound made at 59-Across, but an Italian-derived notation for [More, musically].

Constructor Notes

One of my favorite genres of crossword theme is the representation of an object or game. Lately I've been thinking about puzzles that depict movement, and looking at the timeline of this puzzle, that may have started earlier than I realized. My first stab at this theme was in late 2023. I had the circled elements in place, but the longer theme entries weren't quite coming together. Coming back to it in spring of 2025, the grid fell into place when I realized that STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK were the same length. I especially love the dangling vertical PLUSH TOY at the top of the grid. Hope this one doesn't throw you for a loop!

title: Nell Whittingham obituary
full_text_raw:
My friend Nell Whittingham, who has died aged 96, relished adventure. When her husband Barrie's career took their family to Zambia in the 1960s they had a Piper Tri-Pacer aircraft and flew the Flying Doctor service - Nell also helped with weather reports and logistics. In the 70s they lived in Swaziland and Sudan, then Nigeria, where Nell set up a weather station to monitor wind for the Savannah Sugar Factory. During a stint in Papua New Guinea, she renovated a dug-out canoe and sailed in shark-infested waters.

In 1980 Nell and Barrie moved to Foggathorpe, East Yorkshire, where she discovered the 11-century Norman church of All Saints, Aughton, where later she became churchwarden for more than 30 years.

In the 80s Nell gained a certificate in social studies at Hull University, then a degree in social policy and administration, and master's degrees in care for the elderly, and managing change. She then worked (1989-91) as unit manager for Bridlington Mental Health Resource Base, and resource manager (1991-92) for Grimsby Mental Health Resource Base. She won the East Riding of Yorkshire council chairman's community award, and in 2020 was awarded Maundy Money from Queen Elizabeth II.

Born in Ipstones, Staffordshire, Nell was the daughter of George and Ella Clowes, silk-mill workers who later ran a greengrocers in Leek. Times were hard for Nell and her sister, Lilian. Nell had a strong Christian faith, loved writing letters and had a fantastic memory for people's interests and families. Her family called her "annoyingly positive".

Gaining a scholarship to Leek high school for girls, she then attended Stoke Technical College studying public health, becoming the first female public health inspector for Stoke council. In 1952 she married Barrie Whittingham, a civil engineer, and they settled first in Wiltshire then in Essex, in the town of Corringham, where Nell built a sailing dinghy in the kitchen, and was hands-on with house building tasks, before they set off for Zambia.

Nell loved reading, long-distance walking, gardening, singing and went on a pilgrimage to Iona.

She was tireless in her fundraising for Aughton - a stained-glass window consecrated by the archbishop of York John Sentamu, electricity installation, and mains water for a much-needed toilet and kitchen. She also undertook huge amounts of research into the Catholic rebel Robert Aske from Aughton, the Pilgrimage of Grace, the uprising against Henry VIII and the Suppression of Religious Houses in 1535. Aske was subsequently executed by Henry VIII. Nell's supreme efforts kept Aughton church alive, and her annual Pilgrimage of Grace evenings and afternoon teas are still going.

Barrie died in 1993, and Lilian in 2017. Nell is survived by three sons, David, Mark and Nichols, five grandchildren and great-grandson.

title: Target ultra-processed food to reduce obesity in Britain | Letter
full_text_raw:
James Capon responds to an editorial on the health select committee's call for radical action to regulate food markets

The MPs' report mentioned in your editorial is welcome and overdue (The Guardian view on obesity: put public health before food industry pressure, 15 July). The health select committee is right to clarify that obesity is an engineered outcome, not a failure of willpower. But there's a flaw running through decades of British food policy that risks being repeated: the "high in fat, salt or sugar" framework itself.

"High in fat, salt or sugar" combines three nutrients as though they carry equivalent blame. However, the evidence on weight gain and type 2 diabetes points to sugar and refined carbohydrates as the primary drivers, not fat. Salt matters, chiefly when combined with sugar, but the body needs salt to function. Fat matters because without it many fat-soluble vitamins will just pass through our bodies. We need no sugar at all.

The low-fat, calorie-controlled orthodoxy inherited from flawed nutritional science still shapes labelling, reformulation targets and public understanding, encouraging manufacturers to strip out fat and replace it with sweet-tasting substitutes, while ticking the "healthier" box.

To hold supermarkets and manufacturers to account, the target must be sharpened. The culprit is the ultra-processed food model itself: products engineered for shelf life, craveability and margin, using cheap sugar and refined starch as primary ingredients. Ice-cream or potato crisps sold on rare occasions are fine, but the food system that has made them the cheapest, most heavily advertised, most convenient choice is the problem.

We shouldn't need to romanticise the Greggs sausage roll as some kind of national treasure. Consider it a treat, not a staple. That's the shift in our relationship with ultra-processed food that this report should be pushing for - one built on carbohydrate and sugar reduction, not a blunt fat-and-salt panic that has already failed us.

James Capon

Waterloo, Belgium

title: Suspected money laundering network used real estate vouchers to move NIS 500 million
full_text_raw:
The case was named "Payment Voucher" following the suspects' use of real estate-related vouchers

A Jerusalem District Police central unit and the Israel Tax Authority moved to the overt stage of an investigation into a suspected international financial crime network allegedly involved in laundering hundreds of millions of shekels through fictitious companies, false invoices and real estate payment vouchers, police and tax officials announced on Wednesday.

Three central suspects were arrested on suspicion of receiving something by fraud, money laundering and tax offenses involving an estimated NIS 500 million.

The covert investigation was led by investigators from the Jerusalem District Police central unit's fraud department together with investigators from the Jerusalem and Southern Districts Income Tax Investigations Office. The investigation was launched after suspicions arose that the three were operating an international financial crime mechanism designed to launder money, evade taxes and deliberately conceal income, harming state coffers.

The case was named "Payment Voucher" due to the suspects' extensive use of real estate-related payment vouchers, alongside additional offenses.

During months of investigation, investigators uncovered the suspects' alleged method of operation. According to the suspicion, the three operated an extensive network of fictitious companies and nonprofit organizations in Israel and abroad. Through this network, they allegedly laundered money for local companies, while smuggling funds from overseas and injecting them into Israel.

The alleged method included receiving cash, distributing false invoices and sophisticated concealment of funds through bank transfers, real estate voucher payments and the use of family members' bank accounts.

On July 14, the investigation entered its overt phase, when investigators raided the homes of 16 suspects and arrested several of them for joint questioning. During the raids, dozens of properties were seized that investigators suspect were obtained through fraud and with funds generated from concealed income.

So far, dozens of additional individuals have been questioned. According to investigators, they received and used the services of the central suspects for the purposes of money laundering, concealing income and obtaining benefits by fraud.

As required by the investigation, the detention of two of the central suspects, a 48-year-old man from Kiryat Ye'arim and a 56-year-old man from Tel Aviv, was extended by the court until Thursday.
