title: How will Australia's emergency services cope if satellites go down? With a sextant and a street directory
full_text_raw:
Military and SES personnel being taught analog communication and navigation techniques as experts warn solar flare could knock out 'critical space infrastructure'

Australia's emergency services and military personnel are being trained to read paper maps, navigate without GPS support, and sail by the stars in case something knocks out the nation's space capabilities.

A panel at the 19th Australian space forum in Adelaide on Wednesday was asked to consider what would happen "if we suddenly lost access to critical space infrastructure - no satellites, no GPS, no remote sensing, no secure communications?"

The experts warned that Australians are unaware just how dependent they are on space, and how vulnerable that connection is to enemy attacks and solar flares.

It's "not science fiction", Optus satellite and space systems head, Nick Leake, said.

He described ATM networks going down, emergency services losing their situational awareness, aircraft navigation degrading, defence losing secure communications and remote communities being entirely cut off.

Aviation, freight and energy grid communications all rely on satellites, and financial systems could face "immediate cascading failure", he said. People may only realise their service is being delivered by a satellite when they lose it.

"Most Australians have no idea that space is part of their everyday life," Leake said.

"This isn't science fiction. This is how critical satellite infrastructure is. Australia has one of the highest per capita dependencies on satellite infrastructure in the world.

"Right now, it's largely unguarded."

Flinders University adjunct professor Jackie Craig AM is an expert in cyber and virtual warfare and an incident management team leader with the South Australian state emergency service.

She said emergency services are "increasingly dependent on increasingly vulnerable systems".

She said they now teach members to navigate with street directories and maps instead of phones - a once ubiquitous skill that has become lost in the age of Google Maps.

"What we discovered is the young people of the digital revolution can't actually use a UBD [street directory]. They're also very poor at reading and using maps," she said.

"A lot of us can't navigate."

She said if the satellite systems went down emergency services would be "back to pencil and paper", radios, and hard copies of procedure manuals.

Michael Murphy, deputy chief executive of the Royal Flying Doctor Service SA/NT, said if satellite systems went dark tomorrow, they would continue as normal - for about 24 hours, thanks to inbuilt contingencies and redundancies. Then, they would prioritise life-saving missions, relying on manual procedures and alternative communication methods.

He said they could go "old school" with high frequency radio and use the bush telegraph to share information in an analogue way.

"[And] we've got heaps of really good landmarks, the river systems, deserts, ranges, borders, water. If you're familiar with the land, you'll get around pretty well," he said.

The Australian Defence Force's air commodore, Chris Robson, said planning for a loss of satellite support wasn't "doomsday prepping" or a "scare tactic" but "something we need to be honest about".

"I don't think the general public understands," the space forces group and joint forces space component commander said.

The defence force is already offering sextant training, so members can navigate by the stars, along with terrestrial navigation training. But Robson did not think it would be frequently used.

"I don't think that you will see too many people sitting on the bridge looking at a sextant," he said.

The biggest risk was not an enemy attack, he said, but "that big orange glowing thing that on any single day can have a hiccup and take out a significant portion of our space capabilities".

The panel discussed ways to make the network more resilient, including having satellite redundancy in multiple orbits, more Earth stations, and sovereign satellite capabilities, instead of relying on US giants Amazon and Starlink.

title: 8 Books to Help You Navigate Divorce
full_text_raw:
Whether you're contemplating a split, or in the process of one, these books can help.

There is no single way or universal timeline to go through a divorce. Some people spend years deciding, while others are thrust into it. But no matter the specifics, the process can bring up common challenges: grief, uncertainty, logistical stress and questions about what comes next.

"You'll need practical and therapeutic help," said Kathryn Smerling, a psychotherapist in New York City. "Books can be a good source of both."

While books aren't a replacement for a good lawyer, financial adviser, therapist or support system, Dr. Smerling added, they can fill in gaps and empower you throughout the process.

So we asked psychologists, therapists and other relationship experts to share the books they suggest to their clients, whether they're considering divorce, in the thick of the process or navigating the aftermath.

If you're contemplating the subject

Loving Bravely

by Alexandra H. Solomon

In this 2017 book, Dr. Solomon, a clinical psychologist and adjunct professor at Northwestern University, unpacks relational self-awareness, or the ability to understand one's own patterns, expectations and emotional responses within relationships. This, she argues, is foundational to better connection with others.

full_text_raw:
WEDNESDAY PUZZLE -- It's hard to describe Wednesday crosswords. I think of them as the "You had to be there" puzzles of the solving week. They sometimes defy puzzle logic or pull off a whip-smart visual trick. Others contain rebus elements, and some are just plain witty.

I'd describe Rebecca Goldstein as something of a Wednesday whisperer, as crosswords go. It's not that she constructs Wednesday puzzles exclusively -- she has just four under her belt, in fact -- but that she knows how to keep us guessing, be it with clever sleights of word or visual magic. Today's crossword theme was another delight to uncover. There's a rebus square, a visual joke and a truly elegant design choice. Considering the puzzle's subject, that all seems more than, ahem, fair.

Today's Theme

Circled squares indicate themed fill, so that's probably where we'll find 38D's [Carnival game depicted in this puzzle]. Most of these circles contain standard letters: [Many a tech alum: Abbr.] at 49A is an ENGR -- a baffling shortening of "engineer," incidentally -- which gives us a circled R. The [Toxin in castor beans] at 40A is RICIN, which yields an I. Moving on from left to right, we've got an N from TALON (34A), a G from SINGH (41A) and ... something that doesn't quite fit at 52A and 23D.

The answer to [Risqué game that teenagers might give a whirl?] should be SPIN THE BOTTLE, but BOTTLE is too long a word for the entry spaces. 52A's [Pop top?] should be BOTTLE CAP, but we end up with the same issue. The logical conclusion: We're looking at a rebus square.

For the purposes of the Times Crossword we define rebuses simply as "crossword elements where solvers are asked to write multiple letters in the same square." In this case, those letters form the word BOTTLE. If we treat the square as the object itself, then the letters R, I, N and G arcing toward it amount to a RING TOSS (38D)!

Would it be a carnival game without a high-up [Prize dangling from a 38-Down booth] to be won? The biggest PLUSH TOY at 11A can be yours if you land the toss.

And while the connection probably wasn't intentional, I can't resist pointing out that the phrases at 17A and 60A, STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK, could serve as answers to the clue [Hawk's hook] -- as in, phrases used by carnival barkers hawking their games to hook players in. Eh?

Tricky Clues

14A. Blame the Canadian in me for defaulting to "Sorry!" as the [Cry after an accident] instead of OOPSY.

19A. The question mark at the end of [Seller's bottom lines, for short?] indicates a witty twist, likely in the literal interpretation of a figure of speech. "Bottom lines" refers to a product's bar code, also known as U.P.C.

43A. A question mark may also be a reminder to read the clue twice. It's [Get in bad with?], not "get in bed with." The answer is ABET.

1D. You don't need to get your hands grimy to [Spread dirt] in this sense, i.e., to GOSSIP.

40D. Tense is one of the "must match" elements of crossword clues, but it's easy to get tripped up by "-ed" endings, because past-tense verbs can end in other ways. The answer to [Trampled], for example, is RAN OVER.

51D. PIU is not a sound made at 59-Across, but an Italian-derived notation for [More, musically].

Constructor Notes

One of my favorite genres of crossword theme is the representation of an object or game. Lately I've been thinking about puzzles that depict movement, and looking at the timeline of this puzzle, that may have started earlier than I realized. My first stab at this theme was in late 2023. I had the circled elements in place, but the longer theme entries weren't quite coming together. Coming back to it in spring of 2025, the grid fell into place when I realized that STEP RIGHT UP and TRY YOUR LUCK were the same length. I especially love the dangling vertical PLUSH TOY at the top of the grid. Hope this one doesn't throw you for a loop!

title: Stir-Fry Your Lettuce, Ragù Your Green Beans and Cake Your Coconut
full_text_raw:
Good morning! Today we have for you:

It was my husband's birthday this month, so I baked him a cake. He requested a coconut cake with a fluffy crumb and buttercream frosting, and Lisa Donovan's old-fashioned Southern-style confection was just the thing. I pretty much followed the recipe, with one major tweak: I sprinkled the cake layers with a little dark rum before swirling on the buttercream. Even without the extra rum, it's a guaranteed win for anyone in need of a shaggy showstopper of a cake.

The mom in me says, "Before cake, you should eat a nice, healthful dinner, preferably heavy on the vegetables." May I suggest Hetty Lui McKinnon's stir-fried lettuce with crispy garlic and fried eggs? In Chinese culture, stir-fried lettuce is a symbol of good luck. And the combination of soft, soy-sauced lettuce, crispy garlic and runny fried eggs dripping into the rice makes for a comforting, speedy meal.

View Recipe →

More food for thought

Swordfish with tomatoes: I eat tomatoes almost every day during this glorious time of year. Brett Anderson's easy recipe shows off their savory side as they share the pan with plenty of garlic, olives, anchovies and wine. Searing the swordfish only briefly before finishing it with the tomatoes ensures that the fish stays juicy. Serve it with pasta or rice to sop up the tangy sauce.

Skillet chicken with schmaltzy tomatoes: Or if you're in the mood to pair those gorgeous tomatoes with chicken, try this deeply flavored recipe. To make it, I sear chicken pieces until the skin crisps and renders its fat, then add cherry tomatoes to the pan, letting them simmer until juicy. A little salad of sliced red onion and fresh herbs adds color, crunch and freshness right at the end.

Pasta with green bean ragù: Green beans are also in peak season right now. Take advantage by making Eric Kim's delightful pasta, which also features brawny Italian sausages (sweet or hot), Parmesan and a bright hit of lemon.

Plum and mozzarella salad with serrano-lime dressing: Simple, colorful and tangy with mustard, vinegar and lime juice, Ashley Lonsdale's summery salad makes a hearty side dish or a light main course if you add some slices of sourdough.

Strawberry gooey butter cake: As a St. Louis native, Justine Doiron has thoughts about gooey butter cakes. Here, she ditches the usual cake mix in favor of homemade, topping it with a baked-on cream-cheese layer swirled with fresh strawberry purée.

title: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests
full_text_raw:
Finding widens selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable

Mars once had rivers of magma bubbling beneath its crust, new research suggests. The surprise find makes it more probable that Mars could have supported life and widens the selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable.

Researchers at the University of Oxford studied data gathered by Nasa's Insight Lander, which recorded seismic waves caused by meteorite impacts and Martian quakes. They used the seismic data to analyse a mysterious boundary 15 miles (24km) below the surface of Mars. Their findings, published in Nature Astronomy, showed that the most likely cause for this boundary was molten rock pooling deep underground and stretching sideways for hundreds or even thousands of miles.

Scientists had previously assumed that the volcanoes on Mars were underlain by simple isolated magma chambers, but the new finding suggests a more complex interconnected plumbing system. Such a system would have the potential to make a chemically complex crust, capable of recycling elements and supporting the kind of processes needed to generate an atmosphere and ocean on the surface.

This would also help to regulate the climate - previously thought only to be possible on planets with plate tectonics. And that means rocky planets previously dismissed as uninhabitable because of their lack of plate tectonics now deserve a second look.

title: Thousands of immigrant children risk losing lawyers after Trump aid cuts
full_text_raw:
More than 20,000 unaccompanied children risk going to US immigration court alone after federal funding cuts

Thousands of immigrant children who came to the United States without being accompanied by a parent or guardian are now at imminent risk of losing the attorneys assisting on their legal cases, amid cuts in government funding, advocates warned this week.

The Trump administration has severed ties with nearly a hundred legal organizations across the country that provide immigration advice and has been funneling kids into fast-tracked court hearings.

"The Trump administration is working to strip unaccompanied children of legal representation so they can be deported faster and with less scrutiny. We cannot allow that to happen," said Ana Devereaux, senior managing attorney at the Michigan Immigrant Rights Center.

Federal officials are set to end a contract providing legal counsel to more than 20,000 children on 31 July. They have already refused to reimburse organizations for $65m in work completed since December, attorneys say, unless those organizations agree to violate their young clients' confidentiality and turn over sensitive information, such as un-redacted medical evaluations and data about kids' broader immigration cases, according to Shaina Aber, executive director of the Acacia Center for Justice, the contractor that administers legal services for those kids.

"These sorts of detailed disclosures could provide the government with, really, a roadmap for mass deportation of children," said Aber said.

The federal administration's ultimatum is pressing many of the affected non-profits toward layoffs, hiring freezes or even financial collapse and all but ensuring that young immigrants will have to face court alone.

"Without a lawyer, children win the right to stay in the United States less than 10% of the time. Immigration judges are nearly 100 times less likely to grant relief to a child without counsel," said Elizabeth Young, a former regional deputy chief immigration judge, who resigned last year.

She added: "Due process is the foundation of American justice ... When children are forced to navigate one of the most complex areas of law alone, that promise of fairness becomes little more than an illusion."

Unaccompanied children often reach the US while fleeing human trafficking, persecution, neglect, abuse or abandonment, a reality that the nation's lawmakers have recognized through policies meant to protect some of the world's most vulnerable kids.

But under the second Trump administration, an immigration system that was crafted so children could have their legal claims carefully assessed is being rebuilt to fuel the mass deportation machine, and kids are being ordered deported before other government agencies can process their applications to stay legally, experts warn.

"These children are not and should never be leverage in a political game. They are human beings - kids who have a legally and morally recognized right to have their cases heard," Aber said. "The administration's actions are directed at speeding up their deportation instead of protecting them, but abandoning children to meet arbitrary mass deportation targets is immoral."

The impending funding cliff later this month comes amid reports that federal officials are planning to send unaccompanied children en masse to Texas, where the immigration courts, circuit judges and state leaders are generally friendly to the Trump administration's anti-immigrant agenda.

To do so, federal officials reportedly first turned to the Texas attorney general's office - run by Ken Paxton, one of Donald Trump's fiercest allies - for help representing the kids, then pivoted toward the Texas Indigent Defense Commission, a small state entity tasked with criminal defense, not civil immigration work. Scott Ehlers, the Indigent Defense Commission's executive director, told them their request would likely violate his mandate.

Meanwhile, some of Texas's legal organizations with a long history of representing immigrant kids are on the brink of closure in part because the federal government has not reimbursed them for their services.

Likewise, one major legal provider nationally, Kids in Need of Defense, founded by actor Angelina Jolie and the Microsoft Corporation, announced it was canceling its participation as a subcontractor representing unaccompanied children last month based on $20m in overdue payments.

"You can imagine when organizations of that caliber, with the support that they've had throughout the years, cannot sustain this work, it tells you everything you need to know about the severity of what is happening in this field and what the administration is doing," Aber said.

"And that's happening right now, even before the contract expires. So the damage is already being felt, and I assume that we're going to see hundreds and hundreds of children going to court alone."

title: 'The last picture': A passing boater's photograph may be the 5 adults who drowned in Ohio
full_text_raw:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) -- Marcus L. Martin felt instant trepidation Sunday when he saw five adults wading hip- and waist-deep in the Scioto River. A frequent boater on the Ohio waterway, the Baptist pastor knew the area where they were standing to be treacherous. He believes the people he captured in a photo to be the ill-fated group that drowned that day.

"I just remember being taught that that area was kind of dangerous, in the sense of there being steep slopes" and a quick drop-off into the river, he told The Associated Press. A few years earlier, Martin had warned a pair of young people playing in the water at that same spot to "be very careful."

He saw five adults in the water and two children playing on the grassy bank nearby, tracking the description of the group provided by Delaware County authorities after the drownings.

Martin and his family floated away to enjoy a beautiful summer evening. But when they returned past the spot about two hours later and saw the group still wading in the river, Martin thought to snap a photo.

"I don't know what it was. I said, I just need to capture this picture," he said.

Martin said he knows the area well from 10 years of boating there and considered warning the people of the potential danger. But, unlike when he'd warned the two people earlier, there were two or three boats between him and them and he didn't want to cross between them and cause too many waves in the water.

He's been losing sleep over the decision since news broke of five people drowning that afternoon. It feels "surreal," he said.

"I believe the picture I took may have been the last picture of them being alive," he said.

Delaware County Sheriff Jeffrey Balzer has said authorities believe one of the adults began struggling to swim and the others successively went to that person's aid. All five were swept under and died. The two women's bodies were recovered Sunday and the three other bodies a day later.

Neither Balzer's office nor the local EMS agency immediately responded to requests for verification of the photo and those who appear in it.

Martin said he feels certain the group he photographed is of the five people who perished Sunday; it's rare to see people fishing or swimming in that stretch of the river. He said he attempted to share the picture with both law enforcement and a news reporter at the scene the day after the drownings, but no one seemed interested.

Honduran authorities confirmed Tuesday that four of the five adults were Honduran citizens. One was Jose Mario Pineda Dias, 33, another his wife Marina Suyapa Regalado, 28. The other couple and the fifth individual have yet to be identified.

The government of Honduras said it is working with the U.S. to bring their bodies home. The repatriation process could take at least a month.

An 8-year-old and a 10-year-old, children of one of the couples, were orphaned by the tragedy. They were taken into initial custody by the state of Ohio, but arrangements were being made to reunite them with relatives in Honduras.

full_text_raw:
Damon Gulczynski puzzles over the mysteries of the universe.

THURSDAY PUZZLE -- A warm welcome back to Damon Gulczynski, who makes his 49th appearance in the New York Times Crossword today. While his puzzles have run on every day of the week, he's really in the pocket on the back half. Some of Mr. Gulczynski's wily Thursday themes have included phonetic mistranslations, in-grid punctuation and clues written with letter substitution, and he has uncorked another winner today. That's not meant to intimidate newer Thursday solvers; today's puzzle hides its trick cleverly, but fairly. And, as always, the Wordplay column and its friendly commentariat are here to help. Onward!

Today's Theme

You would be forgiven if you thought that today's puzzle was a rebus crossword, a grid with squares that contain multiple letters. After all, this puzzle has several answers that are evidently correct, but don't fit in the grid -- a telltale sign of a shove-'em-in rebus. Picking up on those signals is an excellent solving instinct, and one that will serve you well for sussing out the tricks of late-week puzzles. But when you anticipate a Thursday puzzle's zig, sometimes it zags. There are no squares that require multiple letters in today's puzzle. In fact, all of the letters are there -- some are just hidden.

At 1-Across, [More than just a disapproving look], describes a "death stare." But only DEATH STAR, the planet-destroying space station from "Star Wars," fits. If you investigate the crossing entry where the E should be, at 14-Down, you'll find that it also has the letter unaccounted for. [Champion, as a cause] should be "espouse," but only SPOUSE fits. The E isn't missing; it's represented by the black square at the intersection of DEATH STAR(E) and (E)SPOUSE.

The same trick appears right next door, at 10-Across. [Scruff of the neck] describes "nape," but only APE fits. The hidden letter is intersected by 15-Down, which is clued with [Budding] to mean "nascent," but only ASCENT works. This time, it's the letter N that's represented by the black square where (N)APE and (N)ASCENT meet.

Why hide these letters in black squares, and how many can you expect to find in the puzzle? The theme revealer's clue provides the key. At 62-Across, [Proposed cosmological phenomenon that could make up 70% of the universe -- and six squares in this puzzle's grid?] solves to DARK ENERGY. There are six dark squares in this puzzle that represent a letter. When read from top to bottom, those hidden letters spell "energy." Note that every entry with a hidden letter is an acceptable word whether the letter is included or not: "Nape" and APE are both valid entries, as are "nascent" and ASCENT. See if you can discover the remaining dark squares, or hit the links below to have the mysteries of the universe revealed.

Tricky Clues

16A. You didn't hear this from me, but ["The Devil's radio"] is another way to describe IDLE GOSSIP. George Harrison, no stranger to the rumor mill, released a song titled "Devil's Radio" in 1987. It was reportedly inspired by a church billboard he had seen that read, "Gossip: The Devil's Radio ... Don't Be a Broadcaster."

19A. [What a pointless game has?] plays with the multiple meanings of "pointless." It's not about a nonsensical game, but rather one with NO SCORE. Sports are a rich vein of coinages and turns of phrase that mean "zero." Other than "goose egg," soccer often also uses "nil" for zero, and shutouts are referred to as "clean sheets." In tennis, "love" means zero, and shutouts are called "bagels."

43A. The [Desert for which an African country is named] is the NAMIB Desert, which stretches along the continent's southwestern coast from Angola to South Africa, though a vast majority of it lies in Namibia, the country in question. The Namib is mostly uninhabited and has a fitting etymology: Its name comes from the Nama language and means "an area where there is nothing."

53A. There's a lot going on in the clue [Wholly, but not holey or holy, e.g.: Abbr.]. To make it more digestible, I set aside the "Abbr." and focus on the remainder. While they're all homophones, "holey" and "holy" are adjectives and only "wholly" is an adverb. The word "adverb" can be abbreviated as ADV.

2D. This one may trip up solvers unfamiliar with American football. The [Word after tight or defensive] is END; tight end and defensive end are both positions in the sport. The Cleveland Browns trading Myles Garrett, the best defensive end in the N.F.L., to the Los Angeles Rams was one of the biggest stories this off-season. Still, it didn't generate the headlines that the off-season activities of a certain tight end did.

Constructor Notes

I got the idea for a "dark" puzzle, in which black squares actually contain letters, and then I started playing around with different candidate theme answers, still unsure what exactly the theme would be. The key, in my mind, was to find entries that would be interesting even without the dark gimmick. When I found DEATH STAR(E), I decided to go with DARK ENERGY, and the rest is cosmic history.

title: Uber, Lyft win court block on NYC law requiring notice before firing drivers
full_text_raw:
July 22 (Reuters) - A federal judge has ruled that New York City cannot prohibit Uber Technologies (UBER.N), opens new tab and Lyft (LYFT.O), opens new tab from deactivating drivers from their apps without advance notice, ruling that the novel law is unconstitutional.

U.S. District Judge Gregory Woods in Manhattan said in a written ruling on Tuesday that the city's law adopted earlier this year benefits a small fraction of drivers while interfering with the ride-hailing companies' right to police the safety of their platforms.

"Uber and Lyft are likely to succeed in showing that the law protects a narrow class of drivers and does not advance the broader ⁠social or economic interest which the U.S. Constitution requires to permit the severe impairment of their contracts," Woods wrote.

The judge issued a preliminary injunction blocking the city from enforcing the law, which was set to take effect July 28, pending the outcome of consolidated lawsuits filed by the companies last month.

Lyft said in a statement provided by a spokesperson that "we're pleased the court recognized the serious safety concerns at the heart of this challenge."

Separately, Uber spokesman Josh Gold said: "The opinion underscores that driver fairness and rider safety can and must go hand in hand."

The New York ⁠City Law Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The law, one of the first of its kind inthe U.S., was passed in January after the New York City Council overwhelmingly overrode a veto by former Mayor Eric Adams, a Democrat. Adams had said, opens new tab that the law would create an expensive ⁠and unwieldy new bureaucracy to handle wrongful deactivation claims.

The law requires that ride-hailing services give drivers 14 days' notice before deactivating them from apps, with an exception for "egregious misconduct," and potentially rehire drivers deactivated ⁠since 2019 solely because they did not receive such notice.

Uber and Lyft in lawsuits filed a day apart in June said that the law violated their due process and free speech ⁠rights under the U.S. Constitution. They said the law threatened to undermine their reputation and goodwill while keeping unsafe drivers, including those accused of sexual misconduct, on the road.

title: The deed thieves targeting New York brownstones
full_text_raw:
As property values rise, more titles are being stolen from homeowners without their knowledge

The backdrop for Spike Lee's 1989 classic film Do the Right Thing is a row of sturdy brownstones in which the residents of Brooklyn's Bedford-Stuyvesant neighbourhood fight with their girlfriends, watch the world go by from upstairs windows and seek refuge after a summer night turns violent.

Brownstones in this same neighbourhood are now among the buildings that activists and legislators are trying to make sure remain in the hands of their owners.

Deed theft, which the New York State attorney-general defines as occurring "when a thief takes the title to a home without the homeowner's knowledge or approval", is a scam that mostly affects the city's elderly brown and Black people. Thefts are increasing. Last year 517 complaints were filed in New York City, mainly in Brooklyn and Queens, up from 149 in 2023.

"For a lot of Black homeowners, their home is their wealth -- they don't have a lot of assets in the form of stocks or bonds," says New York State senator Jabari Brisport, who has worked on legislating against deed theft for years, including classifying it as a form of grand larceny. "To have your entire life savings stolen out from under you . . . it's really distressing."

Deed thieves will often appear with official-looking forms that they say need to be signed so they can go ahead with repairs or other work, but which actually hijack ownership of the property.

Others forge the homeowner's signature on a deed to sign it over to themselves. It may be years before a homeowner receives notice of eviction and realises they were the victim of a scam. The ensuing litigation, if brought, can sometimes take "a decade or longer", says Jacob Inwald, a director of litigation at non-profit Legal Services NYC.

This month, New York's attorney-general Letitia James won her case against a man from Long Island who had criminally possessed two Harlem brownstones worth a combined $4.7mn. One elderly owner had been forced to stay at a shelter after his home was stolen from him.

New York City's democratic socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani, who made housing a central tenet of his campaign, has created an Office for the Prevention of Deed Theft in response to pressure from activists and lawyers.

Real estate scams are a growing problem across the US, but deed theft in New York has a specific history. The brownstones that are now coveted in tree-canopied Brooklyn neighbourhoods, including Bed-Stuy and Crown Heights, were "once deemed ugly and undesirable", says Asad Dandia, Brooklyn borough historian.

Black communities bought homes there during the "white flight" of Irish, Italian and Jewish homeowners to residences outside the city in the mid-20th century, he adds. In some instances, history stretches back even further -- the neighbourhood of Weeksville in Brooklyn, for example, was founded by free Black New Yorkers, including freed slaves two centuries ago.

But as these neighbourhoods have become desirable -- and as much of Manhattan's real estate has morphed into the preserve of the ultra-rich -- prices have appreciated. Now, a Bed-Stuy brownstone could set you back $3mn. "Anywhere property values are rising, there are creative speculators coming up with new ways to scam homeowners," says Inwald.

Some of the most prominent activists on deed theft see the scam as a pernicious form of gentrification. New York City's Black population has dropped by around 200,000 people in the past two decades -- an approximately 9 per cent loss.

"Black people rightfully feel as though we're pushed out of Brooklyn because we can't afford it," says Brisport. "The majority of that is rent but . . . Black homeowners feel pressure from multiple angles (to leave the city)," he continues. "Deed theft is one of the most insidious ones."

But Evangeline Byars, leader of activist group People's Coalition to Stop Deed Theft, who spends her nights as a subway worker and her days organising, places less emphasis on the question of gentrification. "It takes away from the criminal side (of the scam)," she says. "And what we are fighting for is people's homes."

title: EU review of airline ownership rules clouds Apollo's £5.7bn easyJet bid
full_text_raw:
EasyJet shares fell as much as 14 per cent on Wednesday as reports about a looming EU review of airline ownership rules cast doubt over its planned takeover by US asset manager Apollo.

The bloc is seeking to "clarify" provisions on control of airlines by foreign investors to protect "strategic autonomy", according to one official.

The move is the latest twist in a protracted takeover saga for the UK low-cost airline, whose board this month recommended a £5.7bn offer from Apollo that trumped an earlier £5.5bn bid from US private credit group Castlelake.

News of the EU review, first reported by Reuters, sent easyJet's shares down as much as 14 per cent before they recovered some poise to be roughly 10 per cent down in late afternoon trading.

The EU requires airlines to be more than 50 per cent owned by member states or nationals of member states in order to obtain an operating licence, and to be controlled by Europeans, meaning they have a "decisive influence" on the running of the airline.

The rules still apply to easyJet after Brexit, as the low-cost carrier established a subsidiary in Austria to allow it to continue to operate flights within the EU after the UK left the bloc.

The official said the review was not linked to the Apollo takeover bid and formed part of a broader revision of the EU's air services regulations, which also govern rules such as public service obligations for peripheral areas of the EU.

Takeovers of airlines have historically been difficult in Europe, with British Airways owner IAG walking away from a bid to purchase 80 per cent of Spanish carrier Air Europa in 2024 after the European Commission flagged competition concerns.

IAG chief executive Luis Gallego last month told the FT he thought the takeover of easyJet was likely to be "very, very difficult" because of the rules.

EasyJet declined to comment. Apollo and Castlelake did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A person close to the airline said EU regulators had not engaged with it regarding the proposed deals with Apollo and Castlelake.

Good morning! Today we have for you:

It was my husband's birthday this month, so I baked him a cake. He requested a coconut cake with a fluffy crumb and buttercream frosting, and Lisa Donovan's old-fashioned Southern-style confection was just the thing. I pretty much followed the recipe, with one major tweak: I sprinkled the cake layers with a little dark rum before swirling on the buttercream. Even without the extra rum, it's a guaranteed win for anyone in need of a shaggy showstopper of a cake.

The mom in me says, "Before cake, you should eat a nice, healthful dinner, preferably heavy on the vegetables." May I suggest Hetty Lui McKinnon's stir-fried lettuce with crispy garlic and fried eggs? In Chinese culture, stir-fried lettuce is a symbol of good luck. And the combination of soft, soy-sauced lettuce, crispy garlic and runny fried eggs dripping into the rice makes for a comforting, speedy meal.

Swordfish with tomatoes: I eat tomatoes almost every day during this glorious time of year. Brett Anderson's easy recipe shows off their savory side as they share the pan with plenty of garlic, olives, anchovies and wine. Searing the swordfish only briefly before finishing it with the tomatoes ensures that the fish stays juicy. Serve it with pasta or rice to sop up the tangy sauce.

To make it, I sear chicken pieces until the skin crisps and renders its fat, then add cherry tomatoes to the pan, letting them simmer until juicy. A little salad of sliced red onion and fresh herbs adds color, crunch and freshness right at the end.

title: 8 Books to Help You Navigate Divorce

title: Private autopsy raises questions about death Mississippi college football player

The pathologist who conducted ⁠the private autopsy "cannot rule out foul play" without more information, said civil rights lawyer Ben Crump.

Wells' body was found fully clothed and face down on the island on July 6. He had traveled there over the Fourth of July ⁠weekend with three white friends who returned to the mainland without him, Crump said.

The death has drawn national ⁠attention over unanswered questions surrounding his final hours and concerns that deaths of ⁠young Black Americans do not receive adequate scrutiny.

title: Rivers of magma once bubbled beneath crust of Mars, research suggests
full_text_raw:
Finding widens selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable

Mars once had rivers of magma bubbling beneath its crust, new research suggests. The surprise find makes it more probable that Mars could have supported life and widens the selection of rocky planets that may once have been habitable.

Researchers at the University of Oxford studied data gathered by Nasa's Insight Lander, which recorded seismic waves caused by meteorite impacts and Martian quakes. They used the seismic data to analyse a mysterious boundary 15 miles (24km) below the surface of Mars. Their findings, published in Nature Astronomy, showed that the most likely cause for this boundary was molten rock pooling deep underground and stretching sideways for hundreds or even thousands of miles.

Scientists had previously assumed that the volcanoes on Mars were underlain by simple isolated magma chambers, but the new finding suggests a more complex interconnected plumbing system. Such a system would have the potential to make a chemically complex crust, capable of recycling elements and supporting the kind of processes needed to generate an atmosphere and ocean on the surface.

This would also help to regulate the climate - previously thought only to be possible on planets with plate tectonics. And that means rocky planets previously dismissed as uninhabitable because of their lack of plate tectonics now deserve a second look.

title: Great Barrier Reef microbiome mapped as researchers discover 500 bacterial species previously unknown to science
full_text_raw:
Research identifies 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what scientists estimate to be 362,802 different viruses

More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.

Analysing DNA from seawater samples of 48 reefs, researchers have mapped the microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef, documenting more than 360,000 distinct viruses as well as more than 500 new bacterial species not previously known to science.

The research, published in the journal Nature, was led by scientists at the University of Queensland and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).

Dr Yun Kit Yeoh, a senior research scientist at AIMS and a senior author of the paper, described microorganisms as a "very important part of the reef ecosystem" that underpinned marine food chains.

"Many of the microbes on the reef can photosynthesise ... like plants, they can take light energy [and] can convert carbon dioxide into oxygen.

"They are eaten by krill and other zooplankton which are then consumed by other animals.

"We haven't been able to really study a lot of them except for a select few that we can grow properly in the lab on petri dishes."

But recent technological advances have allowed scientists to sequence DNA taken from the environment, giving a fuller picture of these microscopic communities.

The field - known as metagenomics - is akin to solving thousands of jigsaw puzzles simultaneously; a single drop of seawater can contain the DNA of thousands of different microbes.

"We wouldn't have been able to do this, say, 10 years ago, but fortunately computing power keeps increasing at an exponential rate," said Prof Philip Hugenholtz, a microbiologist at the University of Queensland and a senior author on the paper.

The research, which first began more than five years ago, identified 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what the researchers estimate to be 362,802 different viruses.

The analysis also identified 5,283 bacterial and archaeal genomes representing 876 distinct species - 584 of which have never been documented before.

Hugenholtz said those large figures were expected. "This is just how huge the microbial world is," he said. "We know that everywhere we sequence ... there's always new viruses turning up.

"I was a little bit surprised that we found over 500 new bacterial species.

"The human gut and the marine ecosystem I would say are the two most sequenced ecosystems on the planet."

The discovery raises the question as to whether the species were unique to the Great Barrier Reef, or were yet to be discovered in other reef ecosystems, Hugenholtz added.

The researchers believe the mapped microbiome could be used as a reef monitoring tool. "We can now use it to start exploring what makes a healthy reef system," Yeoh said. "Then we can examine how these microbes respond to, say, changes ... associated with climate change, with heat stress, bleaching, human activity, or other environmental perturbations.

"Microbial communities can tell you an awful lot. Often you'll see changes in the microbial populations before you see more visible changes [on the reef]."

The microbes in a particular marine area can indicate whether fishing has occurred in a no-take zone, for example. They can also indicate whether heavy metal contamination has occurred.

"It's quite expensive to get a readout of heavy metals - it's cheaper to get a read out of the changes that they have on microbial communities," Hugenholtz said.

The researchers used long-read sequencing technology, which enables large strands of DNA to be read at one time, without the need to break them into smaller fragments.

Hugenholtz likens it to doing jigsaw puzzles with bigger pieces, "which means you'll be able to put those jigsaw puzzles back together more easily".

title: Sperm whales change 'vowel' sounds when boats are nearby, scientists discover
full_text_raw:
Researchers listening off the Caribbean island of Dominica found variations in the mammals' audible clicks when marine traffic was close

Sperm whales produce a specific pattern of clicking noises when they hear the noise of boats, researchers have found. The pattern is so distinct that the scientists who identified it said they can now use it to predict when ships are nearby.

Researchers from Project Ceti (the Cetacean Translation Initiative), a non-profit research organisation working to decode sperm whale communication, spent four years tuning in on the calls of 15 sperm whales off the coast of Dominica.

They discovered specific differences in sperm whale "codas", the discrete and distinctive patterns of clicks that this species utters to communicate when those whales encountered shipping. Individual click sequences became shorter, and one type became more prominent than another. Their findings are published in the journal Ecological Informatics.

"This research begs the question: are whales talking about the ships, or is it an impact on their voices because the ships are around?," said David Gruber, the founder and chief executive of Project Ceti. "And then if we're able to discern what they're saying about the ships, how might that impact policy and laws?"

Under normal conditions, recordings from one of the whales, named "Atwood", picked up one type of coda comprising five clicks in a 1-1-3 pattern (two clicks preceding three quicker ones), which, Gruber explained, is unique to this specific clan of sperm whales off the Caribbean coast of Dominica. With the background hum of a ship, Atwood issued the same 1-1-3 click rhythm but noticeably faster, with the whale reducing the intervals between each click.

The association was so strong that "in general, from their vocalisations alone, we can predict whether ships are around," said Gašper Beguš, linguistics lead at Project Ceti.

For the study, Beguš and colleagues recorded more than 1,000 codas from the 15-strong sperm whale pod, using audio tags attached to whales by drones to be minimally invasive. Where background shipping noise was detected, it was verified using digital geolocation data to confirm that vessels were in the whale's vicinity when the recording was made.

Several studies have shown that marine animals increase the volume of their vocalisations when there is noise pollution, but the researchers were surprised not to see this trend in the sperm whales, finding that the creatures instead seemed to prioritise altering not just the speed but the types of codas they produced.

This related to previous studies where Project Ceti researchers described the "use of vowels" in sperm whales. Communication among sperm whales has long been viewed as a series of morse code-like clicks, but in that work the team found that if the gaps between individual clicks in a coda sequence were condensed to speed up the recording, they formed a continuous unit of sound that resembled two human vowels - the sounds "aaaa" and "iiii".

In the latest research, in addition to the changing coda tempo, the team identified differences in the prevalence of these two vowel-like sounds in noisy conditions, with sperm whales using the "aaaa" coda more frequently.

"The study is actually one of the first glimpses that the vowels that we discovered might actually carry meaningful information. Because in the presence of shipping noise, they change the way they use those vowels," Beguš said.

Some researchers have criticised Ceti's previous studies, finding fault with its methods and saying that describing whale communication using terms such as "vowels" and "language" stretches the associations between whale and human communication too far. Gruber says they try to address this concern by using terms such as "vowel-like" or "language-like".

Nathan Merchant, an underwater noise specialist at the UK government marine research agency Cefas, who was not involved in the research, said there could be other unknown factors driving the change in whale vocalisations aside from shipping noise. But he said his "hunch" was that the relationship was causal.

A large body of work now showed changes in behaviour and call volume when marine animals encountered shipping noise, Merchant noted. "Something that marks this study out is that it shows changes to the fine-scale content of those calls," he said. "It really adds another dimension of nuance to that story about how underwater noise can affect cetaceans."

He added that it would take more research to determine what these audible changes meant.

"Are they [the whales] just struggling to say the same thing, or are they saying something different in the presence of this noise?" he said. "It's a really intriguing question."

title: Journalists urge correspondents' association to stand up to Trump at rescheduled press dinner
full_text_raw:
NEW YORK (AP) -- Hundreds of former or retired journalists and eight press freedom groups are asking the White House Correspondents' Association to stand up to the Trump administration's recent attacks on the media at its rescheduled dinner this week -- a dinner President Donald Trump says he'll attend.

The first dinner was cut short in April when a gunman, who prosecutors say was trying to assassinate Trump, opened fire at the Washington Hilton. The much smaller rescheduled dinner will take place Friday, with enhanced security precautions, at the capital's Waldorf Astoria Hotel, formerly the Trump International Hotel.

The letter expands on a similar one issued in April, before the first dinner. It notes that since then, "the administration's attacks on journalists and press freedom have become even more egregious."

The letter, organized by former ABC News correspondent Lisa Stark and producer Ian Cameron, cites in particular the recent subpoenas by the Justice Department to New York Times journalists who reported on security concerns over the president's Qatari-gifted Air Force One jet. Additional subpoenas of the journalists' phone records have included even the mother of one reporter, and two spouses.

They want the association to stand up 'forcefully'

The letter also cites threats by Trump to revoke licenses of broadcasters "who refuse to acquiesce to his demands."

"Our message to the White House Correspondents' Association is now more urgent: forcefully stand up for freedom of the press in front of the President, publicly defend the journalists he attacks, and vow to resist his administration's concerted effort to undermine the First Amendment," the letter says.

It notes that the association's president, Weijia Jiang, has defined the dinner's purpose as being "to celebrate the First Amendment and the hard daily work of the journalists who defend it."

"We believe it is hypocritical to celebrate the First Amendment in front of the man who relentlessly attacks it," the letter says. "We urge the WHCA to condemn the administration's actions from the podium and pledge to fight all attempts by his administration to undermine this core pillar of a functioning democracy."

There are multiple signatories

The groups signing on to the letter are the Society of Professional Journalists, the Committee to Protect Journalists, the National Association of Black Journalists, the National Press Photographers Association, the Freedom of the Press Foundation, the Coalition for Women in Journalism, the Radio Television Digital News Association and the Media and Democracy Project.

There are also about 520 individual signatories, mainly retired journalists. Almost all of them signed the April letter as well.

Trump has said he would be attending Friday's rescheduled dinner, calling the plan to go ahead with the event "a sign of Strength and Fortitude."

"This announcement is a very good thing in that we cannot allow Lunatics to change our way of life, or even its scheduling," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

He added that he hadn't decided whether to give his originally intended speech, in which he was widely expected to attack the press. "I don't know whether or not I will give the same rather nasty statements, at least as it concerns certain people, but we will soon find out," he wrote. "In any event, it will be a 'HOT' ticket!"

title: Nell Whittingham obituary
full_text_raw:
My friend Nell Whittingham, who has died aged 96, relished adventure. When her husband Barrie's career took their family to Zambia in the 1960s they had a Piper Tri-Pacer aircraft and flew the Flying Doctor service - Nell also helped with weather reports and logistics. In the 70s they lived in Swaziland and Sudan, then Nigeria, where Nell set up a weather station to monitor wind for the Savannah Sugar Factory. During a stint in Papua New Guinea, she renovated a dug-out canoe and sailed in shark-infested waters.

In 1980 Nell and Barrie moved to Foggathorpe, East Yorkshire, where she discovered the 11-century Norman church of All Saints, Aughton, where later she became churchwarden for more than 30 years.

In the 80s Nell gained a certificate in social studies at Hull University, then a degree in social policy and administration, and master's degrees in care for the elderly, and managing change. She then worked (1989-91) as unit manager for Bridlington Mental Health Resource Base, and resource manager (1991-92) for Grimsby Mental Health Resource Base. She won the East Riding of Yorkshire council chairman's community award, and in 2020 was awarded Maundy Money from Queen Elizabeth II.

Born in Ipstones, Staffordshire, Nell was the daughter of George and Ella Clowes, silk-mill workers who later ran a greengrocers in Leek. Times were hard for Nell and her sister, Lilian. Nell had a strong Christian faith, loved writing letters and had a fantastic memory for people's interests and families. Her family called her "annoyingly positive".

Gaining a scholarship to Leek high school for girls, she then attended Stoke Technical College studying public health, becoming the first female public health inspector for Stoke council. In 1952 she married Barrie Whittingham, a civil engineer, and they settled first in Wiltshire then in Essex, in the town of Corringham, where Nell built a sailing dinghy in the kitchen, and was hands-on with house building tasks, before they set off for Zambia.

Nell loved reading, long-distance walking, gardening, singing and went on a pilgrimage to Iona.

She was tireless in her fundraising for Aughton - a stained-glass window consecrated by the archbishop of York John Sentamu, electricity installation, and mains water for a much-needed toilet and kitchen. She also undertook huge amounts of research into the Catholic rebel Robert Aske from Aughton, the Pilgrimage of Grace, the uprising against Henry VIII and the Suppression of Religious Houses in 1535. Aske was subsequently executed by Henry VIII. Nell's supreme efforts kept Aughton church alive, and her annual Pilgrimage of Grace evenings and afternoon teas are still going.

Barrie died in 1993, and Lilian in 2017. Nell is survived by three sons, David, Mark and Nichols, five grandchildren and great-grandson.

title: Cutting down on ultra-processed foods isn't easy. Here are eight tips that worked for my family
full_text_raw:
Experts say reducing ultra-processed foods can be challenging in a world built around convenience, but these strategies can help make it more manageable

I have been trying to eat fewer ultra-processed foods with my family for five years, and it has been challenging.

Many experts agree that ultra-processed foods (UPF) pose health risks, whether because of unhealthy ingredients, links to disease and environmental impacts, or replacing more nutritious foods. Thus, some consumers - including me - are interested in removing them from their daily diet.

Getting here took time, effort and consistency, but we have had some success. Here are some strategies we used in our family.

1. Eat more plants

Plant foods are some of the easiest, most plentiful substitutes for UPF. Most obvious are fruits and vegetables, but nuts, seeds, popcorn and roasted seaweed are other tasty, nutritious options.

When it comes to introducing fruits and vegetables, the 6 to 12-month age is crucial, says Kary Rappaport, pediatric occupational therapist and the executive director of Solid Starts, an organization that supports parents with feeding their children: "It is an exceedingly important window of time, when most babies are most developmentally open to a wide variety of foods and flavors."

Introducing new foods to older children is similar: use small tastes, different preparations and a child's natural curiosity, she says. Focus on describing the food, rather than whether the child likes it - for example, encourage them to lick or take a bite and notice qualities like sweetness or temperature. "It's not a value judgment on the food," she says.

Additionally, timing matters. "We are all more motivated to try and like things when we're a little bit hungry," says Rappaport. Try "putting out a tray of raw veggies with hummus while you're cooking dinner, during that window where kids are looking to snack", she suggests. On the other hand, don't try to force a hangry child to try new veggies.

"Even when you don't have great options that are fully non-UPF, incorporate vegetables and fruits and raw products as much as possible," says Julia Wolfson, an associate professor in public health at Johns Hopkins University.

2. Buy the best ingredients you can afford

At our local farmers' market, there is a stall selling fantastic apples. When in season, they are consistently crisp, sweet and apple-y. This is true for much of the food at the market.

"Whatever they have in your farmers' market is what is seasonal, and what is seasonal is going to be better," says chef Penny Stankiewicz. "If you go to a standard American grocery store and you buy a perfectly round, somewhat red tomato, it's going to have absolutely no flavor in January. But in August, when it's prime tomato season, you don't have to even do anything to that tomato to make it amazing."

Produce is typically more expensive at a farmer's market, and not everyone has access to one. But the flavor payoff can be huge. Otherwise, try the produce at different grocery stores; additionally, frozen and canned produce is usually preserved at its peak. After you source your produce, learn the best ways to store it so it lasts as long as possible.

3. Openly discuss food, its effects and its origins

Part of my motivation to minimize UPF was not wanting to support powerful corporations that exploited workers, mistreated animals and harmed ecosystems. The more I learned about food systems, the less I wanted to participate in them as a consumer.

Teaching children where food comes from and how to prepare it builds appreciation and understanding. Rappaport also suggests discussing how foods make their bodies feel: for instance, "if I eat too many gummy worms or I only eat a bag of Flamin' Hot Cheetos on our car trip, I'm going to feel bad. It's not gonna sit well in my belly."

Familiarize yourself and your family with the definition of UPF, so that you can identify one by looking at an ingredient list, says Wolfson.

4. Learn to cook

I already knew how to cook, but I studied the science of cooking as we embarked on this project. Now, my from-scratch meals taste better than before, sometimes more so than UPF alternatives.

Often the barriers to cooking are systemic: insufficient time and energy to cook. People may also lack confidence in their kitchen skills. "We need to make it easier for people to cook healthy meals from scratch, and that means making those scratch ingredients more available and affordable, and building those skills from a young age so that people have the confidence and self-efficacy," says Wolfson.

Stankiewicz offers the following tips for newer home cooks:

* Learn techniques: "Once you know how to saute, it doesn't matter what you put in the pan."

* Develop knife skills: "If people want to get more comfortable in the kitchen, they should take a knife skills class. Those skills are a massive upscale for confidence in the kitchen."

* Know your taste: "Know what you like, then create that, because that's the starting place. Don't start by making miso brownies when the core is to make a really good brownie that you like, because then you'll do it again."

Wolfson found in her research that "when people cook more at home, they consume fewer ultra-processed foods." She notes that even when people are cooking frequently, the majority of their calories often still come from UPF. Try not to feel defeated if you notice something similar; this speaks to the ubiquity of UPF, she says: "If you picture a typical American grocery store, almost 70% of the foods in the store are ultra processed ... that's what's mostly available to us."

5. Learn to bake

In terms of replacing UPF, replacing desserts and snacks was an easy sell. I wasn't replacing cookies with carrot sticks; I was replacing them with cookies - sometimes better ones.

Stankiewicz says to approach baking with fearlessness. "Messing up is part of it and is really how you learn," she says, telling me that brownies were created by accident when a baker didn't add enough flour to the cake.

The next step is to find trusted recipe sources. Start with recipes that are not overly intimidating or complicated. Read the recipe through before beginning, then gather the ingredients. Organize the ingredients (mise-en-place) - and then just do it!

6. Make cooking at home easy

Consuming UPF is easy. It takes very little time and mental capacity to, say, unwrap and heat something. Try to make cooking and baking at home similarly easy.

First, master a few dishes. "Find a handful of recipes or techniques that are accessible in terms of ingredients, cost, number of ingredients, and how long they're going to take to make. Then just get really good at those," says Stankiewicz.

Second, build a pantry. Keep a stock of frequently used ingredients. My husband and I maintain a shared shopping list, and if we notice something running low, we update the list.

Third, make more than you need. Leftovers are great. Even better are meals that can be frozen and reheated because your past self did all the work.

7. Prioritize mealtimes

We have a rule at the table: no phones or toys during mealtimes. We have conversations instead (often mundane and not terribly deep). Our meals aren't long; they usually take 20 minutes from when we sit down to when my youngest is done.

"The research is really clear that family meals, where people are eating together, have a huge positive impact on child development across many different areas in terms of school performance, mental health and social engagement," says Rappaport.

It can be difficult when schedules are varied. Rappaport has older children and strives to fit in three dinners together each week around work and extracurriculars. It's less about "having a Norman Rockwell meal at the dinner table" than finding opportunities to engage, she says. "It can be burritos that we got for takeout while we're all sitting at the park waiting for practice to start. I can still find those same benefits, which are that I'm asking about their day. I'm showing interest in them. We are connecting around the food."

8. Be relentlessly consistent - and don't be too hard on yourself

We have not completely eliminated UPF. But for the most part, I try to cook, choose whole food items and purchase better-quality ingredients. Over five years and thousands of decisions, our palates have shifted to prefer non-UPF foods. Cooking and baking have become routine. When you reach the stage where UPF is no longer desirable taste-wise, and regular cooking is as habitual as brushing your teeth, opting out of UPF becomes less daunting.

Without fail, every expert I spoke with emphasized the structural factors that make it difficult for consumers to reduce UPF consumption. Their prevalence, coupled with time and cost pressures mean that UPF often makes the most sense. There will be unexpected work emergencies or illnesses that make cooking from scratch impossible. Some days are full of extracurriculars and social events, and you won't have time to bake or cook. You may attend catered events, meetings or functions where you have no control over the food.

The vast majority of us will eat at least some UPF. Your children will eat UPF - especially at birthday parties and play dates. But that's not failure, just reality. Being realistic about your options can help you stay consistent instead of giving up entirely, and that's ultimately what got me and my family to this point. When it comes to UPF consumption, don't let perfect become the enemy of good.

title: Great Barrier Reef microbiome mapped as researchers discover 500 bacterial species previously unknown to science
full_text_raw:
Research identifies 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what scientists estimate to be 362,802 different viruses

More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.

Analysing DNA from seawater samples of 48 reefs, researchers have mapped the microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef, documenting more than 360,000 distinct viruses as well as more than 500 new bacterial species not previously known to science.

The research, published in the journal Nature, was led by scientists at the University of Queensland and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).

Dr Yun Kit Yeoh, a senior research scientist at AIMS and a senior author of the paper, described microorganisms as a "very important part of the reef ecosystem" that underpinned marine food chains.

"Many of the microbes on the reef can photosynthesise ... like plants, they can take light energy [and] can convert carbon dioxide into oxygen.

"They are eaten by krill and other zooplankton which are then consumed by other animals.

"We haven't been able to really study a lot of them except for a select few that we can grow properly in the lab on petri dishes."

But recent technological advances have allowed scientists to sequence DNA taken from the environment, giving a fuller picture of these microscopic communities.

The field - known as metagenomics - is akin to solving thousands of jigsaw puzzles simultaneously; a single drop of seawater can contain the DNA of thousands of different microbes.

"We wouldn't have been able to do this, say, 10 years ago, but fortunately computing power keeps increasing at an exponential rate," said Prof Philip Hugenholtz, a microbiologist at the University of Queensland and a senior author on the paper.

The research, which first began more than five years ago, identified 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what the researchers estimate to be 362,802 different viruses.

The analysis also identified 5,283 bacterial and archaeal genomes representing 876 distinct species - 584 of which have never been documented before.

Hugenholtz said those large figures were expected. "This is just how huge the microbial world is," he said. "We know that everywhere we sequence ... there's always new viruses turning up.

"I was a little bit surprised that we found over 500 new bacterial species.

"The human gut and the marine ecosystem I would say are the two most sequenced ecosystems on the planet."

The discovery raises the question as to whether the species were unique to the Great Barrier Reef, or were yet to be discovered in other reef ecosystems, Hugenholtz added.

The researchers believe the mapped microbiome could be used as a reef monitoring tool. "We can now use it to start exploring what makes a healthy reef system," Yeoh said. "Then we can examine how these microbes respond to, say, changes ... associated with climate change, with heat stress, bleaching, human activity, or other environmental perturbations.

"Microbial communities can tell you an awful lot. Often you'll see changes in the microbial populations before you see more visible changes [on the reef]."

The microbes in a particular marine area can indicate whether fishing has occurred in a no-take zone, for example. They can also indicate whether heavy metal contamination has occurred.

"It's quite expensive to get a readout of heavy metals - it's cheaper to get a read out of the changes that they have on microbial communities," Hugenholtz said.

The researchers used long-read sequencing technology, which enables large strands of DNA to be read at one time, without the need to break them into smaller fragments.

Hugenholtz likens it to doing jigsaw puzzles with bigger pieces, "which means you'll be able to put those jigsaw puzzles back together more easily".

title: Sperm whales change 'vowel' sounds when boats are nearby, scientists discover
full_text_raw:
Researchers listening off the Caribbean island of Dominica found variations in the mammals' audible clicks when marine traffic was close

Sperm whales produce a specific pattern of clicking noises when they hear the noise of boats, researchers have found. The pattern is so distinct that the scientists who identified it said they can now use it to predict when ships are nearby.

Researchers from Project Ceti (the Cetacean Translation Initiative), a non-profit research organisation working to decode sperm whale communication, spent four years tuning in on the calls of 15 sperm whales off the coast of Dominica.

They discovered specific differences in sperm whale "codas", the discrete and distinctive patterns of clicks that this species utters to communicate when those whales encountered shipping. Individual click sequences became shorter, and one type became more prominent than another. Their findings are published in the journal Ecological Informatics.

"This research begs the question: are whales talking about the ships, or is it an impact on their voices because the ships are around?," said David Gruber, the founder and chief executive of Project Ceti. "And then if we're able to discern what they're saying about the ships, how might that impact policy and laws?"

Under normal conditions, recordings from one of the whales, named "Atwood", picked up one type of coda comprising five clicks in a 1-1-3 pattern (two clicks preceding three quicker ones), which, Gruber explained, is unique to this specific clan of sperm whales off the Caribbean coast of Dominica. With the background hum of a ship, Atwood issued the same 1-1-3 click rhythm but noticeably faster, with the whale reducing the intervals between each click.

The association was so strong that "in general, from their vocalisations alone, we can predict whether ships are around," said Gašper Beguš, linguistics lead at Project Ceti.

For the study, Beguš and colleagues recorded more than 1,000 codas from the 15-strong sperm whale pod, using audio tags attached to whales by drones to be minimally invasive. Where background shipping noise was detected, it was verified using digital geolocation data to confirm that vessels were in the whale's vicinity when the recording was made.

Several studies have shown that marine animals increase the volume of their vocalisations when there is noise pollution, but the researchers were surprised not to see this trend in the sperm whales, finding that the creatures instead seemed to prioritise altering not just the speed but the types of codas they produced.

This related to previous studies where Project Ceti researchers described the "use of vowels" in sperm whales. Communication among sperm whales has long been viewed as a series of morse code-like clicks, but in that work the team found that if the gaps between individual clicks in a coda sequence were condensed to speed up the recording, they formed a continuous unit of sound that resembled two human vowels - the sounds "aaaa" and "iiii".

In the latest research, in addition to the changing coda tempo, the team identified differences in the prevalence of these two vowel-like sounds in noisy conditions, with sperm whales using the "aaaa" coda more frequently.

"The study is actually one of the first glimpses that the vowels that we discovered might actually carry meaningful information. Because in the presence of shipping noise, they change the way they use those vowels," Beguš said.

Some researchers have criticised Ceti's previous studies, finding fault with its methods and saying that describing whale communication using terms such as "vowels" and "language" stretches the associations between whale and human communication too far. Gruber says they try to address this concern by using terms such as "vowel-like" or "language-like".

Nathan Merchant, an underwater noise specialist at the UK government marine research agency Cefas, who was not involved in the research, said there could be other unknown factors driving the change in whale vocalisations aside from shipping noise. But he said his "hunch" was that the relationship was causal.

A large body of work now showed changes in behaviour and call volume when marine animals encountered shipping noise, Merchant noted. "Something that marks this study out is that it shows changes to the fine-scale content of those calls," he said. "It really adds another dimension of nuance to that story about how underwater noise can affect cetaceans."

He added that it would take more research to determine what these audible changes meant.

"Are they [the whales] just struggling to say the same thing, or are they saying something different in the presence of this noise?" he said. "It's a really intriguing question."

title: Strange Milky Way planetary system leaves scientists puzzled
full_text_raw:
WASHINGTON, July 22 (Reuters) - Scientists are documenting a planetary system in the Milky Way galaxy that is so starkly dissimilar to our own solar system that they are struggling to find the proper terminology to describe it.

The system includes a red dwarf star about 40% of the mass of our sun that is orbited by a brown dwarf, a celestial body that blurs the line between planet and star. The brown dwarf, in turn, is orbited by a gaseous Jupiter-sized world, newly discovered using the European Southern Observatory's Chile-based Very Large Telescope.

Using our solar system as a definitional frame of reference, a body that orbits another body that orbits a star should be called a moon -- or in this case an exomoon, because it is beyond our solar system. But the object that orbits the brown dwarf is unlike any of the many moons in our solar system -- all of which are relatively small rocky or icy worlds -- in terms of composition and size.

So what should we call it?

"This will certainly be a matter of debate. In general, most astronomers are fine with the term exosatellite, ⁠at least as a placeholder until we formally adopt definitions for objects like the one we found," said Kevin Hoy, a doctoral student in astrophysics at Universidad Diego Portales in Chile also affiliated with the exomoon research group YEMS, lead author of the study published in the journal Nature, opens new tab.

"We're really hitting the limits of how far we can stretch the words we invented to describe the solar system to describe other systems in this case," Hoy said.

This system is about 71 light-years away from Earth. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km).

The exosatellite possesses at least 90% of the mass of Jupiter, the gas giant that is our solar system's largest planet. It completes an orbit of the brown dwarf every 170 days at a distance about a fifth of that separating Earth and the sun.

'A PANDORA'S BOX'

"I think this discovery has opened a Pandora's box for the scientific community. This type of object is completely new and unusual, truly different from what we are familiar with in our solar system. Now we will have to understand, through theoretical models, how these kinds of objects form and whether they are common or not," said study co-author Alice ⁠Zurlo, a Universidad Diego Portales astrophysicist and YEMS director.

"We deliberately chose not to call it a moon. That's because this object is unlike any moon in our solar system. It's much more massive, and it doesn't orbit a planet -- it orbits a brown dwarf, an object that's somewhere between a planet and a star. Since we've never seen a system quite like this before, we're still figuring out the best way to describe it," Zurlo said.

While more than 6,300 exoplanets -- as planets outside our solar system are known -- have been discovered, finding exomoons has proven more challenging, with only a few good candidates identified.

The researchers are trying to figure out the ⁠origins of the exosatellite.

"It may have formed from the disk of gas and dust around the brown dwarf, just as planets form around stars. Or it may have been captured (gravitationally) by the brown dwarf later on," Zurlo said.

A brown dwarf is neither a star nor a planet, but something in between. They could be considered aspiring stars that during their formative stages did not reach the mass necessary to ignite nuclear fusion at their core ⁠like a star. But they are more massive than the biggest planets.

The one in this system is about 33 times more massive, 50% larger in size and much hotter than Jupiter.

"Because the system is very young, the brown dwarf is still shining with the heat left from its formation," Zurlo said.

Since the first detection of exoplanets in the 1990s, scientists have spotted a wide variety of planetary ⁠systems, some built much like our own and others quite different. The one examined in the new research is an outlier.

"Yep, this system is definitely weird. There was likely a pretty chaotic dynamical history that left it in its current state, but it's really hard to tell exactly what kind of chaos it went through," Hoy said.

Some of Mr. Gulczynski's wily Thursday themes have included phonetic mistranslations, in-grid punctuation and clues written with letter substitution, and he has uncorked another winner today. That's not meant to intimidate newer Thursday solvers; today's puzzle hides its trick cleverly, but fairly. And, as always, the Wordplay column and its friendly commentariat are here to help. Today's Theme

After all, this puzzle has several answers that are evidently correct, but don't fit in the grid -- a telltale sign of a shove-'em-in rebus. Picking up on those signals is an excellent solving instinct, and one that will serve you well for sussing out the tricks of late-week puzzles. In fact, all of the letters are there -- some are just hidden.
