title: Nell Whittingham obituary
full_text_raw:
My friend Nell Whittingham, who has died aged 96, relished adventure. When her husband Barrie's career took their family to Zambia in the 1960s they had a Piper Tri-Pacer aircraft and flew the Flying Doctor service - Nell also helped with weather reports and logistics. In the 70s they lived in Swaziland and Sudan, then Nigeria, where Nell set up a weather station to monitor wind for the Savannah Sugar Factory. During a stint in Papua New Guinea, she renovated a dug-out canoe and sailed in shark-infested waters.

In 1980 Nell and Barrie moved to Foggathorpe, East Yorkshire, where she discovered the 11-century Norman church of All Saints, Aughton, where later she became churchwarden for more than 30 years.

In the 80s Nell gained a certificate in social studies at Hull University, then a degree in social policy and administration, and master's degrees in care for the elderly, and managing change. She then worked (1989-91) as unit manager for Bridlington Mental Health Resource Base, and resource manager (1991-92) for Grimsby Mental Health Resource Base. She won the East Riding of Yorkshire council chairman's community award, and in 2020 was awarded Maundy Money from Queen Elizabeth II.

Born in Ipstones, Staffordshire, Nell was the daughter of George and Ella Clowes, silk-mill workers who later ran a greengrocers in Leek. Times were hard for Nell and her sister, Lilian. Nell had a strong Christian faith, loved writing letters and had a fantastic memory for people's interests and families. Her family called her "annoyingly positive".

Gaining a scholarship to Leek high school for girls, she then attended Stoke Technical College studying public health, becoming the first female public health inspector for Stoke council. In 1952 she married Barrie Whittingham, a civil engineer, and they settled first in Wiltshire then in Essex, in the town of Corringham, where Nell built a sailing dinghy in the kitchen, and was hands-on with house building tasks, before they set off for Zambia.

Nell loved reading, long-distance walking, gardening, singing and went on a pilgrimage to Iona.

She was tireless in her fundraising for Aughton - a stained-glass window consecrated by the archbishop of York John Sentamu, electricity installation, and mains water for a much-needed toilet and kitchen. She also undertook huge amounts of research into the Catholic rebel Robert Aske from Aughton, the Pilgrimage of Grace, the uprising against Henry VIII and the Suppression of Religious Houses in 1535. Aske was subsequently executed by Henry VIII. Nell's supreme efforts kept Aughton church alive, and her annual Pilgrimage of Grace evenings and afternoon teas are still going.

Barrie died in 1993, and Lilian in 2017. Nell is survived by three sons, David, Mark and Nichols, five grandchildren and great-grandson.

title: Target ultra-processed food to reduce obesity in Britain | Letter
full_text_raw:
James Capon responds to an editorial on the health select committee's call for radical action to regulate food markets

The MPs' report mentioned in your editorial is welcome and overdue (The Guardian view on obesity: put public health before food industry pressure, 15 July). The health select committee is right to clarify that obesity is an engineered outcome, not a failure of willpower. But there's a flaw running through decades of British food policy that risks being repeated: the "high in fat, salt or sugar" framework itself.

"High in fat, salt or sugar" combines three nutrients as though they carry equivalent blame. However, the evidence on weight gain and type 2 diabetes points to sugar and refined carbohydrates as the primary drivers, not fat. Salt matters, chiefly when combined with sugar, but the body needs salt to function. Fat matters because without it many fat-soluble vitamins will just pass through our bodies. We need no sugar at all.

The low-fat, calorie-controlled orthodoxy inherited from flawed nutritional science still shapes labelling, reformulation targets and public understanding, encouraging manufacturers to strip out fat and replace it with sweet-tasting substitutes, while ticking the "healthier" box.

To hold supermarkets and manufacturers to account, the target must be sharpened. The culprit is the ultra-processed food model itself: products engineered for shelf life, craveability and margin, using cheap sugar and refined starch as primary ingredients. Ice-cream or potato crisps sold on rare occasions are fine, but the food system that has made them the cheapest, most heavily advertised, most convenient choice is the problem.

We shouldn't need to romanticise the Greggs sausage roll as some kind of national treasure. Consider it a treat, not a staple. That's the shift in our relationship with ultra-processed food that this report should be pushing for - one built on carbohydrate and sugar reduction, not a blunt fat-and-salt panic that has already failed us.

James Capon

Waterloo, Belgium

title: Cutting down on ultra-processed foods isn't easy. Here are eight tips that worked for my family
full_text_raw:
Experts say reducing ultra-processed foods can be challenging in a world built around convenience, but these strategies can help make it more manageable

I have been trying to eat fewer ultra-processed foods with my family for five years, and it has been challenging.

Many experts agree that ultra-processed foods (UPF) pose health risks, whether because of unhealthy ingredients, links to disease and environmental impacts, or replacing more nutritious foods. Thus, some consumers - including me - are interested in removing them from their daily diet.

Getting here took time, effort and consistency, but we have had some success. Here are some strategies we used in our family.

1. Eat more plants

Plant foods are some of the easiest, most plentiful substitutes for UPF. Most obvious are fruits and vegetables, but nuts, seeds, popcorn and roasted seaweed are other tasty, nutritious options.

When it comes to introducing fruits and vegetables, the 6 to 12-month age is crucial, says Kary Rappaport, pediatric occupational therapist and the executive director of Solid Starts, an organization that supports parents with feeding their children: "It is an exceedingly important window of time, when most babies are most developmentally open to a wide variety of foods and flavors."

Introducing new foods to older children is similar: use small tastes, different preparations and a child's natural curiosity, she says. Focus on describing the food, rather than whether the child likes it - for example, encourage them to lick or take a bite and notice qualities like sweetness or temperature. "It's not a value judgment on the food," she says.

Additionally, timing matters. "We are all more motivated to try and like things when we're a little bit hungry," says Rappaport. Try "putting out a tray of raw veggies with hummus while you're cooking dinner, during that window where kids are looking to snack", she suggests. On the other hand, don't try to force a hangry child to try new veggies.

"Even when you don't have great options that are fully non-UPF, incorporate vegetables and fruits and raw products as much as possible," says Julia Wolfson, an associate professor in public health at Johns Hopkins University.

2. Buy the best ingredients you can afford

At our local farmers' market, there is a stall selling fantastic apples. When in season, they are consistently crisp, sweet and apple-y. This is true for much of the food at the market.

"Whatever they have in your farmers' market is what is seasonal, and what is seasonal is going to be better," says chef Penny Stankiewicz. "If you go to a standard American grocery store and you buy a perfectly round, somewhat red tomato, it's going to have absolutely no flavor in January. But in August, when it's prime tomato season, you don't have to even do anything to that tomato to make it amazing."

Produce is typically more expensive at a farmer's market, and not everyone has access to one. But the flavor payoff can be huge. Otherwise, try the produce at different grocery stores; additionally, frozen and canned produce is usually preserved at its peak. After you source your produce, learn the best ways to store it so it lasts as long as possible.

3. Openly discuss food, its effects and its origins

Part of my motivation to minimize UPF was not wanting to support powerful corporations that exploited workers, mistreated animals and harmed ecosystems. The more I learned about food systems, the less I wanted to participate in them as a consumer.

Teaching children where food comes from and how to prepare it builds appreciation and understanding. Rappaport also suggests discussing how foods make their bodies feel: for instance, "if I eat too many gummy worms or I only eat a bag of Flamin' Hot Cheetos on our car trip, I'm going to feel bad. It's not gonna sit well in my belly."

Familiarize yourself and your family with the definition of UPF, so that you can identify one by looking at an ingredient list, says Wolfson.

4. Learn to cook

I already knew how to cook, but I studied the science of cooking as we embarked on this project. Now, my from-scratch meals taste better than before, sometimes more so than UPF alternatives.

Often the barriers to cooking are systemic: insufficient time and energy to cook. People may also lack confidence in their kitchen skills. "We need to make it easier for people to cook healthy meals from scratch, and that means making those scratch ingredients more available and affordable, and building those skills from a young age so that people have the confidence and self-efficacy," says Wolfson.

Stankiewicz offers the following tips for newer home cooks:

* Learn techniques: "Once you know how to saute, it doesn't matter what you put in the pan."

* Develop knife skills: "If people want to get more comfortable in the kitchen, they should take a knife skills class. Those skills are a massive upscale for confidence in the kitchen."

* Know your taste: "Know what you like, then create that, because that's the starting place. Don't start by making miso brownies when the core is to make a really good brownie that you like, because then you'll do it again."

Wolfson found in her research that "when people cook more at home, they consume fewer ultra-processed foods." She notes that even when people are cooking frequently, the majority of their calories often still come from UPF. Try not to feel defeated if you notice something similar; this speaks to the ubiquity of UPF, she says: "If you picture a typical American grocery store, almost 70% of the foods in the store are ultra processed ... that's what's mostly available to us."

5. Learn to bake

In terms of replacing UPF, replacing desserts and snacks was an easy sell. I wasn't replacing cookies with carrot sticks; I was replacing them with cookies - sometimes better ones.

Stankiewicz says to approach baking with fearlessness. "Messing up is part of it and is really how you learn," she says, telling me that brownies were created by accident when a baker didn't add enough flour to the cake.

The next step is to find trusted recipe sources. Start with recipes that are not overly intimidating or complicated. Read the recipe through before beginning, then gather the ingredients. Organize the ingredients (mise-en-place) - and then just do it!

6. Make cooking at home easy

Consuming UPF is easy. It takes very little time and mental capacity to, say, unwrap and heat something. Try to make cooking and baking at home similarly easy.

First, master a few dishes. "Find a handful of recipes or techniques that are accessible in terms of ingredients, cost, number of ingredients, and how long they're going to take to make. Then just get really good at those," says Stankiewicz.

Second, build a pantry. Keep a stock of frequently used ingredients. My husband and I maintain a shared shopping list, and if we notice something running low, we update the list.

Third, make more than you need. Leftovers are great. Even better are meals that can be frozen and reheated because your past self did all the work.

7. Prioritize mealtimes

We have a rule at the table: no phones or toys during mealtimes. We have conversations instead (often mundane and not terribly deep). Our meals aren't long; they usually take 20 minutes from when we sit down to when my youngest is done.

"The research is really clear that family meals, where people are eating together, have a huge positive impact on child development across many different areas in terms of school performance, mental health and social engagement," says Rappaport.

It can be difficult when schedules are varied. Rappaport has older children and strives to fit in three dinners together each week around work and extracurriculars. It's less about "having a Norman Rockwell meal at the dinner table" than finding opportunities to engage, she says. "It can be burritos that we got for takeout while we're all sitting at the park waiting for practice to start. I can still find those same benefits, which are that I'm asking about their day. I'm showing interest in them. We are connecting around the food."

8. Be relentlessly consistent - and don't be too hard on yourself

We have not completely eliminated UPF. But for the most part, I try to cook, choose whole food items and purchase better-quality ingredients. Over five years and thousands of decisions, our palates have shifted to prefer non-UPF foods. Cooking and baking have become routine. When you reach the stage where UPF is no longer desirable taste-wise, and regular cooking is as habitual as brushing your teeth, opting out of UPF becomes less daunting.

Without fail, every expert I spoke with emphasized the structural factors that make it difficult for consumers to reduce UPF consumption. Their prevalence, coupled with time and cost pressures mean that UPF often makes the most sense. There will be unexpected work emergencies or illnesses that make cooking from scratch impossible. Some days are full of extracurriculars and social events, and you won't have time to bake or cook. You may attend catered events, meetings or functions where you have no control over the food.

The vast majority of us will eat at least some UPF. Your children will eat UPF - especially at birthday parties and play dates. But that's not failure, just reality. Being realistic about your options can help you stay consistent instead of giving up entirely, and that's ultimately what got me and my family to this point. When it comes to UPF consumption, don't let perfect become the enemy of good.

title: Our Favorite Pet Fountains Are Perfect for Picky, Dehydrated Cats and Dogs
full_text_raw:
The Pioneer Pet Big Max Stainless Steel Drinking Fountain used to be a pick because of its mostly stainless steel construction, simple-to-fill bowl, and large capacity. But it's one of the noisier models we've tested, and it has several parts, so it's more difficult to clean than our current picks.

The Petkit EverSweet 3 Pro (UVC) Pet Water Fountain is similar in build to our top pick, yet this model has a stainless steel tank and a UVC pump that purportedly can kill bacteria. However, the area a pet drinks from is still plastic, and, unlike the EverSweet Solo 2, this model doesn't have a water-level window.

The Petkit EverSweet Max 2 Cordless UVC Pet Water Fountain can operate cordlessly or plugged into an outlet. When we were using it on battery power, it took much longer than our cordless pick to detect a pet's presence. And this fountain has more pieces to clean than most of our picks.

The FeelNeedy FN-W26 Wireless No Filters Cat Water Fountain has separate clean- and dirty-water chambers, so you don't need to use expensive filters to keep the water clean. You can set the water to refresh on a schedule. But even with frequent changing, the clean water is sitting stagnant in the tank, as opposed to constantly flowing like it does in our picks. And the machine made a loud grinding sound every time it ran out of water.

The Misfans Ceramic Cat Water Fountain is a decent ceramic option, but it was one of the noisiest fountains we tested. And the ceramic top piece slides around on the tank, which may spook a pet. It's also heavy, and the ceramic might shatter if dropped.

The Petlibro Dockstream App Monitoring Water Fountain is an older version of our upgrade pick. It was previously a pick because it's simple to clean, easy to move around, and relatively attractive. But this fountain had a few critical failures in our long-term testing: For one tester, it stopped charging, and another tester discovered the tank had sprung a leak.

The Catit Flower Fountain was a pick for several years, and I've personally owned this one. Although this fountain is attractive, has great capacity, and is easy to take apart and clean, it was also one of the loudest models we tested. The pump motor never stopped making a low, aggravating hum, which we could hear even from the next room over. Several online reviews also mention this buzzing, but it might not bother everyone.

If you prefer ceramic and are willing to pay for it, the PetSafe Drinkwell Seascape Ceramic Pet Water Fountain is a great, albeit heavy, option. The square ceramic tank and bulbous centerpiece are dishwasher-safe, but this model also has more small plastic pieces than our picks, and you still need to wash them by hand. This fountain was also the heaviest one we tested, so it was a pain to carry to and from the sink.

The Catit Stainless Steel Flower Fountain was loud, though not as loud as its plastic counterpart. It has a stainless steel dish and a blue LED light on the pump, similar to our budget pick, but this fountain is nearly twice as expensive. The stainless dish never nested properly in the tank, so it spun around easily, and that could startle some pets.

The Pioneer Pet Raindrop Fountain used to be a pick, and it's still a great fountain if you want an option with more stainless steel than plastic. But it had many of the same issues as its larger sibling, the Big Max.

The Veken Pet Fountain's pump alternated between loud and quiet with unpredictable frequency. After the first week, there was visible dirt staining the inside of the tank where a water line had been. This refused to budge when we washed it with a soft sponge (we avoided using abrasives, so as to not scratch the plastic). Also, the plastic top doesn't sit securely, so it can get knocked off easily.

The PetNF Transparent Cat Water Drinking Fountain's clear plastic tank makes it easy to see when water is low or dirty. But unlike every other fountain we tested, this one lacks a clearly delineated slot or frame for the pump to sit in. That made it difficult to line up the pump with the upper spout tube when we cleaned or refilled the tank. The PetNF fountain's pump also has a tiny lever that tends to fall off during cleaning and can easily get lost.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Pagoda Fountain may look nice in your kitchen, but it has a lot of small parts, so it's a pain to assemble and clean. It's also noisy -- both when it's running normally (the water splashes) and when it's low on water.

The PetSafe Drinkwell 360 Fountain was a nightmare to assemble, and the plastic clasps that held the centerpiece of the fountain in place were not secure enough to keep the fountain together during assembly or use. The extra rings to change the flow from the top of the fountain provided little practical benefit.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Platinum Pet Fountain is made up of many small parts and has lots of nooks and crannies. So it's difficult to keep clean and free of hard-water buildup or slime.

For a low-cost fountain, the Cat Mate Pet Fountain is decent. However, it's cheaply constructed, and it has a tendency to quickly accumulate dirt in all three chambers.

The Catit LED Flower Water Fountain is an upgraded version of the Catit Flower Fountain. It has a blue LED light, which illuminates the fountain at night. And the mini water reservoirs trap water as it falls from the flower petal, so small pets can drink from the standing water, if they choose to. Like that of its predecessor, this fountain's flower petal is removable, so you can control the flow of water. But in testing we had a harder time disconnecting the petal, and that could be a problem for people with limited hand strength. Also, when the flower petal was connected, it never consistently pooled water into the mini reservoirs.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Multi-Tier Dog and Cat Fountain's waterfall feature can get noisy, especially when it's low on water. And setting up this fountain was not an intuitive process.

This article was edited by Harry Sawyers.

title: Video: What Can a Poll Tell Us?
full_text_raw:
Everyone wants to know who's going to win an election, but predicting the outcome isn't a poll's only job. The polling reporter Ruth Igielnik shares how polls are also judged on their ability to reveal the dynamics underlying a race, as well as to uncover how shifting tides and core issues shape the views of the electorate.

A lot of the polls we conduct are about elections and who people prefer. But there's another way that we think about poll accuracy, and that is thinking about the themes of the election. Polls help us reflect back how people are feeling, not just the people around you, but the people you don't hear from. My name is Ruth Igielnik, and I work on the Times-Sienna poll. I do everything from working with our team to write the questionnaire. We field the survey and then analyze the results afterwards. We ask voters how they feel about the economy, how they're feeling about the political parties, how voters are feeling about immigration. In the last 25 years, many of our elections in swing states have come down to one-to-two percentage points, and a typical poll margin of error is about three percentage points. It's very difficult for polls to be that precise when elections are that close. Heading into the 2026 midterms, we try to think of new ways to reach voters. We've experimented with reaching them over a text message and through the mail, and we conduct our polls over the phone, making sure that we have the representative sample that we need in order to be accurate.

title: Prosecutors argue D4vd had financial motivation to kill Celeste Rivas Hernandez
full_text_raw:
Details emerge about how much Interscope Records paid the singer at hearing to determine if there is probable cause for murder case to proceed to trial

Singer D4vd had a multi-million dollar recording deal, an executive at his former label testified on Wednesday, as prosecutors sought to establish the musician had a financial motivation to kill Celeste Rivas Hernandez.

Details emerged around how much Interscope Records was paying the singer, who was born David Anthony Burke, on the second day of a hearing to determine if there is probable cause for him to stand trial for the murder and sexual abuse of Rivas Hernandez.

The teenager's body was found last year in gruesome conditions in a car registered to the musician.

Prosecutors accuse Burke of stabbing Rivas Hernandez, 14, to death at his Los Angeles residence to silence her from divulging the sexual nature of their relationship as his career was on the rise.

Burke has pleaded not guilty to charges that include first-degree murder, "lewd and lascivious acts" with a child under the age of 14, and the mutilation of human remains. His defense team has said their client "was not the cause" of Hernandez's death.

On the first day of hearings on Tuesday, prosecutors showed photos of the dismembered and decomposing body of Rivas Hernandez, and alleged the singer had severely mutilated her body. They also sought to show that the singer used his credit cards to purchase chainsaws, a body bag and a shovel.

The preliminary hearing is expected to last between three and five days.

Burke, now 21, was arrested in April and has been held in custody since then without bail.

If convicted of murder, he could face the death penalty, or life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Rivas Hernandez' family was in court for the start of the hearing on Tuesday. After Burke's arrest in April, the family said in a statement: "Celeste was a beautiful, strong girl who loved to sing and dance. Every Friday night was movie night and we spent wonderful times together. We love her very much and she always told us that she loved us. We miss her deeply. All we want is justice for Celeste."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Whitmer makes 'science of reading' training mandatory for Michigan teachers
full_text_raw:
Michigan elementary school teachers will be required to take literacy training by the 2031-2032 school year, under a new law signed by Gov. Gretchen Whitmer Tuesday.

The law requires K-5 instructors who teach reading or language arts to receive training and requires the state Department of Education to select at least two vendors each year to provide the training.

"We all want results for our kids," Whitmer said at an event in Southfield promoting the new education budget. "And none of us is patient about it, nor should we be. We want those results fast. But here's what we know: literacy is a marathon, it's not a miracle. The steps we're taking now are the first steps down a road ahead. It will take time, but if we give every child a strong early start, using proven methods, offering extra help, we can ensure that every child can read."

The 'science of reading' refers to research about how the brain learns to read. Sometimes the term is used as a shorthand for an emphasis on phonics, which is one aspect of learning to read.

Whitmer has said literacy is her number one priority in her last term, and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have called for changes to how Michigan handles literacy. Just 38.9% of Michigan third graders are proficient in reading, according to state tests, and the state ranks 44th for fourth grade reading on national assessments.

Districts were already required to teach in "evidence-based" ways and screen students for traits of dyslexia beginning with the 2027-28 school year, under laws passed in 2024. Districts must also affirm that teachers have received information about evidence-based literacy practices and related topics.

But the law signed Tuesday takes the requirements a step further by prescribing what type of training is required of K-5 teachers.

The law does not name an education vendor to provide the training, but lawmakers, state superintendent Glenn Maleyko, Whitmer and House Speaker Matt Hall have named LETRS, offered by vendor Lexia, in public appearances or news releases.

"The budget guarantees that not some, not most, but all reading teachers in Michigan complete training to teach students the science of reading methods like phonics," said Whitmer.

Whitmer also signed House Bill 5646, which requires the state superintendent to only approve teacher preparation programs and grant teacher certificates when certain literacy requirements have been met.

Michigan also provides funding for literacy coaches, vetted curricula and for support material for students who are struggling in class. The state has also expanded pre-K access, which has prompted some public school districts to expand classrooms or renovating buildings to accommodate more 4-year-olds.

How long will this training take?

The state has already provided $44 million toward LETRS training for those who want to take it. Otherstates have encouraged or mandated LETRS training, and the majority have made changes to reading policies.

"Today, we celebrate for the students of Michigan!" said state Rep. Nancy DeBoer, R-Holland in a statement. DeBoer sponsored the training requirement legislation.

"Learning to Read will unlock their futures," she said. "We have come together to support our families, our dedicated educators, and our innovative business community. Michigan is worth it!"

The law requires teachers to receive the training but only if the Legislature provides "sufficient" funding.

Although the law will require that the state name two vendors, the new education budget includes another $75 million specifically for LETRS training.

Many teachers across the state have already taken LETRS training. As of July 1, 5,684 educators are in training and 7,460 have completed the training, according to the Michigan Department of Education.

But the training typically takes two years. Some schools offer stipends for teachers to take the training or time during the day for the teacher to train while a substitute teacher watches their classroom.

Michigan teachers with an interim teaching certificate would not be required to take the training.

title: 'He knows what he's doing': Burnham's off-the-cuff remarks inspire headlines and headaches
full_text_raw:
New PM's conversational tone is markedly different to his predecessor's, but carries risk of sowing confusion

Before he became Britain's prime minister, Andy Burnham promised to "do politics differently". Just three days into his time in Downing Street, that approach is already being put to the test.

In the last two days, the prime minister has been accused of performing U-turns over raising the income tax threshold, raising taxes for higher earners and freezing private sector rents.

The minor controversies are mostly a function of the fact Burnham has come into office with a rare combination of not having fixed his policy platform and a habit of speaking openly about his ideas before they are fully formed.

Earlier this week, for example, Burnham said while campaigning in the Makerfield byelection which secured his return to parliament, he heard complaints about the income tax threshold more than any other issue. This prompted speculation he would raise it once he became PM.

Reports on Tuesday suggested he had ruled it out, only for him to clarify on Wednesday that it was still an option. As he did, Burnham expressed surprise that people had put so much stock in his original comments.

"It's funny these days you can't answer a question honestly without then people reading everything else into it," he told broadcasters. "I want to answer questions honestly in this job, as I said before. I think that's all about trust in politics and doing politics differently, and I'm determined to keep working in that way."

He added: "It's just perhaps the way politics is these days and the way people report things, but that was an honest answer."

A similar scenario played out over the issue of freezing private sector rents. Asked by reporters on Monday if such a move could be part of his package to tackle the UK's cost-of-living crisis, the prime minister replied: "We're looking at all of those things."

On Wednesday, however, it was reported that officials are not actively considering such a move.

Burnham has also kickstarted an unexpected debate on releasing prisoners early, saying he would review the policy, which has been one of the government's main tools for easing overcrowding in prisons.

"Andy appears to have just realised he is the prime minister," said one Labour official. "He is a talented communicator and he is right that the media spins messages and this can be a hostile environment. But it is his job to go into that with his eyes wide open.

"He hasn't fought an election or had much scrutiny, and so people are desperately trying to understand what his priorities and platforms are."

For many, Burnham's approach is a necessary response to the buttoned-up way in which his predecessor, Keir Starmer, used to speak and to the modern media environment which demands authenticity above discipline.

His open, conversational style worked well as Greater Manchester mayor, when reporters became used to his off-the-cuff comments during press conferences and he seems determined to bring the same outlook to Downing Street.

"He's not an idiot," said Sean Kemp, who advised the former Liberal Democrat leader Nick Clegg and is now a partner at the political comms firm Hanbury Strategy. "He knows what he's doing, but he doesn't care, and he's going to keep on saying it. And he's done it so much now, I'm starting to think now that he's decided this is just how he does things."

The approach is also reflected in the media he uses to communicate. He has already shown his willingness to use mischievous social media posts to get his message across, and took part in an online question-and-answer session on Reddit shortly after winning the Makerfield byelection.

But the chances of being misunderstood were highlighted in another post-Makerfield interview, with the England footballer turned podcaster Gary Lineker. In comments that were interpreted by some as leaving the door open to a wealth tax and others as ruling it out, he said: "I do believe we need a greater sense of fairness and people feeling that things are being done in the right way and a fair way.

"But at the same time, you know, I don't want to sort of be perceived as somebody who's coming in with grudges and agendas and, you know, going to just immediately find or demonise one group or create a new way of dividing people."

His desire to bypass traditional political journalism is not new, say political communication experts. But it does carry risks. "I think every single prime minister in the last 25 years has tried to do that," said Kemp.

"Then they realise that these are the people reporting day to day on what you are doing, and still, to a great extent, are setting the parameters of how you're viewed."

Guto Harri, who was once communications director to the former prime minister Boris Johnson, said: "He's not an ordinary person any more, he is the first lord of the Treasury and the prime minister of Britain.

"So if he says these things, it is reasonable for the people who hear him to think something will follow. And if something doesn't follow, then people are likely to become cynical quite quickly."

title: Tiny Love Stories: 'A Full, Hiccuping Meltdown Over Nothing'
full_text_raw:
Modern Love in miniature, featuring reader-submitted stories of no more than 100 words.

My daughter's birthday falls three days after my late brother's. Every July, while I hang lanterns and fill gift bags, grief flashes through me. My daughter is 6 and doesn't know she should have an Uncle Jay. He was nine years my junior, a boy I mothered, adored and eventually couldn't save from untreated schizophrenia and suicide. I thought telling her about him would only pass down pain. But grief is not the whole story of his life, or our bond. Soon, I will tell my daughter about my brother, confident that I'll also be able to pass down love. -- Ashley Womble

'Steady as the Sun'

I called my high school friends Anvi and Ashwini in a full, hiccuping meltdown over nothing, a PMS spiral that felt stupidly enormous. Now roommates, both happened to be working from home. Twenty minutes later, they were at my door. No questions, just action: They pulled me out of bed, put shoes on my feet and drove me to get ice cream. We relaxed in the grass in Dolores Park, sharing two pints, watching San Francisco buzz around us. They sat beside me, steady as the sun above, reminding me, without saying a word, that I was never alone. -- Kaanthi Pandhigunta

He Saw Me Before I Could

Fifth grade, hazel eyes, curly hair, honey-toned skin. I was infatuated with him, already tailoring plans for us to fall in love. I confessed my feelings. He gently replied, "Tiff, you're like my boy; you don't really see me that way, do you?" Years passed, his question lingering in my mind. Then one day, walking along the boardwalk, hand in hand with my girlfriend, I saw him again. I smiled, introducing them. His hazel eyes brightened with happiness when he saw that I had found myself and my sexual identity, something he seemed to understand long before I ever could. -- Tiffany Pippins

Never Too Old to Be Mothered

I thought I wanted to be alone with my husband after my son was born, but then my mother brought me breakfast in bed -- banana pancakes, right off the stove, with warmed syrup on the side. She cut them into pieces so I could eat with one hand while holding the baby. They tasted so good that I cried. Today we were with my son at the park. As I chased him with his hat, my mother asked, "Did you get sunscreen on?" "Yes, just need to get his legs," I said. "Not him," she replied, smiling. "You!" -- Virginia Craig

title: Woman, 70, charged with murder of British expat Karen Carter in France
full_text_raw:
The public prosecutor for the region said the suspect had been initially arrested shortly after the murder on 29 April last year

A 70-year-old woman has been charged with the murder of Karen Carter, the British expat found dead in south-western France last year, according to reports.

According to the Dordogne Libre and others, the woman was charged on 2 July with Carter's murder in Tremolat, in the Dordogne, and is "under judicial supervision".

Jacques-Édouard Andrault, the public prosecutor for the region, is quoted as confirming the charge, adding that the suspect had been arrested shortly after the murder on 29 April last year, but was released without charge at the time.

Andrault told reporters: "On July 2nd, the investigating judge in Périgueux formally charged a woman with murder."

He added that "this 70-year-old woman, originally from Trémolat, was taken into custody on April 30, 2025, during a preliminary investigation, before being released".

"Since then, the investigations conducted as part of the judicial inquiry opened on May 7, 2025, have led the investigating judge to indict her," he said, adding "this woman has been placed under judicial supervision".

Carter, a 65-year-old British-South African national, ran two gites (holiday rental homes) in the village of Tremolat, a beautifully renovated 250-year-old farmhouse and neighbouring 18th-century stone barn collectively called Les Chouettes.

She was said to divide her time between the Dordogne and the home she shared with her husband, Alan Carter, in KuGompo City, South Africa.

An autopsy reportedly revealed that Carter died from severe blood loss after being stabbed multiple times, collapsing and dying next to her car.

Eight serious wounds were reportedly noted in total, including to the "chest, abdomen and forearm", as well as "superficial ones on the thigh, shoulder and thumbs".

Carter had reportedly been at a wine-tasting party at Cafe Village Trémolat, described on Facebook as "an association that wants to offer the people of Trémolat and the surrounding area a meeting place", with about 15 other guests, including Eric Chassagne, the village's mayor.

A few days after the attack a then 69-year-old local woman was arrested. She was released without charge shortly after.

It later emerged that Carter was discovered by a 75-year-old businessman, Jean-François Guerrier, with whom she was reportedly in a relationship. The nature of their relationship was seized upon and speculated over by tabloids.

Carter's husband, a former London Stock Exchange worker who was in South Africa at the time of the murder, expressed his shock at the revelations that his wife had "started a relationship" with another man, saying he understood Guerrier was "just a friend of hers".

title: Nell Whittingham obituary
full_text_raw:
My friend Nell Whittingham, who has died aged 96, relished adventure. When her husband Barrie's career took their family to Zambia in the 1960s they had a Piper Tri-Pacer aircraft and flew the Flying Doctor service - Nell also helped with weather reports and logistics. In the 70s they lived in Swaziland and Sudan, then Nigeria, where Nell set up a weather station to monitor wind for the Savannah Sugar Factory. During a stint in Papua New Guinea, she renovated a dug-out canoe and sailed in shark-infested waters.

In 1980 Nell and Barrie moved to Foggathorpe, East Yorkshire, where she discovered the 11-century Norman church of All Saints, Aughton, where later she became churchwarden for more than 30 years.

In the 80s Nell gained a certificate in social studies at Hull University, then a degree in social policy and administration, and master's degrees in care for the elderly, and managing change. She then worked (1989-91) as unit manager for Bridlington Mental Health Resource Base, and resource manager (1991-92) for Grimsby Mental Health Resource Base. She won the East Riding of Yorkshire council chairman's community award, and in 2020 was awarded Maundy Money from Queen Elizabeth II.

Born in Ipstones, Staffordshire, Nell was the daughter of George and Ella Clowes, silk-mill workers who later ran a greengrocers in Leek. Times were hard for Nell and her sister, Lilian. Nell had a strong Christian faith, loved writing letters and had a fantastic memory for people's interests and families. Her family called her "annoyingly positive".

Gaining a scholarship to Leek high school for girls, she then attended Stoke Technical College studying public health, becoming the first female public health inspector for Stoke council. In 1952 she married Barrie Whittingham, a civil engineer, and they settled first in Wiltshire then in Essex, in the town of Corringham, where Nell built a sailing dinghy in the kitchen, and was hands-on with house building tasks, before they set off for Zambia.

Nell loved reading, long-distance walking, gardening, singing and went on a pilgrimage to Iona.

She was tireless in her fundraising for Aughton - a stained-glass window consecrated by the archbishop of York John Sentamu, electricity installation, and mains water for a much-needed toilet and kitchen. She also undertook huge amounts of research into the Catholic rebel Robert Aske from Aughton, the Pilgrimage of Grace, the uprising against Henry VIII and the Suppression of Religious Houses in 1535. Aske was subsequently executed by Henry VIII. Nell's supreme efforts kept Aughton church alive, and her annual Pilgrimage of Grace evenings and afternoon teas are still going.

Barrie died in 1993, and Lilian in 2017. Nell is survived by three sons, David, Mark and Nichols, five grandchildren and great-grandson.

title: Target ultra-processed food to reduce obesity in Britain | Letter
full_text_raw:
James Capon responds to an editorial on the health select committee's call for radical action to regulate food markets

The MPs' report mentioned in your editorial is welcome and overdue (The Guardian view on obesity: put public health before food industry pressure, 15 July). The health select committee is right to clarify that obesity is an engineered outcome, not a failure of willpower. But there's a flaw running through decades of British food policy that risks being repeated: the "high in fat, salt or sugar" framework itself.

"High in fat, salt or sugar" combines three nutrients as though they carry equivalent blame. However, the evidence on weight gain and type 2 diabetes points to sugar and refined carbohydrates as the primary drivers, not fat. Salt matters, chiefly when combined with sugar, but the body needs salt to function. Fat matters because without it many fat-soluble vitamins will just pass through our bodies. We need no sugar at all.

The low-fat, calorie-controlled orthodoxy inherited from flawed nutritional science still shapes labelling, reformulation targets and public understanding, encouraging manufacturers to strip out fat and replace it with sweet-tasting substitutes, while ticking the "healthier" box.

To hold supermarkets and manufacturers to account, the target must be sharpened. The culprit is the ultra-processed food model itself: products engineered for shelf life, craveability and margin, using cheap sugar and refined starch as primary ingredients. Ice-cream or potato crisps sold on rare occasions are fine, but the food system that has made them the cheapest, most heavily advertised, most convenient choice is the problem.

We shouldn't need to romanticise the Greggs sausage roll as some kind of national treasure. Consider it a treat, not a staple. That's the shift in our relationship with ultra-processed food that this report should be pushing for - one built on carbohydrate and sugar reduction, not a blunt fat-and-salt panic that has already failed us.

James Capon

Waterloo, Belgium

title: Cutting down on ultra-processed foods isn't easy. Here are eight tips that worked for my family
full_text_raw:
Experts say reducing ultra-processed foods can be challenging in a world built around convenience, but these strategies can help make it more manageable

I have been trying to eat fewer ultra-processed foods with my family for five years, and it has been challenging.

Many experts agree that ultra-processed foods (UPF) pose health risks, whether because of unhealthy ingredients, links to disease and environmental impacts, or replacing more nutritious foods. Thus, some consumers - including me - are interested in removing them from their daily diet.

Getting here took time, effort and consistency, but we have had some success. Here are some strategies we used in our family.

1. Eat more plants

Plant foods are some of the easiest, most plentiful substitutes for UPF. Most obvious are fruits and vegetables, but nuts, seeds, popcorn and roasted seaweed are other tasty, nutritious options.

When it comes to introducing fruits and vegetables, the 6 to 12-month age is crucial, says Kary Rappaport, pediatric occupational therapist and the executive director of Solid Starts, an organization that supports parents with feeding their children: "It is an exceedingly important window of time, when most babies are most developmentally open to a wide variety of foods and flavors."

Introducing new foods to older children is similar: use small tastes, different preparations and a child's natural curiosity, she says. Focus on describing the food, rather than whether the child likes it - for example, encourage them to lick or take a bite and notice qualities like sweetness or temperature. "It's not a value judgment on the food," she says.

Additionally, timing matters. "We are all more motivated to try and like things when we're a little bit hungry," says Rappaport. Try "putting out a tray of raw veggies with hummus while you're cooking dinner, during that window where kids are looking to snack", she suggests. On the other hand, don't try to force a hangry child to try new veggies.

"Even when you don't have great options that are fully non-UPF, incorporate vegetables and fruits and raw products as much as possible," says Julia Wolfson, an associate professor in public health at Johns Hopkins University.

2. Buy the best ingredients you can afford

At our local farmers' market, there is a stall selling fantastic apples. When in season, they are consistently crisp, sweet and apple-y. This is true for much of the food at the market.

"Whatever they have in your farmers' market is what is seasonal, and what is seasonal is going to be better," says chef Penny Stankiewicz. "If you go to a standard American grocery store and you buy a perfectly round, somewhat red tomato, it's going to have absolutely no flavor in January. But in August, when it's prime tomato season, you don't have to even do anything to that tomato to make it amazing."

Produce is typically more expensive at a farmer's market, and not everyone has access to one. But the flavor payoff can be huge. Otherwise, try the produce at different grocery stores; additionally, frozen and canned produce is usually preserved at its peak. After you source your produce, learn the best ways to store it so it lasts as long as possible.

3. Openly discuss food, its effects and its origins

Part of my motivation to minimize UPF was not wanting to support powerful corporations that exploited workers, mistreated animals and harmed ecosystems. The more I learned about food systems, the less I wanted to participate in them as a consumer.

Teaching children where food comes from and how to prepare it builds appreciation and understanding. Rappaport also suggests discussing how foods make their bodies feel: for instance, "if I eat too many gummy worms or I only eat a bag of Flamin' Hot Cheetos on our car trip, I'm going to feel bad. It's not gonna sit well in my belly."

Familiarize yourself and your family with the definition of UPF, so that you can identify one by looking at an ingredient list, says Wolfson.

4. Learn to cook

I already knew how to cook, but I studied the science of cooking as we embarked on this project. Now, my from-scratch meals taste better than before, sometimes more so than UPF alternatives.

Often the barriers to cooking are systemic: insufficient time and energy to cook. People may also lack confidence in their kitchen skills. "We need to make it easier for people to cook healthy meals from scratch, and that means making those scratch ingredients more available and affordable, and building those skills from a young age so that people have the confidence and self-efficacy," says Wolfson.

Stankiewicz offers the following tips for newer home cooks:

* Learn techniques: "Once you know how to saute, it doesn't matter what you put in the pan."

* Develop knife skills: "If people want to get more comfortable in the kitchen, they should take a knife skills class. Those skills are a massive upscale for confidence in the kitchen."

* Know your taste: "Know what you like, then create that, because that's the starting place. Don't start by making miso brownies when the core is to make a really good brownie that you like, because then you'll do it again."

Wolfson found in her research that "when people cook more at home, they consume fewer ultra-processed foods." She notes that even when people are cooking frequently, the majority of their calories often still come from UPF. Try not to feel defeated if you notice something similar; this speaks to the ubiquity of UPF, she says: "If you picture a typical American grocery store, almost 70% of the foods in the store are ultra processed ... that's what's mostly available to us."

5. Learn to bake

In terms of replacing UPF, replacing desserts and snacks was an easy sell. I wasn't replacing cookies with carrot sticks; I was replacing them with cookies - sometimes better ones.

Stankiewicz says to approach baking with fearlessness. "Messing up is part of it and is really how you learn," she says, telling me that brownies were created by accident when a baker didn't add enough flour to the cake.

The next step is to find trusted recipe sources. Start with recipes that are not overly intimidating or complicated. Read the recipe through before beginning, then gather the ingredients. Organize the ingredients (mise-en-place) - and then just do it!

6. Make cooking at home easy

Consuming UPF is easy. It takes very little time and mental capacity to, say, unwrap and heat something. Try to make cooking and baking at home similarly easy.

First, master a few dishes. "Find a handful of recipes or techniques that are accessible in terms of ingredients, cost, number of ingredients, and how long they're going to take to make. Then just get really good at those," says Stankiewicz.

Second, build a pantry. Keep a stock of frequently used ingredients. My husband and I maintain a shared shopping list, and if we notice something running low, we update the list.

Third, make more than you need. Leftovers are great. Even better are meals that can be frozen and reheated because your past self did all the work.

7. Prioritize mealtimes

We have a rule at the table: no phones or toys during mealtimes. We have conversations instead (often mundane and not terribly deep). Our meals aren't long; they usually take 20 minutes from when we sit down to when my youngest is done.

"The research is really clear that family meals, where people are eating together, have a huge positive impact on child development across many different areas in terms of school performance, mental health and social engagement," says Rappaport.

It can be difficult when schedules are varied. Rappaport has older children and strives to fit in three dinners together each week around work and extracurriculars. It's less about "having a Norman Rockwell meal at the dinner table" than finding opportunities to engage, she says. "It can be burritos that we got for takeout while we're all sitting at the park waiting for practice to start. I can still find those same benefits, which are that I'm asking about their day. I'm showing interest in them. We are connecting around the food."

8. Be relentlessly consistent - and don't be too hard on yourself

We have not completely eliminated UPF. But for the most part, I try to cook, choose whole food items and purchase better-quality ingredients. Over five years and thousands of decisions, our palates have shifted to prefer non-UPF foods. Cooking and baking have become routine. When you reach the stage where UPF is no longer desirable taste-wise, and regular cooking is as habitual as brushing your teeth, opting out of UPF becomes less daunting.

Without fail, every expert I spoke with emphasized the structural factors that make it difficult for consumers to reduce UPF consumption. Their prevalence, coupled with time and cost pressures mean that UPF often makes the most sense. There will be unexpected work emergencies or illnesses that make cooking from scratch impossible. Some days are full of extracurriculars and social events, and you won't have time to bake or cook. You may attend catered events, meetings or functions where you have no control over the food.

The vast majority of us will eat at least some UPF. Your children will eat UPF - especially at birthday parties and play dates. But that's not failure, just reality. Being realistic about your options can help you stay consistent instead of giving up entirely, and that's ultimately what got me and my family to this point. When it comes to UPF consumption, don't let perfect become the enemy of good.

title: Geoffrey King obituary
full_text_raw:
My father, Geoffrey King, who has died aged 82, was a prolific research scientist whose papers on geophysics have been cited more than 30,000 times. His most influential contribution was a 1994 paper, published in the Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America, that revolutionised earthquake forecasting.

After early work at Cambridge University, he moved to the US in 1987 to work at the US Geological Survey in Colorado and then in 1990 to France, where he spent 20 happy years as a research professor at the Institut de Physique du Globe in Paris. He became a naturalised Frenchman and greatly enjoyed telling me how much better France was than the UK.

Born in Kampala, Uganda, Geoffrey was one of the four children of Peggy (nee Wells) and Basil King, both British geologists. Basil was working with the Uganda Geological Survey mapping the Rift Valley. When Basil was appointed to the staff of Glasgow University, the family returned to the UK. Geoffrey went to school in Glasgow, a city he adored, and then Haberdashers' boys' school in Elstree, Hertfordshire. There his final school report ominously said, "[Geoffrey] must appreciate that the future is shaped in the present: it would be a great pity if his ambitions were not realised through a want of determined application."

But at Durham University, my father found himself, albeit by way of all the exciting new freedoms the 1960s offered. He loved ideas and exploring the new; asking questions was exciting, questioning orthodoxy essential. He went on to gain a first in applied physics and then a Cambridge PhD spent in a disused railway tunnel in Yorkshire designing better instruments to record earthquakes.

Geoffrey and his father may remain the only people to have had a (terrible, but scientifically accurate) poem published in the scientific journal Nature. About plate tectonics, it appeared in 1971 - the opening lines read "They put a girdle around the Earth/And named it the Worldwide Rift/It helps explain the ocean floor/And Continental Drift".

The work possibly closest to his heart came later, when he explored how seismically active landscapes gave early humans a survival advantage - the cliffs and rocky features provide natural places to hide, hunt and farm.

When he left the UK in the 1980s, in part, this was disgust at the Thatcher government's policies on tertiary education. I also suspect he annoyed his stuffier academic colleagues, who tried to get him to stick to orthodoxy or - even worse - do some administration.

As a personality, he was mischievous. As a father, he was a whirlwind - fun and always a little rebellious. He adored socialising - being among like-minded people from a range of disciplines was a joy. From his flat in Paris on the right bank of the Seine, he hosted large dinner parties full of wine, cheese and rabbit stews made in an enormous slow cooker. Last year, he told me with conviction: "I've had an amazing life."

Geoffrey and my mother, Anna, separated when I was young. He is survived by me, three grandchildren, Esmé, Juno and Benedict, and his younger twin siblings, Peter and Diana.

title: Rei Ami from 'KPop Demon Hunters' and comedian Ken Jeong take a bite out of 'Shark Week'
full_text_raw:
NEW YORK (AP) -- Rei Ami, whose voice helped fuel the hit movie "KPop Demon Hunters," recently found herself facing plenty of real hunters -- watching from the ocean floor as about 16 reef sharks went on a feeding frenzy.

She was scared, sure. But more than that, she was brought to tears.

"I thought I'd be a bit more petrified, but I was enamored. I was in awe. It was witnessing nature," she says. "You can't put it into words the emotions and the feelings that you experience."

Viewers can watch Rei Ami -- and hear her sing a new K-pop song inspired by her experience with sharks while off the Korean Peninsula -- as Discovery Channel's "Shark Week" kicks off Sunday.

Twenty new, hourlong shows leap deep into the world of the ancient predators, from a record-setting dive attempt into shark-infested waters to trying to find out what triggers giant bull sharks to confront humans.

"Growing up, I always watched 'Shark Week,'" says Rei Ami. "You see those epic commercials, with the great white jumping out and eating the chum and the tuna. That's ingrained in my brain forever."

Actor-comedian Ken Jeong joins her to start the week off with the show "K-Pop Shark Heroes" on Sunday. But while she went on two cage dives and two free dives with hammerheads and reef sharks and bull sharks, he preferred to stay out of the water.

"I'm more of the Christopher Nolan of the shark 'Odyssey' -- just overseeing it," Jeong jokes. "Just overlooking everything. High and dry. That's when I do my best work."

It's a shark-a-thon

The seven nights of new shows ends Aug. 1 with a look at how great whites are moving further up the East Coast and an examination of how thresher sharks use their tails to stun and kill prey.

One highlight is watching high diver Molly Carlson leap 50 feet (15 meters) from a helicopter into a Plexiglas cage in the ocean surrounded by circling reef sharks. She's OK with jumping from enormous heights, but sharks terrify her.

"There was zero chances of me ever swimming with sharks. This was just not on my radar," she says. "That's always been my thing, and so for me to be invited to be on 'Shark Week,' I was like 'Why me?'"

Viewers will see Carlson, who has been frank about her struggles with anxiety, overcome her lifelong fear of sharks. Carlson hopes she can motivate others.

"If I can inspire that next 16-year-old girl who wants to just hide in her room and never come out because she's scared of so many things, then I'm absolutely going to find a way to do this," she says. "You're allowed to be scared and do it anyways. And so I think that was the big purpose behind this project for me."

This year's highlights also include an attempt to locate a rumored 15-foot (4-meter) mako off the coast of Southern California, which would make it the largest ever documented.

Marine biologist Kendyl Berna, a "Shark Week" veteran who co-founded the ecology group Beyond the Reef, says her team of scientists were betting on the fact that a marine heat wave has made mako prey in those waters abundant, allowing the sharks to get bigger.

"Sharks are the cockroaches of the sea because they've been around for 450 million years. They're older than dinosaurs, they're older than trees. Sharks have just been around, but the form that they're taking constantly changes," she says.

'Shark Week' is fun but also educational

"Shark Week" has become a key part of the summer holiday TV schedule, a place where humans safe on land can see ancient apex predators unnervingly glide into view and snap open their jaws, fueling nightmares.

As always, there is a deep respect for the creatures and strong science beneath the amusing titles, sharky puns, dramatic music and racy titles like "Chum Island: Catching a Killer" and "Sharkzilla Takes New York."

"While 'Shark Week' is very entertaining and thrilling, it is at the core very educational. And I think there's still so much misinformation regarding sharks and how they behave," says Rei Ami.

"Through these episodes, people can understand, there's really no reason to fear them, you know? And I hope that message gets received."

Discovery's "Shark Week" has a rival -- National Geographic's "SharkFest," which also has hours of sharky content. And there's Amazon Studios' new movie "The Devil's Mouth," which has bull sharks terrorizing college students in a flooded cave system.

"Shark Week" also has practical advice about what to do when you find yourself face-to-snout with a shark, a rising concern from Korea to Brooklyn as interactions increase. The advice is clear: Stop splashing.

"It's even more imperative that humans know how to act and react in a situation when they are in the waters and they see a shark," says Rei Ami. "It would really, I think, help the public to understand how these apex predators work and behave."

title: Great Barrier Reef microbiome mapped as researchers discover 500 bacterial species previously unknown to science
full_text_raw:
Research identifies 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what scientists estimate to be 362,802 different viruses

More than a decade after the human microbiome was comprehensively mapped, scientists have now identified the vast communities of microbes that make up the Great Barrier Reef.

Analysing DNA from seawater samples of 48 reefs, researchers have mapped the microbiome of the Great Barrier Reef, documenting more than 360,000 distinct viruses as well as more than 500 new bacterial species not previously known to science.

The research, published in the journal Nature, was led by scientists at the University of Queensland and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).

Dr Yun Kit Yeoh, a senior research scientist at AIMS and a senior author of the paper, described microorganisms as a "very important part of the reef ecosystem" that underpinned marine food chains.

"Many of the microbes on the reef can photosynthesise ... like plants, they can take light energy [and] can convert carbon dioxide into oxygen.

"They are eaten by krill and other zooplankton which are then consumed by other animals.

"We haven't been able to really study a lot of them except for a select few that we can grow properly in the lab on petri dishes."

But recent technological advances have allowed scientists to sequence DNA taken from the environment, giving a fuller picture of these microscopic communities.

The field - known as metagenomics - is akin to solving thousands of jigsaw puzzles simultaneously; a single drop of seawater can contain the DNA of thousands of different microbes.

"We wouldn't have been able to do this, say, 10 years ago, but fortunately computing power keeps increasing at an exponential rate," said Prof Philip Hugenholtz, a microbiologist at the University of Queensland and a senior author on the paper.

The research, which first began more than five years ago, identified 808,585 viral genomes belonging to what the researchers estimate to be 362,802 different viruses.

The analysis also identified 5,283 bacterial and archaeal genomes representing 876 distinct species - 584 of which have never been documented before.

Hugenholtz said those large figures were expected. "This is just how huge the microbial world is," he said. "We know that everywhere we sequence ... there's always new viruses turning up.

"I was a little bit surprised that we found over 500 new bacterial species.

"The human gut and the marine ecosystem I would say are the two most sequenced ecosystems on the planet."

The discovery raises the question as to whether the species were unique to the Great Barrier Reef, or were yet to be discovered in other reef ecosystems, Hugenholtz added.

The researchers believe the mapped microbiome could be used as a reef monitoring tool. "We can now use it to start exploring what makes a healthy reef system," Yeoh said. "Then we can examine how these microbes respond to, say, changes ... associated with climate change, with heat stress, bleaching, human activity, or other environmental perturbations.

"Microbial communities can tell you an awful lot. Often you'll see changes in the microbial populations before you see more visible changes [on the reef]."

The microbes in a particular marine area can indicate whether fishing has occurred in a no-take zone, for example. They can also indicate whether heavy metal contamination has occurred.

"It's quite expensive to get a readout of heavy metals - it's cheaper to get a read out of the changes that they have on microbial communities," Hugenholtz said.

The researchers used long-read sequencing technology, which enables large strands of DNA to be read at one time, without the need to break them into smaller fragments.

Hugenholtz likens it to doing jigsaw puzzles with bigger pieces, "which means you'll be able to put those jigsaw puzzles back together more easily".

title: Widow of Malcolm-Jamal Warner Sues His Mother for $1.2 Million
full_text_raw:
Tenisha Delilah Warner said in a lawsuit filed in Georgia that she was entitled to the money according to a premarital agreement.

The widow of the actor Malcolm-Jamal Warner is suing his mother to recover at least $1.2 million from a family trust, claiming she was owed money from a premarital agreement, according to court documents.

The suit was filed on Monday in DeKalb County Superior Court in Georgia, one year after Mr. Warner, who rose to fame playing Theo Huxtable on "The Cosby Show," died at 54 when he drowned at a beach in Costa Rica.

In the lawsuit, Mr. Warner's wife, Tenisha Delilah Warner, names Mr. Warner's mother, Pamela Warner, as the defendant in her role as the successor trustee of a Warner family revocable trust dated Oct. 7, 1996.

The 1996 trust was created when Mr. Warner was 26 years old, 20 years before he and his wife met, and states that he was unmarried and had no children, according to the suit.

Tenisha Delilah Warner, in a statement emailed by a representative on Wednesday, said Mr. Warner had been close to finalizing a new estate plan to replace the "stale plan."

"Sadly, he was unable to do so before we lost him," she said.

Tenisha Delilah Warner's lawyers did not reply to emails seeking comment. The lawsuit said she was seeking a judgment based on an alleged breach of contract.

Pamela Warner and her lawyers did not immediately reply to email requests for comment on Wednesday.

"For the last year, I have attempted to privately settle my beloved husband's complicated estate and honor his last wishes," Tenisha Delilah Warner said in her statement. "Malcolm had every intention to provide for our 9-year-old daughter and me."

The lawsuit says she and Mr. Warner had in place a premarital agreement when they married on May 23, 2022. The filing said he had agreed to buy a $1 million life insurance policy, and to pay her $16,000 on each anniversary of their marriage. It alleged that he did not do so.

Mr. Warner, the filing alleges, also did not deliver on an agreement to fund a Roth IRA for her during their marriage, and did not pay her a $5,000 monthly salary, as promised, for working as his chief of staff and assistant. It claims the total owed to her is $1,276,042.46.

title: Our Favorite Pet Fountains Are Perfect for Picky, Dehydrated Cats and Dogs
full_text_raw:
The Pioneer Pet Big Max Stainless Steel Drinking Fountain used to be a pick because of its mostly stainless steel construction, simple-to-fill bowl, and large capacity. But it's one of the noisier models we've tested, and it has several parts, so it's more difficult to clean than our current picks.

The Petkit EverSweet 3 Pro (UVC) Pet Water Fountain is similar in build to our top pick, yet this model has a stainless steel tank and a UVC pump that purportedly can kill bacteria. However, the area a pet drinks from is still plastic, and, unlike the EverSweet Solo 2, this model doesn't have a water-level window.

The Petkit EverSweet Max 2 Cordless UVC Pet Water Fountain can operate cordlessly or plugged into an outlet. When we were using it on battery power, it took much longer than our cordless pick to detect a pet's presence. And this fountain has more pieces to clean than most of our picks.

The FeelNeedy FN-W26 Wireless No Filters Cat Water Fountain has separate clean- and dirty-water chambers, so you don't need to use expensive filters to keep the water clean. You can set the water to refresh on a schedule. But even with frequent changing, the clean water is sitting stagnant in the tank, as opposed to constantly flowing like it does in our picks. And the machine made a loud grinding sound every time it ran out of water.

The Misfans Ceramic Cat Water Fountain is a decent ceramic option, but it was one of the noisiest fountains we tested. And the ceramic top piece slides around on the tank, which may spook a pet. It's also heavy, and the ceramic might shatter if dropped.

The Petlibro Dockstream App Monitoring Water Fountain is an older version of our upgrade pick. It was previously a pick because it's simple to clean, easy to move around, and relatively attractive. But this fountain had a few critical failures in our long-term testing: For one tester, it stopped charging, and another tester discovered the tank had sprung a leak.

The Catit Flower Fountain was a pick for several years, and I've personally owned this one. Although this fountain is attractive, has great capacity, and is easy to take apart and clean, it was also one of the loudest models we tested. The pump motor never stopped making a low, aggravating hum, which we could hear even from the next room over. Several online reviews also mention this buzzing, but it might not bother everyone.

If you prefer ceramic and are willing to pay for it, the PetSafe Drinkwell Seascape Ceramic Pet Water Fountain is a great, albeit heavy, option. The square ceramic tank and bulbous centerpiece are dishwasher-safe, but this model also has more small plastic pieces than our picks, and you still need to wash them by hand. This fountain was also the heaviest one we tested, so it was a pain to carry to and from the sink.

The Catit Stainless Steel Flower Fountain was loud, though not as loud as its plastic counterpart. It has a stainless steel dish and a blue LED light on the pump, similar to our budget pick, but this fountain is nearly twice as expensive. The stainless dish never nested properly in the tank, so it spun around easily, and that could startle some pets.

The Pioneer Pet Raindrop Fountain used to be a pick, and it's still a great fountain if you want an option with more stainless steel than plastic. But it had many of the same issues as its larger sibling, the Big Max.

The Veken Pet Fountain's pump alternated between loud and quiet with unpredictable frequency. After the first week, there was visible dirt staining the inside of the tank where a water line had been. This refused to budge when we washed it with a soft sponge (we avoided using abrasives, so as to not scratch the plastic). Also, the plastic top doesn't sit securely, so it can get knocked off easily.

The PetNF Transparent Cat Water Drinking Fountain's clear plastic tank makes it easy to see when water is low or dirty. But unlike every other fountain we tested, this one lacks a clearly delineated slot or frame for the pump to sit in. That made it difficult to line up the pump with the upper spout tube when we cleaned or refilled the tank. The PetNF fountain's pump also has a tiny lever that tends to fall off during cleaning and can easily get lost.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Pagoda Fountain may look nice in your kitchen, but it has a lot of small parts, so it's a pain to assemble and clean. It's also noisy -- both when it's running normally (the water splashes) and when it's low on water.

The PetSafe Drinkwell 360 Fountain was a nightmare to assemble, and the plastic clasps that held the centerpiece of the fountain in place were not secure enough to keep the fountain together during assembly or use. The extra rings to change the flow from the top of the fountain provided little practical benefit.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Platinum Pet Fountain is made up of many small parts and has lots of nooks and crannies. So it's difficult to keep clean and free of hard-water buildup or slime.

For a low-cost fountain, the Cat Mate Pet Fountain is decent. However, it's cheaply constructed, and it has a tendency to quickly accumulate dirt in all three chambers.

The Catit LED Flower Water Fountain is an upgraded version of the Catit Flower Fountain. It has a blue LED light, which illuminates the fountain at night. And the mini water reservoirs trap water as it falls from the flower petal, so small pets can drink from the standing water, if they choose to. Like that of its predecessor, this fountain's flower petal is removable, so you can control the flow of water. But in testing we had a harder time disconnecting the petal, and that could be a problem for people with limited hand strength. Also, when the flower petal was connected, it never consistently pooled water into the mini reservoirs.

The PetSafe Drinkwell Multi-Tier Dog and Cat Fountain's waterfall feature can get noisy, especially when it's low on water. And setting up this fountain was not an intuitive process.

This article was edited by Harry Sawyers.

title: Strange Milky Way planetary system leaves scientists puzzled
full_text_raw:
WASHINGTON, July 22 (Reuters) - Scientists are documenting a planetary system in the Milky Way galaxy that is so starkly dissimilar to our own solar system that they are struggling to find the proper terminology to describe it.

The system includes a red dwarf star about 40% of the mass of our sun that is orbited by a brown dwarf, a celestial body that blurs the line between planet and star. The brown dwarf, in turn, is orbited by a gaseous Jupiter-sized world, newly discovered using the European Southern Observatory's Chile-based Very Large Telescope.

Using our solar system as a definitional frame of reference, a body that orbits another body that orbits a star should be called a moon -- or in this case an exomoon, because it is beyond our solar system. But the object that orbits the brown dwarf is unlike any of the many moons in our solar system -- all of which are relatively small rocky or icy worlds -- in terms of composition and size.

So what should we call it?

"This will certainly be a matter of debate. In general, most astronomers are fine with the term exosatellite, ⁠at least as a placeholder until we formally adopt definitions for objects like the one we found," said Kevin Hoy, a doctoral student in astrophysics at Universidad Diego Portales in Chile also affiliated with the exomoon research group YEMS, lead author of the study published in the journal Nature, opens new tab.

"We're really hitting the limits of how far we can stretch the words we invented to describe the solar system to describe other systems in this case," Hoy said.

This system is about 71 light-years away from Earth. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, 5.9 trillion miles (9.5 trillion km).

The exosatellite possesses at least 90% of the mass of Jupiter, the gas giant that is our solar system's largest planet. It completes an orbit of the brown dwarf every 170 days at a distance about a fifth of that separating Earth and the sun.

'A PANDORA'S BOX'

"I think this discovery has opened a Pandora's box for the scientific community. This type of object is completely new and unusual, truly different from what we are familiar with in our solar system. Now we will have to understand, through theoretical models, how these kinds of objects form and whether they are common or not," said study co-author Alice ⁠Zurlo, a Universidad Diego Portales astrophysicist and YEMS director.

"We deliberately chose not to call it a moon. That's because this object is unlike any moon in our solar system. It's much more massive, and it doesn't orbit a planet -- it orbits a brown dwarf, an object that's somewhere between a planet and a star. Since we've never seen a system quite like this before, we're still figuring out the best way to describe it," Zurlo said.

While more than 6,300 exoplanets -- as planets outside our solar system are known -- have been discovered, finding exomoons has proven more challenging, with only a few good candidates identified.

The researchers are trying to figure out the ⁠origins of the exosatellite.

"It may have formed from the disk of gas and dust around the brown dwarf, just as planets form around stars. Or it may have been captured (gravitationally) by the brown dwarf later on," Zurlo said.

A brown dwarf is neither a star nor a planet, but something in between. They could be considered aspiring stars that during their formative stages did not reach the mass necessary to ignite nuclear fusion at their core ⁠like a star. But they are more massive than the biggest planets.

The one in this system is about 33 times more massive, 50% larger in size and much hotter than Jupiter.

"Because the system is very young, the brown dwarf is still shining with the heat left from its formation," Zurlo said.

Since the first detection of exoplanets in the 1990s, scientists have spotted a wide variety of planetary ⁠systems, some built much like our own and others quite different. The one examined in the new research is an outlier.

"Yep, this system is definitely weird. There was likely a pretty chaotic dynamical history that left it in its current state, but it's really hard to tell exactly what kind of chaos it went through," Hoy said.
