title: British universities slip down in global rankings
full_text_raw:
Change in methodology used to rate institutions means only Cambridge University makes it into top five

British universities have slipped down the latest international rankings, with only Cambridge making it into the top five institutions in the world - taking joint third place in a list dominated by big American universities.

According to the QS World University Rankings, regarded as the most authoritative of its kind, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) is once again named the best university in the world, with Harvard climbing to second place from fourth last year.

The UK still has four universities in the top 10 in the world. One of the biggest casualties, however, was London's Imperial College, which in 2014 was ranked equal second with Cambridge but this year dropped to eighth position because of a change in the methodology used to rate universities.

Oxford University and University College London (UCL) have both slipped down the tables; having been ranked equal fifth last year, Oxford slipped to sixth and UCL to seventh. Kings College London, ranked 16th in 2014, has dropped three places to 19.

Stanford University in California comes in at joint third with Cambridge, climbing from seventh last year; the California Institute of Technology is fifth, with ETH Zurich (the Federal Swiss Institute of Technology) in ninth place and Chicago University in 10th.

UK winners include the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), which climbs from 71 to 35, a beneficiary of the changes to the QS methodology.

Previously the QS rankings favoured universities strong in research, which is generated largely by the medical sciences, but changes have been made in order to give better recognition to institutions that are outstanding in arts and humanities but produce few citations.

As a result, Imperial, a leading research-intensive institution which produces an impressive array of citations every year, dropped six places despite performing well in every other respect.

Warwick University enters the world's top 50 at 48, up from 61 last year; Durham moves up from 92 to 61, St Andrews is at 68 from 88 last year and Southampton takes 81st position, up from 94.

Two Singaporean universities make the top 15 for the first time; the National University of Singapore (12) is the top Asian institution with Nanyang Technological University at 13.

Ben Sowter, QS head of research said: "That the LSE is a world-class institution is not news. Indeed, they have been a firm fixture in the QS top 100 for over a decade, but in any ranking system that places emphasis on medicine and sciences, their strength in their areas of specialty are never likely to shine as brightly as they ought to.

"The QS methodology now evens the playing field and LSE climbs 36 places to be counted, rightfully, amongst the world's top 40."

John O'Leary, a member of the QS global advisory board, added: "The UK remains second only to the US as a higher education destination. The leading universities may have lost ground, but they still make up four of the top 10 in the world.

"Ironically, their strength in medicine and science has cost some of them because the new methodology rewards a more balanced portfolio, but it is good news for the likes of Durham and Warwick, as well as LSE."

The US has 49 institutions in the top 200, ahead of the UK with 30, the Netherlands (12), Germany (11), Canada, Australia, and Japan (8) and China (7).

London is the only city in the world with four universities in the top 50; Boston and New York have three and Paris, Sydney, Hong Kong and Beijing all have two.

The mayor of London, Boris Johnson, said: "London is unequivocally the education capital of the world. With four of our universities in the top 40, the city's education sector is going from strength to strength, attracting the world's top talent and producing the next generation of great thinkers and leaders."

LSE's director, Prof Craig Calhoun, said: "LSE's latest global university ranking as the best social science institution in the UK and second best in the world is testament to both the school and London's reputation as a world class centre for education.

"For 120 years, we have been located in the heart of London, providing outstanding teaching and research which focuses on real-world problems and helps shape government policy at the highest level."

title: Politician's claim Earth's magnetic poles could flip if NT doesn't use more groundwater criticised by experts
full_text_raw:
NT minister for trade and business Robyn Cahill makes scientifically inaccurate claims while pushing to make territory 'datacentre capital of the globe'

A Northern Territory minister has been criticised for scientifically inaccurate claims that groundwater in the Northern Territory needs to be used to prevent the Earth's magnetic poles from flipping.

The NT minister for trade and business, Robyn Cahill, made the claim while speaking in Darwin last week about the government's push to make the territory "the datacentre capital of the globe".

"For datacentres, the water supply is already in existence. It's mainly subterranean," she said. "The water supply that Darwin has is extraordinary."

"There's scientific evidence to suggest that we have so much water underground in the Northern Territory that it actually impacts the axis of the Earth when we have a really bad wet season, so we need to use some of it otherwise we might find ourselves flipping the poles again."

The Environment Centre NT's executive director, Kirsty Howey, described Cahill's claim as "completely cooked".

"The minister appears to believe that the Northern Territory's wet season can alter Earth's axis, which has no scientific basis," Howey said. "It's frightening that the people in charge of regulating dangerous industries like fracking and datacentres seem to lack even a high-school understanding of water science."

Dr Dylan Irvine, a groundwater hydrology expert at Charles Darwin University, told ABC Darwin: "We're not at risk of the poles flipping ... I'm not concerned about the Earth tipping or flipping of poles."

The Earth's most recent major geomagnetic reversal - in which the positions of magnetic north and magnetic south flip - is known as the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal, and occurred an estimated 780,000 years ago. The flip is not instantaneous: scientific analysis suggests reversals take 7,000 years on average to occur.

A recent temporary flip of the poles, classified as an "excursion" rather than a full geomagnetic reversal - occurred 42,000 years ago and lasted for about 1,000 years.

"This is driven by processes that happen in the deep Earth ... that happen in the Earth's core ... not so much groundwater systems," Irvine said.

Experts have warned, however, about the impact massive datacentre projects will have on already strained water resources, particularly in hotter climates where centres require more energy or water to keep cool.

The ECNT is calling for a public ban on fracking and datacentres so their impacts on the NT's climate and water supplies can be properly considered.

"We don't want to see our precious aquifers drained for AI while we get nothing in return," Howey said. "We don't want to be the datacentre capital of the globe - we want safe drinking water and a livable future for our kids."

According to the NT government, as many as a dozen datacentre developers are interested in the region.

"We will be the place all the hyperscalers come to have their datacentres here," Cahill said last week.

On Wednesday, the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, announced the government had granted Beetaloo Digital - a subsidiary of gas company Beetaloo Energy - an exclusive commitment over 185 ha of land near Darwin, for "a massive project involving an integrated AI datacentre and on-site gas-fired power generation".

The project would be "powered by up to 2GW of on-site power generation fuelled by Beetaloo gas", according to a government statement.

For comparison, 2GW is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 2m households.

It comes after the announcement of another hyperscale centre, Energy North's Project Ares, a 1GW project proposed for Murranji station in the NT's Barkly region.

Cahill was contacted for comment.

title: Total solar eclipse books out hotels two years in advance in New Zealand city
full_text_raw:
Dunedin will be the focal point, having last experienced such an eclipse in 1163 - before any humans reached New Zealand

Hotels are booking out two years in advance in the New Zealand city of Dunedin as it prepares for the region's first total solar eclipse in more than 850 years.

At 4.17pm on 22 July 2028, the moon will pass in front of the sun, casting a roughly 100km-wide shadowy band across parts of southern New Zealand. Everywhere within that band - from tourist hotspot Queenstown in the west to Dunedin city in the east - will be plunged into daytime darkness for 2 minutes and 51 seconds.

Despite there being two years still to go, hotels are already fielding booking inquiries, including the Dunedin Leisure Lodge, which by Thursday was fully booked for its "solar eclipse package" that includes complimentary eclipse glasses.

Dr Ian Griffin, an astronomer and director of Tūhura Otago Museum, said: "The last one visible from Dunedin was in 1163, which was before humans reached New Zealand.

"So we will be the first people in Dunedin ever to see a solar eclipse from this part of the world, which is quite exciting."

It will also be the first total solar eclipse visible anywhere in New Zealand since 1965.

"That three minutes of darkness, if it's clear, will be absolutely memorable for anybody who sees it," Griffin said.

On Wednesday, Dunedin's museum started the clock for the two-year countdown, in what is tipped to be a major tourism event for the city. Roughly 35,000 visitors are expected to descend on the city, which has a population of 130,000.

Griffin, meanwhile, has been preparing for the eclipse since 2013.

"I did buy my house all those years ago based on the fact that you could see the eclipse from it," he said.

The eclipse will happen in the middle of New Zealand's winter, just after the country celebrates Matariki - the Māori new year. Matariki is the Māori name for a cluster of stars known elsewhere as the Pleiades. The constellation is visible from New Zealand for 11 months of the year, but disappears from the skies for a month in winter, reappearing around the time of the winter solstice.

Dunedin is planning a night-sky festival beginning with Matariki and going through to the eclipse.

"It's actually unique anywhere around the world," Griffin said. "We've got the cultural holiday celebrating the night sky, and then will be following it about 10 days later with a fantastic eclipse."

The Dunedin mayor, Sophie Barker, said anticipation for the eclipse was being felt across the city. "This remarkable event is now firmly on the horizon."

title: Country diary: The eyebright paradox: a sunny healer and tiny parasitic thief | Paul Evans
full_text_raw:
The Marches, Shropshire: Eyebrights are ancient herbs used to cure eye problems, but they also penetrate grass roots to siphon off water and nutrients

A sight for sore eyes. Eyebrights flower in the short turf of Old Racecourse Common as sunlight burns a hole through rowan trees to cast sunset colours on the grass. The eyebrights are annuals with tiny flowers, 4mm-11mm long with a violet vibe, a white corolla with purple marks and a central flash of yellow.

There are about 20 British eyebright species, some of which are endemic. Their genetic complexity makes them an arcane group of plants and a taxonomic puzzle to all but their most dedicated acolytes. "Life's too short to key out [make a precise identification of] eyebrights," one botanist told me.

For the sake of argument, this one is Euphrasia officinalis agg, an aggregate of species, microspecies and hybrids, one of which is E nemorosa, the common eyebright. They belong to Orobanchaceae, the family that also includes lousewort, toothwort and yellow rattle. Like these, the eyebrights are parasitic, or at least hemi-parasitic, capable of independent living but also sending out roots to penetrate the roots of grasses to siphon water and nutrients from them, like wiring into streetlights to nick the 'leccy. This reduces grass dominance and changes the composition of the turf.

Euphrasia comes from the Greek word for cheerfulness, obvious when you get down to look into their faces, even through the smudgy lenses of my specs. According to the medieval Doctrine of Signatures, objects in nature have trademark characteristics that are key to their influence on human conditions, so gazing at these flowers looking back with such a bright, sunny disposition can help us see and feel better. Following on from intuitions and symbolism, eyebright is an ancient medicinal herb with properties such as aucubin and iridoid glycosides, lignans and flavonoids used in tinctures and compresses to cure eye problems. They also promote wellbeing and were burned as an incense to aid divination.

So, is the future bright for eyebrights? A lack of grazing and encroaching bracken, recently cut here, is a common problem for short-turf habitats. Conventional conservation of distinctive species has to be balanced with the conservation of processes that create the extraordinary evolution of eyebright diversity for these shapers of place and their richly storied lives.

title: Pompeii: Out of Time With Tom Hiddleston review - you will cringe so hard you turn to cheese
full_text_raw:
The actor emotes his way through Vesuvius's catastrophic eruption in a docudrama that is embarrassing and exhausting - but undeniably entertaining. Prepare to be Hiddlestoned!

There's such a fine line between "cheese" and "cringe", is there not? Come, walk it with me and Tom Hiddleston in Pompeii: Out of Time With Tom Hiddleston. Let's see how many of us survive the eruptions of embarrassment that attend our journey!

This is a National Geographic documentary-drama, which means that even the factual bits are emotionally scripted and there's CGI money and speaking parts for the re-enactments. And there is Tom (he has looked very deeply into my eyes throughout all three episodes, so I feel we are on first-name terms now), wringing every drop of feeling from every moment with the untrammelled appetite of a born actor.

We begin! Dramatically! With Tom! Telling us - in weirdly ungrammatical fashion - that Pompeii was destroyed in "a single day that are the most harrowing anyone on this Earth has ever experienced". Then he drops his voice. And explains that although a day is not long, it does mean there is hope for individual survival. He looks deep into my eyes, into your eyes, into all eyes, into eyes past and not yet born, and intones: "A day. A chance."

You have been Hiddlestoned. While you recover, opening credits roll.

As the programme proper begins, informal Tom greets us. He vouchsafes us the intimate personal knowledge that he actually visited Pompeii with two friends in 1998, when he was 17. There are photos to prove it! Tom is young and happy and just like us except taller and handsomer and a born actor destined for a career that blends lucrative and prestigious work in perfect proportions! Pompeii, he confides in us and our eyes, inspired him to learn Latin, study classics at an unnamed university and pursue acting "to bring people back". Crikey. It's lucky he didn't just bugger off to Ibiza for a month. His life and Britain's cultural export ledger could have been so different.

Tom meets Prof Steven L Tuck, leader of the Pompeii Survivors' Project and labelled in the onscreen caption as "Helpful Classicist", which, once further experts have been cheesily introduced as "Helpful Archaeologist", "Helpful Geoscientist" and so on, I very much enjoy. He is there to help Tom find three Pompeiians whose stories he can trace through that fateful day in AD79 when Mount Vesuvius began to rain tonnes of rock and magma down on the defenceless towns below.

Prof Tuck shows Tom some ancient records and inscriptions and Tom, who has the Latin, translates them. The first candidate they find is a boy called Lucius Avianius (which, if my own Latin does not desert me, translates as "Lucy Birdyus"). Tom looks - nay, surely is! - deep in thought. "If I'm going to tell Avianius's story," he says at last, raising his soulful eyes to our bog-standard eyes, "I need to combine the historical evidence with what I do as an actor. I need" - voice drop, eyes soulfuller - "to walk alongside him, through the streets in his shoes." The Romans had the same word for "story" and "history", he says. "Evidence and imagination intermingled," he continues, knotting his fingers together. Consider me awed.

The second potential survivor is a bathhouse owner called Julia - mistakenly translated by Tom at first as "Julius". Oh, Tom! But then another expert explains that women held property and power in the old days and that Julia even did it with the stigma of illegitimacy attached to her. This causes Tom to sigh in compassion and admiration and name her "Impossible Julia". At this point, I find myself cringing so hard I nearly turn to cheese, which is an unexpected turn of events but not an entirely unpleasant sensation.

On we go, with Tom interviewing more Helpful Experts, including a disaster psychologist, who explains why people don't necessarily run for the hills literally or metaphorically at the first sign of trouble but might try to find, say, family first. "Of course," breathes Tom. "That's who you'd go to. It's who I'd go to." I regretfully make a mark in the "cringe" column.

Tom enthuses educatedly over Pliny, stands aside graciously for more ash- and pumice-occluded re-enactments, and hopes wildly for success in the rescue mission launched by the Roman fleet from the Bay of Naples. Occasionally, though, he is overcome by the thought of the suffering unfolding over the day as the full force of the volcano is unleashed. Born actors are easily stricken. But they are very brave. They soldier on until the contract is fulfilled and the money inarguably due.

I suppose I would have to look back at my first documentary-drama presented by a born actor and profess myself entertained but exhausted by the constant prospect of the whole teetering thing collapsing into utter humiliation for all involved. But if I were younger, less cynical, a nicer person in any way, I would have loved it and it would have got me a bit more interested in the ancient world. Contract fulfilled.

title: Orcas seen ramming prey so hard it explodes may be playing game
full_text_raw:
Scientists believe sunfish-smashing behaviour could be form of entertainment or to help younger whales feed

Orcas have been observed ramming into giant fish so hard that the prey explode, possibly as a form of gory entertainment.

On several occasions, orcas were observed to hold sunfish in their jaws while a second whale smashed into the target at high speed, causing it to break into thousands of pieces. Since the fish had already been killed, scientists suggested the behaviour may represent a form of play.

Dr Kathryn Ayres, a scientist at non-profit organisation Beneath The Waves, said: "We think this may help younger orcas feed more easily or it could also just be for fun. Orcas are known for playing with their food."

Ayres captured the first fish-ramming event on a GoPro camera in July 2024 and can be heard shrieking in shock on the audio.

"When you see a multi-ton apex predator charge a massive fish at that speed right next to your boat, the sheer acoustic thud and the resulting explosion of tissue are overwhelming," said Erick Higuera, a marine biologist and wildlife cinematographer at Mexican non-profit Conexiones Terramar and co-author of the research.

Sunfish are among the world's largest fish, growing to more than three metres long and weighing up to 2,000kg. They are commonly hunted and eaten by orcas.

In Ayres' footage, a female orca is seen gripping the tail of a sunfish carcass while an adult male accelerates towards it. Just before impact, the female releases the dead fish and there is an audible crunch as the male strikes the target, leaving behind a plume of white fragments. A juvenile whale is subsequently seen eating the small pieces of flesh, while the adult orcas feed on the remains of the main carcass.

In a second instance, captured by a tourism operator in September 2025, an adult female orca was spotted holding out a dead sunfish, while a second orca executed a high-speed ramming manoeuvre, breaking it into thousands of pieces. The events were recorded in the Gulf of California, off the coast of Mexico, but it is unclear whether the same orcas were involved.

One hypothesis is that ramming is used to break the tough, rubbery sunfish into bite-size pieces for juveniles, whose jaws are smaller. But orcas are also known for social fads and boisterous games that do not have an obvious practical purpose. In the 1980s, a pod of orcas started carrying dead salmon on their head like hats, a trend that was recently revived. A subpopulation off the coast of Spain and Portugal has attracted attention for unusual interactions with boats.

"They throw kelp at each other, surf in boat wakes and engage in intricate tactical games," said Higuera. "Play is a core pillar of orca society."

Whatever the purpose of the behaviour, it demonstrates an impressive level of cognitive sophistication, requiring the planning and coordination of several steps, according to the findings reported in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

Eco-tour operators increasingly use underwater drones and cameras, which are capturing new behaviours that are of interest to scientists. But there are also concerns about the disruptive impact of wildlife tourism, with Mexico issuing new regulations on swimming with orcas last year.

"If we can maintain a respectful distance and protect these animals, continuing this collaboration with tour operators will allow us to safely document mysteries of ocean life that would otherwise remain completely hidden from science," said Higuera.

title: Splatoon Raiders Review: Paint, Paint, Everywhere, and Not a Friend to Ink
full_text_raw:
Instead of competitive multiplayer, Splatoon Raiders has you take on fishlike enemies with an array of weapons and gadgets.

The challenge in reviewing most Nintendo games is that, more often than not, it feels less like considering a piece of narrative art than evaluating a playground: The slide has frictionless and smooth mechanics. The swing set has a satisfying arc. The seesaw, on the other hand, is dreadfully imbalanced.

As silly as this sounds, it aligns with how I feel about a game like Splatoon Raiders, which lives and dies by how fun its experiences are as toys and as rides, but offers little else.

It's too easy to chalk this up to Raiders being a game made for children. Plenty of media made for children, like the early Pixar film canon, have deep, emotional narratives that reach all ages.

The characters in Raiders -- the anonymous "Mechanic" and three goofy bandmates -- are all high-pitched, diminutive and childlike, with all the worldly concerns of an old Nicktoons roster. They all wear bright colors. Yet adults are invited to enjoy this spectacle, as if we could engage in chaotic paintball warfare without spraining a knee or throwing out our backs, laughing maniacally as we dash about coating everything in color within this safe digital simulacra.

Childlike frivolity is what is undeniably at work in Raiders. Its matches consist of facing down armies of crawling fishlike enemies, which range from tiny pipsqueaks to gargantuan whales. Your character must coat them with a nearly endless supply of ink until they explode in bursts of color.

Over the course of the game you'll unlock weapon categories familiar to most who have played early Splatoon games: rapid-firing squirt pistols, paint brushes, rollers and even glob-tossing buckets. Raiders also offers an assortment of gadgets, allowing you to fire bazookas, use a dash to zip and leap around the stage, and even drop auto-firing turrets and floating mines.

The gameplay additions in Raiders build upon a solid foundation established by the first three Splatoon games. New bells and whistles are needed because Raiders lacks the competitive play mode that defined previous games, which allowed players to battle their squid kid characters against one another in colorful arenas. Those shootouts came with an inherent drama because of the random and unpredictable choices made by other human players, trumping the algorithmic choices of even the most sophisticated enemies.

Lackluster single-player modes have always been an Achilles' heel of Splatoon, which leaned on multiplayer brilliance. They mostly consisted of puzzle stages, and felt linear and slow next to the freewheeling and fast-paced arenas. Raiders tries to address this concern by taking the series down a purely noncompetitive path.

That approach, when it works, involves mounting and delirious chaos as enemies pour out of sewer grates and flood the stage with their undulating mass. They may be slow and stupid, but as their numbers pile up, the challenge becomes figuring out how to dispatch them all before getting overwhelmed.

This style of encounter, though effective, has its limits. Aside from specific challenge levels, most of the game's raids occur in wide-open spaces, occasionally spread between island clusters or boxed within underground caverns. The challenge is not navigating its levels -- minimalist slices of the franchise's past multiplayer arenas -- but overcoming its ludicrous enemy count.

Frustratingly, your character's fancy skills have a lot of potential for tackling interesting spatial challenges, but are instead put in service solely to survive these arenas. Few and far between are larger, complex battles against boss types, which offer glimmers of an approach that squares your squid's astonishing agility against building-size adversaries and vertiginous levels. Far more often, things are kept blindingly simple, mostly a test ground for your gadgets.

It's all fun enough, as a playground with well-designed jungle gyms and monkey bars. But it feels so small and insignificant as a result. The side characters, while a lively troupe, perform with one-note pantomimes of enthusiasm. They are so jazzed to be here, and are only ever varying levels of jazzed.

The occasional obstacle emerges in their unchanging goal of hoovering up every last trinket and treasure that these islands offer. But once you inevitably clear each level, the minor disappointment is wiped away by maximalist effervescence.

Raiders does have a cooperative online mode that promises to be fun and chaotic, with up to four players facing off against teeming fishy hordes that fill the screen with so many particles that one can almost forgive Nintendo for not including a local multiplayer option. The game is otherwise a lonely affair. It's just you and the incessant rattle of your sidekicks, constantly reminding you to keep your head up about some challenging raid or making sure you don't forget about that new compass that's popped up!

The island setting of Raiders starts off covered in fog and shrouded in mystery. It could be anything, could take the story anywhere. But there really isn't that much to see, not much offered besides the momentary chance to slide and swing and grasp at an ephemeral childhood innocence.

Splatoon Raiders is available on the Switch 2.

title: Vietnam reaffirms trade talks, urges US to conclude trade investigation
full_text_raw:
HANOI, July 23 (Reuters) - Vietnam's foreign ministry said on Thursday that it remained committed to bringing trade negotiations with the United States to a conclusion, urging Washington to wrap up its Section 301 investigation into the southeast Asian country.

The appeal came after a meeting between U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vietnam's Foreign Minister Le Hoai Trung on the sidelines of an ASEAN summit in ⁠Manila, where the two sides discussed ways to strengthen ties and rebalance trade.

It follows more than a year of talks between Hanoi and its largest export market, with U.S. President Donald Trump's temporary 10% global tariff on goods shipped from Vietnam scheduled to expire on Friday.

Vietnam is facing three separate Trump administration probes targeting Hanoi for allegedly distorting trade through excess capacity, ⁠intellectual property violations, and the use of goods produced by forced labour.

Vietnam called for the United States to conclude the Section 301 investigation with a decision that fully recognises Vietnam's efforts, the ⁠foreign ministry said in a statement.

Section 301 of U.S. trade law is a provision that authorises investigations into alleged unfair trade practices.

Trung ⁠said Vietnam is willing to facilitate U.S. firms in expanding their investment and business activities in the country.

The U.S. ⁠trade deficit with Vietnam reached $75.3 billion in the first half of this year, an annual increase of 21%, Vietnam's government data showed.

title: African Rainbow Minerals approves Bokoni platinum project, nickel mine restart
full_text_raw:
July 23 (Reuters) - African Rainbow Minerals (ARM) (ARIJ.J), opens new tab said on Thursday its board has approved a phased 15.2 billion rand ($927.28 million) upgrade of its Bokoni platinum group metal operations as well as the resumption of nickel mining at Nkomati.

The diversified South African miner said in a statement the outlook for PGMs, mostly used in autocatalysts which curb vehicle emissions, remains positive despite the expected impact of battery electric vehicles, which do not require emission control.

The Bokoni project expansion will add a ⁠new 120,000 metric ton per month platinum group metal concentrator to the existing 60,000 ton per month plant, which will be refurbished, ARM said. The new concentrator is expected to be commissioned in 2030.

ARM said it expects the Bokoni project to reach steady state in 2032, with annual output between 350,000 and 400,000 ounces of PGMs from that year. The company produced 615,719 ounces of PGMs in its financial year to June 2025.

ARM suspended operations ⁠at Bokoni in June 2025, saying the smaller 60,000 ton per month mining and milling capacity was insufficient to offset fixed costs and sustain profitability.

The company, which also has iron ore, manganese and coal assets, said it was restarting ⁠open-pit mining operations and nickel concentrate production at Nkomati after agreeing a conditional off-take deal with Sweden's Boliden (BOL.ST), opens new tab.

The Nkomati mine was placed on care and maintenance in ⁠2021 due to persistent financial losses driven by rising operational costs and weak nickel prices.

ARM, which took full control of Nkomati in July 2025 ⁠following the exit of former joint venture partner Nornickel, plans to spend $46 million on the nickel mining restart, producing 56,065 tons of nickel concentrate annually.

title: Pompeii: Out of Time With Tom Hiddleston review - you will cringe so hard you turn to cheese
full_text_raw:
The actor emotes his way through Vesuvius's catastrophic eruption in a docudrama that is embarrassing and exhausting - but undeniably entertaining. Prepare to be Hiddlestoned!

There's such a fine line between "cheese" and "cringe", is there not? Come, walk it with me and Tom Hiddleston in Pompeii: Out of Time With Tom Hiddleston. Let's see how many of us survive the eruptions of embarrassment that attend our journey!

This is a National Geographic documentary-drama, which means that even the factual bits are emotionally scripted and there's CGI money and speaking parts for the re-enactments. And there is Tom (he has looked very deeply into my eyes throughout all three episodes, so I feel we are on first-name terms now), wringing every drop of feeling from every moment with the untrammelled appetite of a born actor.

We begin! Dramatically! With Tom! Telling us - in weirdly ungrammatical fashion - that Pompeii was destroyed in "a single day that are the most harrowing anyone on this Earth has ever experienced". Then he drops his voice. And explains that although a day is not long, it does mean there is hope for individual survival. He looks deep into my eyes, into your eyes, into all eyes, into eyes past and not yet born, and intones: "A day. A chance."

You have been Hiddlestoned. While you recover, opening credits roll.

As the programme proper begins, informal Tom greets us. He vouchsafes us the intimate personal knowledge that he actually visited Pompeii with two friends in 1998, when he was 17. There are photos to prove it! Tom is young and happy and just like us except taller and handsomer and a born actor destined for a career that blends lucrative and prestigious work in perfect proportions! Pompeii, he confides in us and our eyes, inspired him to learn Latin, study classics at an unnamed university and pursue acting "to bring people back". Crikey. It's lucky he didn't just bugger off to Ibiza for a month. His life and Britain's cultural export ledger could have been so different.

Tom meets Prof Steven L Tuck, leader of the Pompeii Survivors' Project and labelled in the onscreen caption as "Helpful Classicist", which, once further experts have been cheesily introduced as "Helpful Archaeologist", "Helpful Geoscientist" and so on, I very much enjoy. He is there to help Tom find three Pompeiians whose stories he can trace through that fateful day in AD79 when Mount Vesuvius began to rain tonnes of rock and magma down on the defenceless towns below.

Prof Tuck shows Tom some ancient records and inscriptions and Tom, who has the Latin, translates them. The first candidate they find is a boy called Lucius Avianius (which, if my own Latin does not desert me, translates as "Lucy Birdyus"). Tom looks - nay, surely is! - deep in thought. "If I'm going to tell Avianius's story," he says at last, raising his soulful eyes to our bog-standard eyes, "I need to combine the historical evidence with what I do as an actor. I need" - voice drop, eyes soulfuller - "to walk alongside him, through the streets in his shoes." The Romans had the same word for "story" and "history", he says. "Evidence and imagination intermingled," he continues, knotting his fingers together. Consider me awed.

The second potential survivor is a bathhouse owner called Julia - mistakenly translated by Tom at first as "Julius". Oh, Tom! But then another expert explains that women held property and power in the old days and that Julia even did it with the stigma of illegitimacy attached to her. This causes Tom to sigh in compassion and admiration and name her "Impossible Julia". At this point, I find myself cringing so hard I nearly turn to cheese, which is an unexpected turn of events but not an entirely unpleasant sensation.

On we go, with Tom interviewing more Helpful Experts, including a disaster psychologist, who explains why people don't necessarily run for the hills literally or metaphorically at the first sign of trouble but might try to find, say, family first. "Of course," breathes Tom. "That's who you'd go to. It's who I'd go to." I regretfully make a mark in the "cringe" column.

Tom enthuses educatedly over Pliny, stands aside graciously for more ash- and pumice-occluded re-enactments, and hopes wildly for success in the rescue mission launched by the Roman fleet from the Bay of Naples. Occasionally, though, he is overcome by the thought of the suffering unfolding over the day as the full force of the volcano is unleashed. Born actors are easily stricken. But they are very brave. They soldier on until the contract is fulfilled and the money inarguably due.

I suppose I would have to look back at my first documentary-drama presented by a born actor and profess myself entertained but exhausted by the constant prospect of the whole teetering thing collapsing into utter humiliation for all involved. But if I were younger, less cynical, a nicer person in any way, I would have loved it and it would have got me a bit more interested in the ancient world. Contract fulfilled.

title: Orcas seen ramming prey so hard it explodes may be playing game
full_text_raw:
Scientists believe sunfish-smashing behaviour could be form of entertainment or to help younger whales feed

Orcas have been observed ramming into giant fish so hard that the prey explode, possibly as a form of gory entertainment.

On several occasions, orcas were observed to hold sunfish in their jaws while a second whale smashed into the target at high speed, causing it to break into thousands of pieces. Since the fish had already been killed, scientists suggested the behaviour may represent a form of play.

Dr Kathryn Ayres, a scientist at non-profit organisation Beneath The Waves, said: "We think this may help younger orcas feed more easily or it could also just be for fun. Orcas are known for playing with their food."

Ayres captured the first fish-ramming event on a GoPro camera in July 2024 and can be heard shrieking in shock on the audio.

"When you see a multi-ton apex predator charge a massive fish at that speed right next to your boat, the sheer acoustic thud and the resulting explosion of tissue are overwhelming," said Erick Higuera, a marine biologist and wildlife cinematographer at Mexican non-profit Conexiones Terramar and co-author of the research.

Sunfish are among the world's largest fish, growing to more than three metres long and weighing up to 2,000kg. They are commonly hunted and eaten by orcas.

In Ayres' footage, a female orca is seen gripping the tail of a sunfish carcass while an adult male accelerates towards it. Just before impact, the female releases the dead fish and there is an audible crunch as the male strikes the target, leaving behind a plume of white fragments. A juvenile whale is subsequently seen eating the small pieces of flesh, while the adult orcas feed on the remains of the main carcass.

In a second instance, captured by a tourism operator in September 2025, an adult female orca was spotted holding out a dead sunfish, while a second orca executed a high-speed ramming manoeuvre, breaking it into thousands of pieces. The events were recorded in the Gulf of California, off the coast of Mexico, but it is unclear whether the same orcas were involved.

One hypothesis is that ramming is used to break the tough, rubbery sunfish into bite-size pieces for juveniles, whose jaws are smaller. But orcas are also known for social fads and boisterous games that do not have an obvious practical purpose. In the 1980s, a pod of orcas started carrying dead salmon on their head like hats, a trend that was recently revived. A subpopulation off the coast of Spain and Portugal has attracted attention for unusual interactions with boats.

"They throw kelp at each other, surf in boat wakes and engage in intricate tactical games," said Higuera. "Play is a core pillar of orca society."

Whatever the purpose of the behaviour, it demonstrates an impressive level of cognitive sophistication, requiring the planning and coordination of several steps, according to the findings reported in the journal Frontiers in Ethology.

Eco-tour operators increasingly use underwater drones and cameras, which are capturing new behaviours that are of interest to scientists. But there are also concerns about the disruptive impact of wildlife tourism, with Mexico issuing new regulations on swimming with orcas last year.

"If we can maintain a respectful distance and protect these animals, continuing this collaboration with tour operators will allow us to safely document mysteries of ocean life that would otherwise remain completely hidden from science," said Higuera.

title: Andy Burnham's high-risk start may help him get ahead of political pain
full_text_raw:
Good morning. Andy Burnham has completed putting together his first front bench. He has, sensibly, largely kept many ministers of state in place. This makes sense because ministers of state are the real engines of delivery across government and this ensures less disruption.

He has also made some quite big bets in terms of who he has chosen to alienate, and on putting such a big focus on reforms to Whitehall itself. Some thoughts on both of those in today's note.

O Brother, where art thou?

The more things change, the more they stay the same: when former prime minister Harold Macmillan mused on putting together his new government, he set out the "many considerations" that he had to bear in mind, and who exactly it had to accommodate:

The right, centre, and left of the party; the extreme 'Suez' group; the extreme opposition to Suez; the loyal centre -- and last, but not least, U and non-U (to use the jargon that Nancy Mitford has popularised) that is, Eton, Winchester, etc on the one hand; Board School and grammar school on the other.

Modern prime ministers have to do something similar: keep their party's right, centre and left flanks aligned, but instead of making sure that Eton, Winchester and Charterhouse are represented alongside grammars and a handful of elementary schools, they have to take care over sex, geography and ethnicity.

Men hold three out of four of the great offices of state but Burnham has restored the Women and Equalities post to a full, standalone cabinet post, a key demand of many in the women's Parliamentary Labour Party. Meanwhile, everyone knows that the second person in this government is not the chancellor, the home secretary or the foreign secretary: it's the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, Louise Haigh. So as a result there is not much disquiet on that front as there otherwise would be.

Just as Macmillan had to accommodate various schools of thought on the Suez Crisis, the Conservative government under Theresa May needed to balance Remainers and Leavers; Ed Miliband needed to balance Blairites and Brownites, and so on.

Burnham has opted to make few accommodations to the minority of MPs and ministers who remained loyal to Keir Starmer right to the end. Only Pat McFadden, whose plans for welfare Burnham is strongly signed up to, remains in place.

I think this is unlikely to come back to bite him: ultimately the Starmer loyalists are not a particularly ideologically united bunch. If you are going to annoy a group of people, it's best to annoy a group who contain many internal policy disagreements.

What looks more risky is that it has also been a pretty brutal reshuffle for Wes Streeting's allies. None of the MPs in the most vocal bit of his supporters club -- Zubir Ahmed, Naushabah Khan, Tom Rutland or Joe Morris, who resigned from Starmer's government, not Jess Phillips, nor any of his most vocal parliamentary supporters on the backbenches -- have been given ministerial jobs.

Taken together, that seems like a hostage to fortune to me. I think it is sensible to choose putting one of these blocs completely outside the government but not both. If the government gets into difficulties, Burnham may come to regret that.

But I wonder if Burnham is perhaps planning to get ahead of possible trouble by seeking a mandate of his own in short order. This new government has kicked off its life with a surprising level of reform to Whitehall structures. Some of these changes are exciting and timely in my view (creating a proper office of the prime minister, for example). Others are a retrograde step (scrapping DSIT, or the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology, and folding it back into the business department).

I'll write about what I think are the good, the bad and the mixed of these changes soon, but the thing about Whitehall reform is that it inevitably eats into the time that a government can actually spend delivering anything, and this government really only has 18 months left in which it might be able to do so.

This is the difficult trade-off for governments considering Whitehall reform: if you don't do it, you're left trying to make changes with structures you don't like. Do it and you lose the time you could instead be focusing directly on vote-moving issues. I just wonder if one reason this government is happy to focus on Whitehall reform and happy to make big swings in terms of who is in and who is out of the government is that its Plan A is to spend the next month communicating the idea of change, in the hope of getting a fresh mandate from the country and, as a result, the parliamentary party sooner rather than later.

Now try this

I always find it reassuring when occasionally I leave the cinema or the theatre thinking "well, that was a complete waste of time", as it shows that I am trying new things. And on that basis I suppose I am glad I saw Rosebush Pruning at the cinema, but save yourselves is my advice. Danny Leigh's review is here.

title: Pride organisers vow to march in Romanian city that has blocked event four years in a row
full_text_raw:
Oradea is only major city in EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride plans

Campaigners in a Romanian city have vowed to go ahead with plans for a Pride march after local authorities denied them permission for the fourth consecutive year.

Since 2023, campaigners in the western city of Oradea - population 180,000 - have sought authorisation for Pride events. Each year, however, they have come up against opposition, turning Oradea into the only major city in the EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride plans.

"Every year the local authorities have managed to find legal or technical excuses to ban Oradea Pride events," said Iulian Ditiu, the co-founder and president of ARK Oradea, the local organisers of Pride.

In 2024, for example, they were told that none of the city's parks were available at the times requested, he said. The following year, campaigners provided local authorities with 12 potential routes for the march, only to be told that none of the routes were possible.

Before this year's proposed march, slated to be held on Saturday, organisers submitted more than 100 route options. On Wednesday the city said that none of the routes were viable as they overlapped with other events or with major public infrastructure works.

The city's mayor, who is from a party that describes itself as liberal, conservative and Christian democratic, did not reply to a request for comment from the Guardian.

Ditiu pointed to the wider significance of the consecutive bans. "It feels like the message that they are trying to send our way is that we're not welcome here," he said. "They have never said out loud that they are banning Pride for LGBT reasons. They're always hiding behind technical reasons."

As organisers grapple with the possibility of another ban, their plight has attracted international attention. Before this year's march, 152 organisations from 30 countries signed a statement calling on officials to allow the march to take place in "complete safety" and in line with EU law.

"After four consecutive years in which the Pride march has been unable to take place, there can be no question of administrative or logistical difficulties," the statement noted. "When an authority consistently prevents a community from assembling peacefully, a principle that concerns all citizens is undermined."

Their appeal, delivered recently to the local administration in Oradea, drew a direct comparison between Oradea and Budapest, where Hungary's former leader Viktor Orbán and his rightwing populist movement had sought to ban Pride events. "In recent years, the restriction of Pride marches has become, in several European states, an indicator of democratic backsliding and the weakening of the rule of law," the statement said.

Ditiu said that he and other organisers were planning to go ahead with the march on Saturday despite the lack of permission, in a repeat of the decision made last year. In 2025, between 500 and 600 people turned up to an unauthorised march, with nine people later receiving fines that amounted to the equivalent of about €4,000 (£3,420) he said.

This time representatives from several diplomatic missions have already said they will participate, as well as the Romanian ombudsman, he said.

The resulting situation was both "encouraging and disappointing", said Ditiu. On one hand, "the institutions that are supposed to protect the rights of every community are trying to use our community as a scapegoat", he said. "But many more people are behind us, many more people understand what the stakes are."

He pointed to the wave of international solidarity they had received as an example. "This is not an LGBT issue. This is a democratic issue, it's about the freedom to public assembly," he said. "And if the local LGBT community here in Oradea can be denied this basic human right without any repercussion, it can happen pretty much anywhere in Europe for pretty much any community."

title: British universities slip down in global rankings
full_text_raw:
Change in methodology used to rate institutions means only Cambridge University makes it into top five

British universities have slipped down the latest international rankings, with only Cambridge making it into the top five institutions in the world - taking joint third place in a list dominated by big American universities.

According to the QS World University Rankings, regarded as the most authoritative of its kind, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) is once again named the best university in the world, with Harvard climbing to second place from fourth last year.

The UK still has four universities in the top 10 in the world. One of the biggest casualties, however, was London's Imperial College, which in 2014 was ranked equal second with Cambridge but this year dropped to eighth position because of a change in the methodology used to rate universities.

Oxford University and University College London (UCL) have both slipped down the tables; having been ranked equal fifth last year, Oxford slipped to sixth and UCL to seventh. Kings College London, ranked 16th in 2014, has dropped three places to 19.

Stanford University in California comes in at joint third with Cambridge, climbing from seventh last year; the California Institute of Technology is fifth, with ETH Zurich (the Federal Swiss Institute of Technology) in ninth place and Chicago University in 10th.

UK winners include the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), which climbs from 71 to 35, a beneficiary of the changes to the QS methodology.

Previously the QS rankings favoured universities strong in research, which is generated largely by the medical sciences, but changes have been made in order to give better recognition to institutions that are outstanding in arts and humanities but produce few citations.

As a result, Imperial, a leading research-intensive institution which produces an impressive array of citations every year, dropped six places despite performing well in every other respect.

Warwick University enters the world's top 50 at 48, up from 61 last year; Durham moves up from 92 to 61, St Andrews is at 68 from 88 last year and Southampton takes 81st position, up from 94.

Two Singaporean universities make the top 15 for the first time; the National University of Singapore (12) is the top Asian institution with Nanyang Technological University at 13.

Ben Sowter, QS head of research said: "That the LSE is a world-class institution is not news. Indeed, they have been a firm fixture in the QS top 100 for over a decade, but in any ranking system that places emphasis on medicine and sciences, their strength in their areas of specialty are never likely to shine as brightly as they ought to.

"The QS methodology now evens the playing field and LSE climbs 36 places to be counted, rightfully, amongst the world's top 40."

John O'Leary, a member of the QS global advisory board, added: "The UK remains second only to the US as a higher education destination. The leading universities may have lost ground, but they still make up four of the top 10 in the world.

"Ironically, their strength in medicine and science has cost some of them because the new methodology rewards a more balanced portfolio, but it is good news for the likes of Durham and Warwick, as well as LSE."

The US has 49 institutions in the top 200, ahead of the UK with 30, the Netherlands (12), Germany (11), Canada, Australia, and Japan (8) and China (7).

London is the only city in the world with four universities in the top 50; Boston and New York have three and Paris, Sydney, Hong Kong and Beijing all have two.

The mayor of London, Boris Johnson, said: "London is unequivocally the education capital of the world. With four of our universities in the top 40, the city's education sector is going from strength to strength, attracting the world's top talent and producing the next generation of great thinkers and leaders."

LSE's director, Prof Craig Calhoun, said: "LSE's latest global university ranking as the best social science institution in the UK and second best in the world is testament to both the school and London's reputation as a world class centre for education.

"For 120 years, we have been located in the heart of London, providing outstanding teaching and research which focuses on real-world problems and helps shape government policy at the highest level."

title: Politician's claim Earth's magnetic poles could flip if NT doesn't use more groundwater criticised by experts
full_text_raw:
NT minister for trade and business Robyn Cahill makes scientifically inaccurate claims while pushing to make territory 'datacentre capital of the globe'

A Northern Territory minister has been criticised for scientifically inaccurate claims that groundwater in the Northern Territory needs to be used to prevent the Earth's magnetic poles from flipping.

The NT minister for trade and business, Robyn Cahill, made the claim while speaking in Darwin last week about the government's push to make the territory "the datacentre capital of the globe".

"For datacentres, the water supply is already in existence. It's mainly subterranean," she said. "The water supply that Darwin has is extraordinary."

"There's scientific evidence to suggest that we have so much water underground in the Northern Territory that it actually impacts the axis of the Earth when we have a really bad wet season, so we need to use some of it otherwise we might find ourselves flipping the poles again."

The Environment Centre NT's executive director, Kirsty Howey, described Cahill's claim as "completely cooked".

"The minister appears to believe that the Northern Territory's wet season can alter Earth's axis, which has no scientific basis," Howey said. "It's frightening that the people in charge of regulating dangerous industries like fracking and datacentres seem to lack even a high-school understanding of water science."

Dr Dylan Irvine, a groundwater hydrology expert at Charles Darwin University, told ABC Darwin: "We're not at risk of the poles flipping ... I'm not concerned about the Earth tipping or flipping of poles."

The Earth's most recent major geomagnetic reversal - in which the positions of magnetic north and magnetic south flip - is known as the Brunhes-Matuyama reversal, and occurred an estimated 780,000 years ago. The flip is not instantaneous: scientific analysis suggests reversals take 7,000 years on average to occur.

A recent temporary flip of the poles, classified as an "excursion" rather than a full geomagnetic reversal - occurred 42,000 years ago and lasted for about 1,000 years.

"This is driven by processes that happen in the deep Earth ... that happen in the Earth's core ... not so much groundwater systems," Irvine said.

Experts have warned, however, about the impact massive datacentre projects will have on already strained water resources, particularly in hotter climates where centres require more energy or water to keep cool.

The ECNT is calling for a public ban on fracking and datacentres so their impacts on the NT's climate and water supplies can be properly considered.

"We don't want to see our precious aquifers drained for AI while we get nothing in return," Howey said. "We don't want to be the datacentre capital of the globe - we want safe drinking water and a livable future for our kids."

According to the NT government, as many as a dozen datacentre developers are interested in the region.

"We will be the place all the hyperscalers come to have their datacentres here," Cahill said last week.

On Wednesday, the NT chief minister, Lia Finocchiaro, announced the government had granted Beetaloo Digital - a subsidiary of gas company Beetaloo Energy - an exclusive commitment over 185 ha of land near Darwin, for "a massive project involving an integrated AI datacentre and on-site gas-fired power generation".

The project would be "powered by up to 2GW of on-site power generation fuelled by Beetaloo gas", according to a government statement.

For comparison, 2GW is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of approximately 2m households.

It comes after the announcement of another hyperscale centre, Energy North's Project Ares, a 1GW project proposed for Murranji station in the NT's Barkly region.

Cahill was contacted for comment.

title: Total solar eclipse books out hotels two years in advance in New Zealand city
full_text_raw:
Dunedin will be the focal point, having last experienced such an eclipse in 1163 - before any humans reached New Zealand

Hotels are booking out two years in advance in the New Zealand city of Dunedin as it prepares for the region's first total solar eclipse in more than 850 years.

At 4.17pm on 22 July 2028, the moon will pass in front of the sun, casting a roughly 100km-wide shadowy band across parts of southern New Zealand. Everywhere within that band - from tourist hotspot Queenstown in the west to Dunedin city in the east - will be plunged into daytime darkness for 2 minutes and 51 seconds.

Despite there being two years still to go, hotels are already fielding booking inquiries, including the Dunedin Leisure Lodge, which by Thursday was fully booked for its "solar eclipse package" that includes complimentary eclipse glasses.

Dr Ian Griffin, an astronomer and director of Tūhura Otago Museum, said: "The last one visible from Dunedin was in 1163, which was before humans reached New Zealand.

"So we will be the first people in Dunedin ever to see a solar eclipse from this part of the world, which is quite exciting."

It will also be the first total solar eclipse visible anywhere in New Zealand since 1965.

"That three minutes of darkness, if it's clear, will be absolutely memorable for anybody who sees it," Griffin said.

On Wednesday, Dunedin's museum started the clock for the two-year countdown, in what is tipped to be a major tourism event for the city. Roughly 35,000 visitors are expected to descend on the city, which has a population of 130,000.

Griffin, meanwhile, has been preparing for the eclipse since 2013.

"I did buy my house all those years ago based on the fact that you could see the eclipse from it," he said.

The eclipse will happen in the middle of New Zealand's winter, just after the country celebrates Matariki - the Māori new year. Matariki is the Māori name for a cluster of stars known elsewhere as the Pleiades. The constellation is visible from New Zealand for 11 months of the year, but disappears from the skies for a month in winter, reappearing around the time of the winter solstice.

Dunedin is planning a night-sky festival beginning with Matariki and going through to the eclipse.

"It's actually unique anywhere around the world," Griffin said. "We've got the cultural holiday celebrating the night sky, and then will be following it about 10 days later with a fantastic eclipse."

The Dunedin mayor, Sophie Barker, said anticipation for the eclipse was being felt across the city. "This remarkable event is now firmly on the horizon."

title: Country diary: The eyebright paradox: a sunny healer and tiny parasitic thief | Paul Evans
full_text_raw:
The Marches, Shropshire: Eyebrights are ancient herbs used to cure eye problems, but they also penetrate grass roots to siphon off water and nutrients

A sight for sore eyes. Eyebrights flower in the short turf of Old Racecourse Common as sunlight burns a hole through rowan trees to cast sunset colours on the grass. The eyebrights are annuals with tiny flowers, 4mm-11mm long with a violet vibe, a white corolla with purple marks and a central flash of yellow.

There are about 20 British eyebright species, some of which are endemic. Their genetic complexity makes them an arcane group of plants and a taxonomic puzzle to all but their most dedicated acolytes. "Life's too short to key out [make a precise identification of] eyebrights," one botanist told me.

For the sake of argument, this one is Euphrasia officinalis agg, an aggregate of species, microspecies and hybrids, one of which is E nemorosa, the common eyebright. They belong to Orobanchaceae, the family that also includes lousewort, toothwort and yellow rattle. Like these, the eyebrights are parasitic, or at least hemi-parasitic, capable of independent living but also sending out roots to penetrate the roots of grasses to siphon water and nutrients from them, like wiring into streetlights to nick the 'leccy. This reduces grass dominance and changes the composition of the turf.

Euphrasia comes from the Greek word for cheerfulness, obvious when you get down to look into their faces, even through the smudgy lenses of my specs. According to the medieval Doctrine of Signatures, objects in nature have trademark characteristics that are key to their influence on human conditions, so gazing at these flowers looking back with such a bright, sunny disposition can help us see and feel better. Following on from intuitions and symbolism, eyebright is an ancient medicinal herb with properties such as aucubin and iridoid glycosides, lignans and flavonoids used in tinctures and compresses to cure eye problems. They also promote wellbeing and were burned as an incense to aid divination.

So, is the future bright for eyebrights? A lack of grazing and encroaching bracken, recently cut here, is a common problem for short-turf habitats. Conventional conservation of distinctive species has to be balanced with the conservation of processes that create the extraordinary evolution of eyebright diversity for these shapers of place and their richly storied lives.

The recalled eggs ⁠were available at Kroger (KR.N), opens new tab stores in Texas and Louisiana and Brookshire Grocery stores in states including Oklahoma, Arkansas, and Mississippi, the FDA said.

Midwest Poultry Services and Kroger did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment outside regular business hours, while Brookshire Grocery could not be immediately reached.

No ⁠illnesses reported were linked to the Midwest Poultry Services eggs as of the announcement, the FDA added.

Midwest Poultry Services has halted distributing eggs produced on ⁠its Texas farms, the health regulator added.

Salmonella enteritidis is a bacterium that can live on either the outside or ⁠inside of eggs and cause foodborne illness. Symptoms include cramps, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, chills, ⁠fever, and possibly headache within 12 to 72 hours after eating.

title: How to Eat a 2,000-Pound Fish? These Orcas Choose to Pulverize It.
full_text_raw:
Marine biologists in Mexico captured video of a strange maneuver that killer whales used to shred their meal.

Ocean sunfish are the largest bony fish in the world -- some species can weigh more than 2,000 pounds and span 14 feet from top to bottom fin. Their impressive size and thick skin usually deter predators.

But off the coast of Baja California, a group of orcas has adopted a brutal way of hunting sunfish: With an unusual maneuver, the orcas pulverize the giants. Erick Higuera, a marine biologist at Conexiones Terramar, a scientific organization, described the attacks as "violent" and "chaotic," but also "highly calculated."

Mr. Higuera first witnessed the hunting strategy in 2021. Orcas tossed around a sunfish "like a Frisbee" before making it "explode," he said. Now, in a study published Thursday in Frontiers in Ethology, Mr. Higuera and his colleagues described two events filmed in 2024 and 2025.

In the two videos, an adult orca held the carcass of a sharp-tail sunfish in its mouth. Then, another adult swam at high speed toward the sunfish. The first orca released it, and the second rammed into it, fragmenting the sunfish. As pieces floated about, a juvenile orca began eating.

"It's like soccer," Mr. Higuera said. "Everyone has a role."

Scientists have documented orcas preying on sunfish, also known as mola, for several decades. In the Gulf of California, the feeding behavior was first reported in the 1990s.

In January, Mr. Higuera and another group of scientists published a study reporting more than 20 encounters between orcas and sunfish. Orca calves were present for eight of them. Female orcas may be using sunfish to train their young, or just for entertainment, the authors wrote in the earlier study.

But the sunfish in the earlier observations were not shredded as much as the prey in the videos, suggesting the fragmentation strategy may be specific to the sharp-tail sunfish.

Robert Pitman, a marine ecologist at Oregon State University who was not involved in the research, saw the behavior as perhaps logical. Sunfish skin is made up of so-called dermal denticles, similar to the rough, toothlike scales that sharks have.

By ramming the fish, Dr. Pitman said, killer whales may get at their prey without wearing down their teeth. "Nothing that they do surprises me anymore," he said.

Marianne Nyegaard, a marine biologist at Auckland War Memorial Museum who was not involved in the research, has studied ocean sunfish and documented many orca interactions with them.

"I was really pleased to see someone had taken the behavior and kind of described it in detail," she said.

"Sunfishes are often seen as these big, weird, irrelevant fish that are a bit of a curiosity," Dr. Nyegaard said. "They're not really seen as part of the ecosystem." The new study, she said, helps bring sunfish into "mainstream ecology."

Luke Rendell, a marine biologist at the University of St. Andrews, said that sunfish know-how might persist in this group of orcas for generations through cultural inheritance.

And ramming behavior is not unique to the sunfish hunt, Dr. Rendell added. He pointed to the widely reported interactions between orcas and boats off the Iberian Peninsula, where orcas have rammed and sunk several vessels.

"In both cases, bashing up something they find in their environment leads to new knowledge," Dr. Rendell said. "Food, in this study, and fun games, in the case of the boat interactions."

title: Pride organisers vow to march in Romanian city that has blocked event four years in a row
full_text_raw:
Oradea is only major city in EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride plans

Campaigners in a Romanian city have vowed to go ahead with plans for a Pride march after local authorities denied them permission for the fourth consecutive year.

Since 2023, campaigners in the western city of Oradea - population 180,000 - have sought authorisation for Pride events. Each year, however, they have come up against opposition, turning Oradea into the only major city in the EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride plans.

"Every year the local authorities have managed to find legal or technical excuses to ban Oradea Pride events," said Iulian Ditiu, the co-founder and president of ARK Oradea, the local organisers of Pride.

In 2024, for example, they were told that none of the city's parks were available at the times requested, he said. The following year, campaigners provided local authorities with 12 potential routes for the march, only to be told that none of the routes were possible.

Before this year's proposed march, slated to be held on Saturday, organisers submitted more than 100 route options. On Wednesday the city said that none of the routes were viable as they overlapped with other events or with major public infrastructure works.

The city's mayor, who is from a party that describes itself as liberal, conservative and Christian democratic, did not reply to a request for comment from the Guardian.

Ditiu pointed to the wider significance of the consecutive bans. "It feels like the message that they are trying to send our way is that we're not welcome here," he said. "They have never said out loud that they are banning Pride for LGBT reasons. They're always hiding behind technical reasons."

As organisers grapple with the possibility of another ban, their plight has attracted international attention. Before this year's march, 152 organisations from 30 countries signed a statement calling on officials to allow the march to take place in "complete safety" and in line with EU law.

"After four consecutive years in which the Pride march has been unable to take place, there can be no question of administrative or logistical difficulties," the statement noted. "When an authority consistently prevents a community from assembling peacefully, a principle that concerns all citizens is undermined."

Their appeal, delivered recently to the local administration in Oradea, drew a direct comparison between Oradea and Budapest, where Hungary's former leader Viktor Orbán and his rightwing populist movement had sought to ban Pride events. "In recent years, the restriction of Pride marches has become, in several European states, an indicator of democratic backsliding and the weakening of the rule of law," the statement said.

Ditiu said that he and other organisers were planning to go ahead with the march on Saturday despite the lack of permission, in a repeat of the decision made last year. In 2025, between 500 and 600 people turned up to an unauthorised march, with nine people later receiving fines that amounted to the equivalent of about €4,000 (£3,420) he said.

This time representatives from several diplomatic missions have already said they will participate, as well as the Romanian ombudsman, he said.

The resulting situation was both "encouraging and disappointing", said Ditiu. On one hand, "the institutions that are supposed to protect the rights of every community are trying to use our community as a scapegoat", he said. "But many more people are behind us, many more people understand what the stakes are."

He pointed to the wave of international solidarity they had received as an example. "This is not an LGBT issue. This is a democratic issue, it's about the freedom to public assembly," he said. "And if the local LGBT community here in Oradea can be denied this basic human right without any repercussion, it can happen pretty much anywhere in Europe for pretty much any community."

title: Sweden's far right party says it won the arguments. Now it wants a share of power
full_text_raw:
STOCKHOLM, July 23 (Reuters) - After championing huge policy shifts in Sweden by propping up a minority centre-right government for four years, the far-right Sweden Democrats say they have won the political arguments and now deserve a share of power for themselves.

But it is a demand that could prove a step too far for voters in an election in September, and potentially bring down Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. The prime minister, who once told a Holocaust survivor he would never cooperate with the Sweden Democrats, now says he has lifted those "red lines".

Sweden, the stalwart of European socialism for generations, has undergone a startling rightward shift in policy and public opinion in recent years, especially over immigration in a country where one person in five was born abroad.

The number of asylum seekers last year was down 97% from the peak a decade ago. One of Europe's most welcoming immigration systems has become one of its most stringent: newcomers face employment restrictions, language and culture tests, and reduced welfare payouts. Immigrants who break the law can be swiftly expelled, and others are offered payments to leave voluntarily.

The changes were all championed by the Sweden Democrats, who spent the past four years providing 73 votes in the 349-seat Riksdag to support the centre-right government from outside Kristersson's coalition.

Party leader Jimmie Akesson says that arrangement has run its course, and his party must now ⁠become a full-blown member of the coalition, controlling most of the key ministries in the cabinet if the right wins the vote.

"It's been a clear demand from us ahead of this election. Either we are in government or we are in opposition," Akesson told Reuters in an interview. "We have shown that we can cooperate, it has gone better than most people expected."

After the election, the Sweden Democrats expect to control at least three of the most powerful ministries -- justice, defence, foreign affairs or finance, Akesson said.

"I think that is reasonable if you look at the balance of power within our bloc," he said. He would allow Kristersson to remain as prime minister, he added: "I can do without travelling around the world and shaking hands."

ONCE OSTRACISED

The Sweden Democrats were once ostracised by all of Sweden's mainstream parties, including Kristersson's main centre-right Moderates.

But at a joint press conference with Akesson in April, the prime minister officially lifted the taboo: "We have done away with red lines that can limit our cooperation and want to form a stable majority government after the election," he announced. "That's a strength for Sweden."

Voters so far appear unconvinced. A major poll in June showed support for the governing bloc including the Sweden Democrats at just 42.6%, with the loosely aligned centre-left opposition led by the Social Democrats receiving 55.2%.

"Kristersson is caught between a rock and a hard place. He can't form a government without the Sweden Democrats, but they might also scare off too many voters," ⁠said Gothenburg University Political Science Professor Jonas Hinnfors.

Winning Kristersson's public acceptance was "a monumental journey" for the Sweden Democrats, Hinnfors said. "They weren't just a small party, they were also a taboo party, a pariah party that no one wanted to touch with pliers."

NEO-NAZI ROOTS

The Sweden Democrats acknowledge that some members had roots in neo-Nazism and white supremacy when the party was founded in the 1980s, but say such figures have since been weeded out.

Akesson, 47, joined the party in the 1990s and became party leader in 2005. Since then, he has pushed relentlessly for mainstream acceptance. A keyboardist in a Viking rock band, he cultivates an informal persona and is usually seen in a suit without a tie.

The rise of the Sweden Democrats has forced other parties to alter their positions, especially on immigration and crime. In 2015, ⁠when more than a million asylum seekers entered Europe mainly from Syria, Sweden proudly took in more per capita than any other EU country, with Prime Minister Stefan Lofven, a Social Democrat, saying his Europe "didn't build walls".

Now, with policy having shifted and the numbers of new immigrants having already plummeted, the Sweden Democrats' focus has shifted toward demands that the existing foreign-born population espouse Swedish values, language and customs.

The party calls for banning traditional Islamic dress for women, tearing down mosques that preach Islamic radicalism, increasing expulsions and raising financial ⁠incentives for those who leave voluntarily.

"We want the complete abolition of multiculturalism," said Mattias Karlsson, seen as the party's chief ideologist.

While opinion polls suggest support for the Sweden Democrats remains fairly steady at around a fifth of the electorate, the agreement to allow them into a future government has hurt other parties in Kristersson's coalition.

The Liberals, who now provide the ruling coalition with 16 seats, saw several high-profile representatives quit and the party's support fall below the 4% threshold needed to ⁠win seats.

The Sweden Democrats' "values are as far from mine as possible. To be in government with them is unthinkable," said Liberal lawmaker Malin Sjoberg Hogrell, who quit her party's governing board and announced she would not seek re-election to parliament.

Opposition parties say Kristersson's deal with the Sweden Democrats means the only way to keep the far right out of power is now to vote for the left.

"Kristersson would be the weakest prime minister in Sweden's history," Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson told a news conference. "That government would only last until the day Jimmie Akesson decides it's time for him to become prime minister."

Reporting by Johan Ahlander Editing by Niklas Pollard and Peter Graff
